Modafinil is a mainstay of treatment but Australian access through the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme requires a confirmed diagnosis with objective sleep study evidence, and empirical treatment would remove the ability to obtain that evidence. Stimulant treatment before diagnosis also risks masking another sleep disorder (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy).

Obstructive sleep apnoea is argued against by the absence of snoring or witnessed apnoeas, a body mass index of 22 kg/m2, undisturbed nocturnal sleep and naps that are refreshing rather than unrefreshing. Oximetry would also miss the daytime findings that carry the diagnosis (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy).

Insufficient sleep syndrome and delayed sleep phase are the common causes of student sleepiness, but he already sleeps eight hours on a regular schedule and neither explains episodes of sudden bilateral muscle weakness with preserved awareness. Three months of watchful waiting also risks another failed semester (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy).

Sudden bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion with retained awareness, together with sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations and refreshing naps, is the classic tetrad, and confirmation requires overnight polysomnography to exclude other causes followed the next day by a multiple sleep latency test. The diagnostic thresholds are a mean sleep latency of 8 minutes or less with two or more sleep onset rapid eye movement periods (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy).

explanation.summary: Insomnia disorder requires difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep at least three nights a week for at least three months with daytime consequences, despite adequate opportunity for sleep. The most common and most reversible maintaining factor is extending time in bed to compensate, which lowers sleep efficiency and strengthens the association between bed and being awake. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia combines sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive restructuring, relaxation and sleep hygiene, and it is first line because its benefits persist after treatment ends whereas hypnotic benefits do not. Before diagnosing primary insomnia, screen for obstructive sleep apnoea, restless legs syndrome, depression, alcohol use, shift work and medications such as stimulants and corticosteroids. Where medication is needed as a bridge, the recommendation is the lowest effective dose intermittently for no more than two to four weeks with an agreed exit plan.
key_points: Insomnia disorder needs symptoms three nights a week for three months with daytime impact
Excessive time in bed lowers sleep efficiency and maintains the problem
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is first line and outlasts hypnotics
Sleep hygiene alone is the weakest single component and is not adequate treatment
Hypnotics are for short term intermittent use with a planned exit
explanation.pearls: Sleep restriction sets time in bed to roughly the average total sleep time from the diary, with a floor of five hours, and expands it by fifteen minutes each week once sleep efficiency exceeds 85 per cent, which is why the therapy briefly makes people sleepier before it makes them better.

options.rationale: Benzodiazepine hypnotics are recommended only for short term intermittent use of up to two to four weeks because tolerance, rebound insomnia and dependence develop with nightly use, and three months of unmonitored supply invites all three. The fact that it worked previously reflects its short term efficacy rather than its suitability for a chronic problem (Source: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence).

Low dose quetiapine is widely prescribed off label for sleep but has no efficacy evidence for insomnia disorder and carries metabolic, extrapyramidal and cardiac risk. Her difficulty is maintaining sleep rather than initiating it, so a sedating agent addresses the wrong part of the night (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

A sedating antidepressant is a reasonable choice when insomnia accompanies a depressive disorder, but her score of 4 with preserved enjoyment does not support that diagnosis. Treating primary insomnia with an antidepressant also brings weight gain and daytime sedation without addressing the behavioural maintenance of the problem (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is first line for chronic insomnia disorder in Australian and international guidance, with effects that outlast hypnotics, and its sleep restriction component directly targets the nine and a half hours in bed that are diluting her sleep. Her prolonged time in bed and clock watching are the maintaining behaviours the program is designed to reverse (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Insomnia).

Sleep hygiene education as a stand alone treatment performs barely better than control in trials and is the weakest component of the multi part therapy, because it does not change the time in bed or the conditioned arousal that maintain chronic insomnia. It is included within the structured program rather than used instead of it (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Insomnia).

explanation.summary: Fabricated or induced illness is a form of child abuse in which a carer exaggerates, fabricates or produces symptoms and signs, leading to unnecessary and often invasive medical intervention. The signature features are a history that only one person can corroborate, symptoms that resolve when the carer is absent, investigations that are persistently normal, multiple hospitals and specialists involved, and a carer who is unusually comfortable in the medical environment and who pushes for further procedures. It is a diagnosis about the child's care rather than about the carer's psychopathology, so the assessment focuses on assembling a chronology of all health contacts across services rather than on interviewing the carer. Australian doctors are mandatory reporters and the threshold for notification is a reasonable belief of significant harm, not proof. Mortality is estimated at around 6 to 10 per cent and siblings are at risk, so any notification asks about them as well.
key_points: Events witnessed by only one carer with consistently normal investigations is the core pattern
The chronology assembled across all health services is the key diagnostic instrument
Notification requires reasonable belief of harm, not proof, and doctors are mandatory reporters
Confrontation before a coordinated plan increases risk to the child
Siblings should be considered in any notification
explanation.pearls: Request the records from every hospital and general practice involved before speaking with the family, because the diagnosis is usually made by seeing eleven admissions in one place rather than by any single clinical finding, and each service typically knows about only its own two or three.

sources.label: RANZCP: Fabricated or induced illness in a child
Royal Children's Hospital: Child abuse and neglect

options.rationale: Early confrontation before a coordinated plan is in place commonly precipitates removal of the child from hospital, transfer to another health service and escalation of the reported symptoms, all of which increase risk. Any conversation with the family happens after the statutory notification and within an agreed multidisciplinary plan (Source: RANZCP: Fabricated or induced illness in a child).
source_refs: RANZCP: Fabricated or induced illness in a child

options.rationale: Covert surveillance raises significant legal and ethical problems, requires police and executive authorisation where it is used at all, and is never the initial step taken by a treating team. The threshold for notification is reasonable suspicion of harm, which has already been reached without it (Source: RANZCP: Fabricated or induced illness in a child).
source_refs: RANZCP: Fabricated or induced illness in a child

options.rationale: Doctors are mandatory reporters in every Australian state and territory and the threshold is a reasonable belief of significant harm, which is met by invasive procedures and repeated admissions for events that only ever occur in one person's presence with uniformly normal investigations. Convening the treating teams, the general practitioner and child protection assembles the chronology from all services, which is the single most important diagnostic step in these cases (Source: RANZCP: Fabricated or induced illness in a child).
source_refs: RANZCP: Fabricated or induced illness in a child

options.rationale: There is no consistent psychiatric profile in these cases and a normal assessment of the carer does not lower the risk to the child, so making the referral the gateway step delays protection. Assessment of the carer has a place later, within the child protection plan rather than ahead of it (Source: RANZCP: Fabricated or induced illness in a child).
source_refs: RANZCP: Fabricated or induced illness in a child

options.rationale: Ordering more of an investigation that has already been comprehensively normal continues the pattern of escalating intervention that is itself the harm, and each admission carries its own risks. Further testing is warranted only if a new clinical finding emerges (Source: Royal Children's Hospital: Child abuse and neglect).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital: Child abuse and neglect

explanation.summary: Illness anxiety disorder is characterised by preoccupation with having or acquiring a serious illness for at least six months, with somatic symptoms that are absent or mild, high health anxiety and either excessive health related behaviours or maladaptive avoidance. It is distinguished from somatic symptom disorder, in which distressing physical symptoms are prominent, and the DSM-5 revision split the former diagnosis of hypochondriasis along exactly this line. The disorder is maintained by a cycle of bodily attention, catastrophic interpretation, checking and reassurance seeking, in which each normal result gives short lived relief and increases the need for the next. Care and avoidance seeking subtypes both occur, and the avoidant subtype can present late with genuine pathology missed through avoidance of medical contact. Cognitive behavioural therapy is first line, a serotonin reuptake inhibitor is an effective alternative or addition, and the single most useful structural change is moving to appointments at fixed intervals with one consistent doctor.
key_points: Preoccupation with illness for six months with minimal somatic symptoms defines the diagnosis
Reassurance relieves anxiety briefly and then strengthens the cycle
Cognitive behavioural therapy is first line, with a serotonin reuptake inhibitor as an alternative
Scheduled rather than symptom triggered review breaks the reinforcement pattern
The avoidant subtype risks genuine pathology being missed
explanation.pearls: Set appointments at fixed intervals such as every four weeks regardless of symptoms, and agree in advance that new investigations require a new objective sign rather than a new worry, because this single arrangement reduces both consultations and investigation rates substantially.

sources.label: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders

options.rationale: Repeated investigation is the central maintaining factor in this condition because each normal result provides relief that lasts days and then strengthens the need for the next test. Reassurance seeking is the behaviour being treated, not the treatment (Source: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders

options.rationale: Another specialist opinion repeats the same reassurance cycle at greater cost and reinforces the belief that the previous assessments may have missed something. It differs from repeat imaging only in the form the reassurance takes (Source: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders

options.rationale: A short-acting benzodiazepine taken at peaks of anxiety functions as a safety behaviour that prevents the natural extinction of the anxiety, and it carries tolerance and dependence risk over a fourteen month problem. Where medication is used in this condition it is a serotonin reuptake inhibitor taken regularly (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Cognitive behavioural therapy targeting catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations, checking and reassurance seeking has the strongest evidence in this disorder, with effects sustained at follow up. Scheduling appointments at fixed intervals rather than in response to symptoms breaks the link between worry and medical contact, which is the behavioural half of the treatment (Source: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders

options.rationale: Advice to stop checking without a structured program rarely succeeds, and reviewing only when symptoms change makes medical contact contingent on symptoms, which rewards symptom focus. Fixed interval review does the opposite (Source: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders

explanation.summary: Notifiable conduct under the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law comprises practising while intoxicated by alcohol or drugs, sexual misconduct in the course of practice, placing the public at substantial risk of harm through practice that departs significantly from accepted standards, and placing the public at substantial risk of harm by practising with an impairment. The 2020 reforms deliberately raised the threshold for treating practitioners for the impairment and standards limbs to substantial risk of harm, in order to encourage doctors to seek health care, but the intoxication and sexual misconduct limbs were not softened. Western Australia exempts treating practitioners from mandatory notification altogether and Queensland has its own variation, so jurisdiction matters. An impairment that is being appropriately treated and is not placing patients at substantial risk does not require notification, which is the point most often misunderstood. Doctors health advisory services operate in every state and territory and offer confidential assessment, and referral to them sits alongside rather than instead of any obligation that has been triggered.
key_points: Practising while intoxicated by alcohol is notifiable conduct with no softened threshold
The 2020 reforms raised the treating practitioner threshold only for the impairment and standards limbs
Western Australia exempts treating practitioners entirely and Queensland differs
An impairment under appropriate treatment without substantial risk is not notifiable
Notification and continuing to provide care are not alternatives
explanation.pearls: Tell the practitioner patient in the consultation that you are required to notify and why, because doing so preserves the therapeutic relationship far more often than a notification they learn about later from the regulator.

sources.label: Medical Board of Australia: Good medical practice

options.rationale: Confidentiality is not absolute and yields where a practitioner has practised while intoxicated, because the risk transfers to patients who cannot consent to it. Treating her is necessary but is not an alternative to the notification (Source: Ahpra: Guidelines for mandatory notifications).

Doctors health services are a valuable support and should be offered, but referral to them does not discharge a mandatory obligation once the practitioner has practised while intoxicated. They are the complement to the notification rather than a substitute for it (Source: Ahpra: Guidelines for mandatory notifications).

Delegating the judgement to an employer does not satisfy a personal statutory obligation that rests with the practitioner who forms the reasonable belief, and it discloses her health information to a party with no clinical role. Employers have their own separate notification duties (Source: Ahpra: Guidelines for mandatory notifications).

Withdrawing care removes the one therapeutic relationship she has disclosed to, makes future help seeking less likely and still leaves the obligation unmet. Practitioner patients are entitled to the same continuity of care as anyone else (Source: Medical Board of Australia: Good medical practice).
source_refs: Medical Board of Australia: Good medical practice

options.rationale: Practising while intoxicated by alcohol is one of the four forms of notifiable conduct under the National Law, and her account of starting operating lists still affected meets that threshold irrespective of whether any patient has been harmed. Treating practitioners in Victoria are not exempt, and the notification is made while the therapeutic relationship continues, with an explanation to her of what you must do and why (Source: Ahpra: Guidelines for mandatory notifications).

explanation.summary: Sexual dysfunction is among the most common and most under reported adverse effects of serotonergic antidepressants, affecting between 25 and 70 per cent of patients depending on how it is measured, and it involves desire, arousal and orgasm to differing degrees. Distinguishing it from the sexual dysfunction of depression itself is done on timing, since drug related effects begin within the first weeks of treatment or a dose increase while depressive dysfunction improves as mood improves. Management options are watchful waiting, dose reduction, a drug holiday, switching to a lower risk agent, or augmentation, and the choice depends on how stable the mood is and what has already been tried. Paroxetine has the highest reported rates and agomelatine, mirtazapine, moclobemide, bupropion and vortioxetine the lowest. Any switch is made with attention to discontinuation symptoms and to the risk of relapse during the changeover, usually by cross tapering rather than abrupt substitution.
key_points: Sexual dysfunction affects a large minority to a majority of patients on serotonergic antidepressants
Onset within weeks of starting or increasing the dose distinguishes it from depressive dysfunction
Tolerance develops in only a minority so waiting is rarely the answer
Relapse on a previous dose reduction removes that option from the list
Agomelatine, mirtazapine, moclobemide and vortioxetine carry the lowest rates
explanation.pearls: Ask about sexual function before starting an antidepressant and again at the four week review, because a baseline recorded before treatment is the only way to separate a drug effect from the sexual dysfunction that depression itself causes in around 40 per cent of patients.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines

options.rationale: Antidepressant treatment is continued for at least six to twelve months after remission of a first episode to prevent relapse, and this man has already relapsed once on dose reduction at five months. Ceasing entirely would trade a side effect for a recurrence (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Sexual dysfunction from serotonin reuptake inhibition affects up to half of patients, rarely improves with time and is dose related, and his relapse on dose reduction has already closed off the simplest alternative. Agents such as agomelatine, mirtazapine, moclobemide and vortioxetine carry substantially lower rates and allow effective treatment to continue (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

A phosphodiesterase inhibitor helps erectile dysfunction, and his erections are normal on waking and during activity, so the problem lies with desire and orgasm rather than with tumescence. It targets a mechanism that is not the one affected here (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

Dose reduction is a reasonable first strategy in general, but it has already been tried at exactly this dose and produced return of early morning waking and low mood within a fortnight. Repeating a failed intervention risks a second relapse (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Tolerance to sexual adverse effects develops in only a minority and his symptoms have persisted for eight months, so waiting is not supported. Unaddressed sexual dysfunction is also one of the leading reasons patients stop antidepressants without telling their doctor (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines).
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines

explanation.summary: Decision making capacity is presumed in adults, is specific to the decision at hand and to the moment, and is assessed on whether the person can understand the relevant information, retain it long enough to use it, weigh it, and communicate a choice. A patient may retain capacity for simple decisions while lacking it for a complex one, and intoxication, delirium, pain and head injury all cause it to fluctuate over hours. Where capacity is absent and treatment is urgently necessary to prevent serious harm, the common law doctrine of necessity permits that treatment, and it authorises the minimum restriction needed to deliver it. Mental health legislation is a separate pathway that applies only to mental illness and is not a general tool for uncooperative patients. Anticoagulation transforms an apparently minor head injury, since delayed intracranial haemorrhage can present hours later in a patient who initially had a normal conscious state, which is why imaging thresholds are far lower in these patients.
key_points: Capacity is decision specific, time specific and requires understanding, retention, weighing and communication
Failure to retain information for minutes is direct evidence that capacity is absent
The common law doctrine of necessity authorises urgent treatment and minimal restriction
Mental health legislation applies to mental illness and not to intoxication alone
A signed refusal form does not confer capacity or legal protection
explanation.pearls: Anticoagulated patients need a computed tomogram after any head strike even with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 15 and no other risk factors, and a period of observation afterwards, because delayed haemorrhage occurs in around 1 to 2 per cent despite an initially normal scan.

sources.label: RANZCP: Assessment of decision making capacity
Medical Board of Australia: Good medical practice

options.rationale: A signed form records a refusal but does not create the capacity to make it, and a patient who cannot retain the information for five minutes cannot weigh it. The signature offers no legal protection where capacity is absent (Source: Medical Board of Australia: Good medical practice).
source_refs: Medical Board of Australia: Good medical practice

options.rationale: Mental health legislation applies to a person with or suspected of having a mental illness requiring assessment or treatment, and acute alcohol intoxication with a head injury is not that. Using the wrong statutory instrument is both unlawful and unnecessary when another lawful basis exists (Source: RANZCP: Assessment of decision making capacity).
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment of decision making capacity

options.rationale: Substitute consent processes are designed for decisions that can wait for the appointed decision maker to be identified and consulted, not for an emergency where delay itself is the harm. A person responsible also cannot authorise detention of a patient trying to leave (Source: RANZCP: Assessment of decision making capacity).
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment of decision making capacity

options.rationale: Capacity is decision specific and is absent here because he cannot retain or weigh the information, so the emergency doctrine permits treatment necessary to prevent serious harm using the least restrictive means, with staff remaining with him while he is observed. Capacity fluctuates with falling alcohol levels, so it is reassessed rather than being settled once (Source: RANZCP: Assessment of decision making capacity).
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment of decision making capacity

options.rationale: Sedating a patient with a possible intracranial bleed removes the neurological observations that are the main means of detecting deterioration, and he is irritable rather than a danger to himself or others. Chemical restraint is the last resort after verbal de escalation and constant observation have failed (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Prolonged grief disorder entered DSM-5-TR in 2022 and requires the death of a close person at least twelve months earlier for adults, with persistent intense yearning or preoccupation on most days, together with at least three of identity disruption, disbelief, avoidance of reminders, intense emotional pain, difficulty reintegrating, emotional numbness, a sense that life is meaningless and intense loneliness. It affects roughly 7 to 10 per cent of bereaved adults and is more likely after a sudden or violent death, the death of a child or partner, and where the relationship was highly dependent. It is separated from major depression by the focus of the symptoms on the deceased rather than pervasive anhedonia and worthlessness, and the two can coexist. Grief focused psychotherapy is the treatment with the best evidence, with antidepressants reserved for comorbid depression. Passive wishes not to wake and thoughts of joining the deceased are common and require explicit risk assessment at every review.
key_points: Diagnosis requires at least twelve months since the death in adults
Persistent yearning plus identity disruption, avoidance or a sense of meaninglessness are core
Preserved enjoyment and reactive mood argue against major depression
Grief focused psychotherapy outperforms supportive counselling and antidepressants
Benzodiazepines during bereavement are associated with worse outcomes
explanation.pearls: Ask directly about wishes to join the deceased and about kept possessions used to maintain proximity, because passive death wishes appear in a large proportion of this disorder and are the symptom most often missed when a depression screening score is used as the assessment.

options.rationale: Grief that remains this intense and disabling at nineteen months, with persistent avoidance, identity disruption and no return to work, has passed beyond the expected trajectory and meets diagnostic criteria in its own right. Reassurance at this point delays an effective treatment by another half year (Source: RANZCP: Prolonged grief disorder).

Structured grief focused psychotherapy, which combines exposure to avoided reminders and to the story of the death with work on restoring goals and relationships, outperforms both general supportive counselling and antidepressants for this disorder in randomised trials. Her nightly voicemail listening and avoidance of the bedroom are the proximity seeking and avoidance behaviours that the therapy directly targets (Source: RANZCP: Prolonged grief disorder).

Antidepressants treat a co occurring depressive episode but have not been shown to improve the core grief symptoms, and her preserved enjoyment of her grandchildren with reactive mood and stable appetite does not support major depression. Medication is added for comorbidity rather than used as the primary treatment (Source: RANZCP: Prolonged grief disorder).

Benzodiazepines given during bereavement have been associated with worse grief outcomes, most likely because they blunt the emotional processing that recovery depends on, and they carry dependence risk over a problem measured in years. Her six hours of sleep is also not the target symptom (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Supportive counselling and peer groups help uncomplicated grief but have repeatedly underperformed grief focused therapy in trials of this disorder, because they do not include the exposure component. It differs from the correct option specifically in leaving the avoidance untreated (Source: RANZCP: Prolonged grief disorder).

explanation.summary: Tourette syndrome requires multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic present for more than a year with onset before age eighteen, and the tics characteristically wax and wane, shift location over time, worsen with stress or excitement and diminish during absorbing activity. The premonitory urge and brief voluntary suppressibility distinguish tics from chorea, dystonia, myoclonus and seizures, and suppression is typically followed by a rebound burst. Around 85 per cent of children have a coexisting condition, most often attention deficit hyperactivity disorder or obsessive compulsive disorder, and these frequently cause more functional impairment than the tics themselves. Treatment is directed at impairment rather than at tic frequency, and comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics is first line, with alpha 2 agonists and then antipsychotics reserved for tics that remain distressing or injurious. Psychoeducation for the school is a substantial intervention in its own right, since much of the distress comes from peer response rather than from the movements.
key_points: Tourette syndrome needs multiple motor tics plus a vocal tic for over a year with onset before eighteen
A premonitory urge with suppressibility and rebound distinguishes tics from other movements
Coexisting attention and obsessive compulsive symptoms are present in most children
Treatment targets impairment rather than tic frequency
Behavioural therapy is first line, ahead of alpha 2 agonists and antipsychotics
explanation.pearls: Screen every child with tics for obsessive compulsive symptoms and attention difficulties, because in most referred children it is the coexisting condition rather than the tics that is driving the school problem and it responds to a different treatment.

options.rationale: Comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics, which teaches awareness of the premonitory urge and a competing response, is first line for tics causing distress or impairment and has effect sizes comparable to medication without adverse effects. His clear description of a premonitory urge and of suppressibility indicates he has the awareness the therapy depends on (Source: RANZCP: Tic disorders in children).

Antipsychotics reduce tics but carry weight gain, metabolic effects, sedation, hyperprolactinaemia and a small risk of tardive dyskinesia in a child who is achieving at year level and has no injuries. They are reserved for severe or injurious tics that have not responded to behavioural treatment (Source: RANZCP: Tic disorders in children).

An alpha 2 agonist is the usual first medication when drug treatment is needed, particularly with coexisting attention problems, and it is better tolerated than an antipsychotic. It still sits after behavioural therapy in the sequence, and sedation and postural hypotension are common (Source: RANZCP: Tic disorders in children).

Most tics do improve substantially through adolescence, but he is now avoiding school, which is impairment requiring treatment now rather than a natural history to wait out. Reassurance alone also leaves the coexisting obsessive compulsive and attention symptoms unassessed (Source: RANZCP: Tic disorders in children).

Botulinum toxin has a role for a single severe focal motor or vocal tic, such as a painful neck jerk or a loud disruptive vocalisation, and cannot address multiple tics across several muscle groups. It differs from the correct option in being a targeted treatment for a problem he does not have (Source: RANZCP: Tic disorders in children).

explanation.summary: Australian guidelines advise healthy adults to drink no more than 10 standard drinks per week and no more than four on any one day to reduce the lifetime risk of alcohol related disease and injury, thresholds that many patients substantially exceed without recognising it. Hazardous or risky drinking, meaning consumption above these limits without a diagnosed use disorder, is far more prevalent than dependence and is where brief intervention has its strongest evidence. The intervention takes five to 15 minutes, combining personalised feedback on intake relative to the guidelines, clear advice to reduce, and a collaboratively agreed goal, and it reliably reduces consumption in non-dependent drinkers. Its effect is much weaker in established dependence, where pharmacotherapy with naltrexone or acamprosate plus psychosocial treatment is appropriate. Biochemical markers such as gamma-glutamyl transferase and mean corpuscular volume are insensitive and should never be used to reassure a patient that their intake is safe.
key_points: Australian limits are no more than 10 standard drinks weekly and no more than four in a day
Hazardous drinking without dependence is the group where brief intervention works best
Personalised feedback on intake relative to guideline limits is the active component
Normal liver enzymes and mean corpuscular volume do not exclude alcohol related harm
Pharmacotherapy and specialist referral are reserved for established dependence
explanation.pearls: Ask patients to describe a typical week in drinks rather than accepting a summary word like social, then total it aloud: quantifying 22 standard drinks against a limit of 10 is the feedback step that drives the reduction.

sources.label: NHMRC: Australian Guidelines to Reduce Health Risks from Drinking Alcohol

options.rationale: She is drinking at hazardous levels without dependence, which is exactly the group in whom a short structured intervention delivered opportunistically produces a measurable reduction in consumption. Personalised feedback comparing her intake to the recommended limits is the active ingredient, and she has already shown surprise that makes her receptive. (Source: NHMRC: Australian Guidelines to Reduce Health Risks from Drinking Alcohol)
source_refs: NHMRC: Australian Guidelines to Reduce Health Risks from Drinking Alcohol

options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy is indicated for moderate to severe alcohol use disorder, and she meets no criteria for dependence such as craving, loss of control, tolerance or withdrawal. It would be considered if brief intervention failed and dependence features emerged. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Specialist referral is reserved for dependence, complex comorbidity or failed primary care management, and using it here would be disproportionate and add delay. Most hazardous drinking is managed effectively in general practice. (Source: NHMRC: Australian Guidelines to Reduce Health Risks from Drinking Alcohol)
source_refs: NHMRC: Australian Guidelines to Reduce Health Risks from Drinking Alcohol

options.rationale: Medicated withdrawal is required only when physical dependence is present with a risk of seizures or delirium, and she has no withdrawal history at all. Inpatient withdrawal is indicated for severe dependence, previous complicated withdrawal or unsafe home circumstances. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Normal biochemistry does not exclude harm, since liver enzymes are insensitive markers that stay normal in most hazardous drinkers, and the risks include cancer, injury and cardiovascular disease. This reassurance would actively reinforce the behaviour. (Source: NHMRC: Australian Guidelines to Reduce Health Risks from Drinking Alcohol)
source_refs: NHMRC: Australian Guidelines to Reduce Health Risks from Drinking Alcohol

explanation.summary: Post-traumatic stress disorder following childbirth affects a few per cent of women and considerably more after emergency caesarean, severe haemorrhage or perceived threat to life, yet it is routinely missed because perinatal screening focuses on depression. The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale is not designed to detect it, so a low score provides no reassurance when the history describes re-experiencing, avoidance, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and hyperarousal persisting beyond a month. The consequences extend beyond the mother, since avoidance of maternity services can delay contraception, cervical screening and antenatal care in a subsequent pregnancy, and some women avoid further childbearing altogether or request caesarean without discussion. Trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing are the first line treatments, with medication reserved for those who cannot access or do not respond to them. A structured birth afterthoughts discussion with the obstetric team has a separate role in explaining what happened and planning future births, distinct from psychological treatment.
key_points: Depression screening tools do not detect post-traumatic stress after birth
Diagnosis requires re-experiencing, avoidance and hyperarousal persisting beyond one month
Trauma-focused psychological therapy is first line; medication is second line
Single session debriefing is ineffective and may worsen outcomes
Avoidance of health services threatens contraception, screening and future antenatal care
explanation.pearls: Ask directly about intrusive memories and avoidance of the hospital in any woman with a traumatic birth, because the Edinburgh scale can be well under the depression cut-off, as here at 8, while full post-traumatic stress disorder is present.

sources.label: Phoenix Australia: Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health
Centre of Perinatal Excellence: Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.rationale: Medication is second line for this disorder and is used when trauma-focused psychological therapy is unavailable, declined or ineffective, or where there is significant comorbid depression. Her depression screening is low and the presentation is dominated by re-experiencing and avoidance. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health

options.rationale: Re-experiencing, avoidance and hyperarousal persisting beyond a month after a life threatening birth event indicate post-traumatic stress disorder, for which trauma-focused psychological therapy is the first line treatment with the strongest evidence. Referral to a clinician familiar with perinatal care matters because ongoing contact with maternity services is often unavoidable. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health
Centre of Perinatal Excellence: Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.rationale: Single session psychological debriefing does not prevent or treat post-traumatic stress and there is evidence it can worsen outcomes in some people. A clinical review of what happened during the birth is valuable for understanding and future planning, but it is not a treatment for established symptoms. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health

options.rationale: Symptoms persisting for five months with functional avoidance have moved well beyond an expected acute stress response, and watchful waiting has a place only in the first month after the event. Delay risks entrenchment and avoidance of necessary health care. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are not recommended in this disorder because they impair the emotional processing that trauma-focused therapy depends on and carry dependence risk. Their role is limited to specific short term indications unrelated to the core treatment. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health

explanation.summary: Stimulants for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder are Schedule 8 controlled drugs in Australia, and prescribing requires an authority from the relevant state or territory health department that is generally tied to one named prescriber, with rules on who may initiate treatment varying between jurisdictions. Real time prescription monitoring is now operating nationally and allows any prescriber to see dispensing of controlled drugs across prescribers and pharmacies, making the pattern of multiple concurrent prescribers immediately visible. Features that raise concern about misuse or diversion include requests for a specific short-acting formulation, requests for dose escalation, lost or stolen prescriptions, use outside prescribed times for recreational or performance purposes, and reluctance to allow contact with previous prescribers. The safe response is to decline to prescribe on the day while explaining the reasoning clearly, arrange verification of the diagnosis and authority, and offer assessment for a possible stimulant use disorder, since irritability at refusal is common and does not by itself indicate a threat. Refusing to prescribe is not refusing to care, and the offer of ongoing review is central to the response.
key_points: Stimulants are controlled drugs requiring a state or territory authority tied to a named prescriber
Real time prescription monitoring reveals multiple concurrent prescribers across jurisdictions
Requests for short-acting preparations, dose escalation and recreational use are misuse markers
Verify diagnosis and authority before any supply, including a bridging supply
Regulatory concerns go to the state health department rather than to police
explanation.pearls: Check real time prescription monitoring before prescribing any Schedule 8 medicine to a new patient, and where misuse is suspected, document the specific findings and the reasons for declining rather than recording only that the request was refused.

options.rationale: Providing any supply before confirming the diagnosis and the authority endorses a pattern that the monitoring data already flags as concerning, and it makes subsequent refusal harder. Bridging supply is reasonable only when records confirm an established authorised treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Switching the formulation does not resolve the absence of a confirmed diagnosis or a valid prescribing authority, and stimulants require state authorisation regardless of the preparation chosen. A modified release formulation is a sensible clinical preference once treatment is properly established. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

The monitoring system is a clinical safety tool and the appropriate escalation is to the state health department regulator, not law enforcement, and treating a possible substance use disorder as a criminal matter drives patients away from care. Police involvement would be relevant only to a specific criminal act such as a forged script. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Multiple prescribers across two states, requests for dose escalation, insistence on immediate release preparations and recreational use are established markers of misuse, and stimulants are controlled drugs requiring a state authority tied to a single prescriber. Declining while keeping the door open with a clear plan and an offer of assessment maintains the therapeutic relationship without prescribing unsafely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Prescribing any treatment for a condition that has not been confirmed is inappropriate, and this agent takes weeks to act so it does not meet the need he is describing. It becomes a reasonable option once a diagnosis is established and stimulant misuse is a concern. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Adjustment disorder describes clinically significant emotional or behavioural symptoms arising within three months of an identifiable stressor, causing distress out of proportion to what would be expected or meaningful functional impairment, without meeting criteria for another mental disorder. It is among the most common presentations in general practice yet is frequently either dismissed as an understandable reaction or over-diagnosed as depression, and the distinction carries real treatment consequences. The features that argue against a depressive episode are preserved mood reactivity, retained capacity for enjoyment, absence of pervasive worthlessness or guilt, and preserved appetite and psychomotor function. First line management is psychological rather than pharmacological, addressing problem solving, activity scheduling and the practical stressors, since antidepressants have limited evidence in this condition. Symptoms are expected to resolve within six months of the stressor or its consequences ending, and the diagnosis should be revisited if they persist or deepen, particularly since work related injury with prolonged absence is itself a risk factor for progression to a depressive episode.
key_points: Symptoms begin within three months of an identifiable stressor and fall short of another disorder
Preserved mood reactivity and retained enjoyment argue against a depressive episode
Generalised anxiety disorder requires at least six months of worry across multiple domains
Psychological and practical intervention is first line; antidepressants have limited evidence
Reassess the diagnosis if symptoms persist, since progression to depression is common
explanation.pearls: Prolonged work absence is itself a predictor of poor recovery, so early graded return to modified duties alongside psychological support does more for the mood symptoms than waiting for full physical recovery before considering work.

sources.label: beyondblue: Clinical Practice Guidelines for Depression

options.rationale: A depressive episode requires low mood or anhedonia present most of the day nearly every day for at least two weeks, and he retains genuine enjoyment and mood reactivity with preserved appetite and no worthlessness or guilt. His distress is real but does not meet the symptom threshold. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

This requires excessive worry across multiple domains on more days than not for at least six months, whereas his worry is confined to the consequences of a specific event seven weeks ago. Duration and breadth are the features that separate the two. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

This diagnosis requires depressed mood for most days over at least two years, and his symptoms began two weeks after an injury seven weeks ago with no prior history. The distinguishing feature is chronicity, which is absent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

This requires disproportionate thoughts and behaviours about somatic symptoms, and his shoulder injury is a real verified injury with proportionate concern about its consequences. It would apply if his preoccupation exceeded what the injury and its prognosis warranted. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Emotional symptoms beginning within three months of an identifiable stressor, causing distress out of proportion to expectations and impairing function, but falling short of criteria for another disorder, define this diagnosis. Preserved mood reactivity, intact enjoyment and absence of worthlessness are the features that keep it below the threshold for a depressive episode. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: beyondblue: Clinical Practice Guidelines for Depression

explanation.summary: Depression in fathers and non-birthing partners during the perinatal period affects around one in ten, with the peak incidence between three and six months after the birth, later than the peak for mothers. It is systematically under-recognised because services, screening programs and public messaging are oriented towards the birthing parent, and because men more often present with irritability, anger, withdrawal, somatic complaints and increased substance use rather than expressed sadness. Risk factors include depression in the partner, a personal history of mental illness, poor relationship quality, financial stress, sleep deprivation and unplanned pregnancy. The consequences extend to the child, with associations with adverse emotional and behavioural outcomes independent of maternal mood, and to the couple relationship. Australian perinatal guidance recommends that fathers and partners be considered for screening and offered assessment when concerns arise, with treatment following the standard approach to depression, using psychological therapy first line for mild to moderate illness and adding an antidepressant for moderate to severe or unresponsive presentations.
key_points: Around one in ten fathers experience perinatal depression, peaking three to six months after birth
Presentation is often irritability, withdrawal and increased substance use rather than expressed sadness
Partner depression is a major risk factor, but paternal depression occurs independently of it
Effects on child emotional and behavioural outcomes are independent of maternal mood
Treatment follows standard depression management with psychological therapy first line
explanation.pearls: The baby's immunisation visits are among the few reliable contacts a new father has with health services, so a direct question about his own mood at the six week and four month visits is the most practical case-finding opportunity available.

sources.label: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.rationale: Four months of persistent symptoms with functional impairment, withdrawal from the baby and increased alcohol use is well beyond a normal adjustment and needs treatment. Watchful waiting is reasonable for mild transient symptoms in the first weeks. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.rationale: Perinatal mental health guidance explicitly includes fathers and non-birthing partners, and his partner has already screened normally and reports coping. Redirecting care away from the person with symptoms would leave a treatable illness untreated. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.rationale: The increased drinking followed the mood symptoms rather than preceding them, so treating it in isolation delays care for the primary problem. Alcohol reduction should be addressed alongside treatment rather than as a prerequisite for it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

He describes a depressive episode of at least moderate severity in the postnatal period, which affects roughly one in ten fathers and warrants the same assessment and treatment as in any other adult, beginning with structured risk assessment and psychological therapy. Addressing the alcohol increase at the same time treats a factor that will otherwise undermine recovery. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.rationale: Parenting support addresses skills and confidence but is not a treatment for a moderate depressive episode, and his withdrawal reflects the illness rather than a skills deficit. It is a useful adjunct once his mood is being treated. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

explanation.summary: Hypnotic agents acting at the benzodiazepine receptor, including the non-benzodiazepine z-drugs, are recommended only for short term use of two to four weeks because tolerance to the hypnotic effect develops quickly while the adverse effects persist. In older adults these agents roughly double the risk of falls and hip fracture and contribute to daytime sedation, cognitive impairment and motor vehicle accidents, and long term use is a recognised deprescribing priority. Withdrawal must be gradual, typically reducing by around a quarter of the dose every one to two weeks with slower steps at lower doses, because abrupt cessation causes rebound insomnia that patients interpret as proof they still need the drug. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is the first line treatment for chronic insomnia and outperforms medication in the long term, with sleep restriction and stimulus control the components that carry most of the effect. Success depends on framing the taper collaboratively, since patients who feel the medicine is being removed against their wishes rarely complete it.
key_points: These agents are indicated for two to four weeks only; tolerance develops while harms persist
In older adults they approximately double the risk of falls and hip fracture
Abrupt cessation causes rebound insomnia that drives relapse and reinforces perceived need
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is first line and outperforms medication long term
Substituting another hypnotic maintains dependence rather than resolving it
explanation.pearls: Taper by roughly 25 per cent of the dose every one to two weeks, slowing further below half the starting dose, and warn the patient in advance that two to three nights of worse sleep after each reduction is expected withdrawal rather than proof the drug is still needed.

options.rationale: Swapping one hypnotic for another maintains dependence and preserves the falls and cognitive risk that prompted the review. A cross-over to a longer acting agent is sometimes used to facilitate withdrawal, but not as ongoing therapy at an unchanged dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Abrupt cessation after four years of nightly use provokes rebound insomnia and withdrawal that predictably drives relapse, which is exactly what happened on her two previous attempts. A handout alone is also inadequate as the psychological component of treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Addressing the consequence while leaving the cause untouched ignores that the hypnotic is the principal modifiable contributor to her falls and cognitive complaints. Falls services work best alongside deprescribing rather than instead of it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Slow tapering with the patient's agreement prevents the rebound insomnia that has defeated her previous attempts, and the structured psychological therapy is first line treatment for chronic insomnia and substantially raises the success rate of withdrawal. Combining the two addresses both the dependence and the underlying sleep disorder. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Tricyclic antidepressants add anticholinergic burden, orthostatic hypotension and cognitive impairment, compounding rather than relieving her falls and memory concerns. Sedating antidepressants are considered only when a coexisting mood disorder justifies them. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Clozapine remains the only agent with established efficacy in treatment resistant schizophrenia, and its monitoring program is built around agranulocytosis, yet gastrointestinal hypomotility is both more common and more lethal. The drug has potent anticholinergic and antiserotonergic effects on the gut, slowing colonic transit in the majority of patients and producing a spectrum that runs from constipation through faecal impaction to paralytic ileus, toxic megacolon, ischaemia and perforation. Case fatality once ileus develops is high, and deaths substantially outnumber those from agranulocytosis. Patients frequently do not report the symptom, partly through negative symptoms and reduced interoceptive awareness, so bowel function must be asked about at every review rather than waiting for a complaint. Prophylactic laxatives are recommended for all patients on clozapine, and constipating co-prescriptions such as anticholinergics and opioids should be avoided or minimised.
key_points: Gastrointestinal hypomotility causes more clozapine deaths than agranulocytosis
Patients under-report bowel symptoms, so ask directly at every review
Myocarditis typically occurs in the first four to eight weeks, not after years of stable therapy
Prophylactic laxatives are recommended for all patients taking clozapine
Suspected ileus needs imaging and surgical review, not further oral laxatives
explanation.pearls: Avoid adding anticholinergic agents such as benzatropine to a patient on clozapine, since the combined gut slowing is a recognised precipitant of ileus, and prescribe a regular osmotic laxative from initiation rather than waiting for constipation to be reported.

options.rationale: His neutrophil count is normal and haematological monitoring is up to date, so agranulocytosis does not explain abdominal distension and vomiting. Withholding clozapine for more than 48 hours also forces a slow retitration with risk of psychotic relapse. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Clozapine induced myocarditis occurs characteristically within the first four to eight weeks of treatment and presents with tachycardia, fever and chest symptoms rather than nine days of constipation with distension. It remains an important complication but the timing and presentation do not fit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Oral laxatives alone are inadequate once obstruction is suspected, and stimulant agents can precipitate perforation in a distended atonic bowel. Laxatives are the mainstay of prevention and of treating uncomplicated constipation, not of suspected ileus. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Symptomatic treatment delays recognition of a condition with a case fatality far exceeding that of agranulocytosis, and many antiemetics further slow gut transit. Antiemetics are appropriate once obstruction has been excluded. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Nine days without bowel action, vomiting and a distended tympanic abdomen in a patient on clozapine indicates gastrointestinal hypomotility progressing towards ileus, which carries a mortality substantially higher than agranulocytosis and demands urgent imaging and surgical assessment. Recognising it requires actively asking about bowels, since patients rarely volunteer the symptom. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Corticosteroid induced neuropsychiatric effects are common, dose dependent and frequently misattributed to a primary psychiatric disorder, particularly when a patient has no prior history. Risk rises steeply above the equivalent of 40 mg of prednisolone daily, and symptoms typically emerge within the first two weeks of treatment. The presentations span elevated mood, irritability and psychosis at higher doses, depression which is more common with prolonged therapy, and cognitive disturbance, with a prior psychiatric history a much weaker predictor than is often assumed. Management centres on reducing the corticosteroid to the lowest dose that controls the underlying disease, in negotiation with the treating team rather than unilaterally, since abrupt cessation risks both disease flare and adrenal insufficiency. Symptomatic treatment uses an antipsychotic for elevated or psychotic presentations and an antidepressant for depressive ones, and most episodes resolve within days to weeks of dose reduction.
key_points: Risk rises steeply above the equivalent of 40 mg of prednisolone daily
Symptoms usually appear within the first two weeks of treatment
Elevated and psychotic presentations predominate acutely; depression predominates with prolonged use
Delirium is excluded by preserved attention and the absence of a fluctuating course
Reduce the dose in negotiation with the treating team rather than stopping abruptly
explanation.pearls: Document the reaction prominently, because recurrence on re-exposure is common and a patient who has had steroid induced mania may warrant prophylactic antipsychotic cover if a future high dose course is unavoidable.

options.rationale: A mood stabiliser committing her to long term therapy and monitoring is not justified when a clear pharmacological precipitant is present and the syndrome typically resolves with dose reduction. Lithium would be considered if manic episodes recurred independent of steroid exposure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

The temporal link to high dose corticosteroid with no prior mood history identifies a substance induced mood disturbance, so the priority is to reduce the causative exposure as far as her asthma safely allows while a short course of an antipsychotic controls the acute symptoms. Most cases resolve within days to weeks of dose reduction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Abrupt cessation after six days of high dose therapy risks both loss of asthma control and adrenal insufficiency if her exposure is longer than documented. The correct approach is the fastest safe reduction negotiated with the respiratory team, not immediate withdrawal. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Her presentation is elevated and expansive rather than depressed, and an antidepressant would risk worsening the elevated mood state. Antidepressants have a place in the depressive form of steroid induced mood disturbance, which is actually more common overall. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Delirium requires disturbed attention and awareness with a fluctuating course, and she is fully oriented with stable attention and no perceptual disturbance. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia are best approached as communication of an unmet need rather than as a target for sedation, and a structured search for precipitants precedes any medication decision. The standard sequence examines physical causes including pain, constipation, urinary retention, infection, sensory impairment and medication effects, then environmental and interpersonal triggers such as noise, overstimulation, unfamiliar carers and the manner in which personal care is delivered. Pain is the most frequently missed contributor because people with moderate to severe dementia cannot report it reliably, and observational pain scales or an empirical trial of regular simple analgesia are the practical responses. Antipsychotics carry a clear increase in stroke and all cause mortality in older people with dementia, so they are reserved for severe distress or risk after non-pharmacological measures have failed, used at the lowest effective dose with informed consent from the substitute decision maker and a defined plan for withdrawal. Australian aged care regulation requires documented justification and review of any psychotropic used for behaviour.
key_points: Treat behaviour as an unmet need and search systematically for precipitants first
Pain is the most commonly missed driver because self report is unreliable in dementia
Agitation confined to personal care and movement points strongly to a pain trigger
Antipsychotics increase stroke and mortality risk and require consent and a withdrawal plan
Benzodiazepines worsen falls and confusion and can cause paradoxical agitation
explanation.pearls: A trial of regular scheduled paracetamol, rather than as required dosing, is the single highest yield intervention for agitation in moderate dementia, and benefit should be assessed over about two weeks before escalating to any psychotropic.

options.rationale: An antipsychotic may eventually be justified but not before untreated pain has been addressed, and a 12 week review is far too long given the stroke and mortality risk. Where an antipsychotic is used, review is recommended at around four to 12 weeks with an explicit plan to withdraw. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Untreated pain is among the commonest reversible drivers of agitation in dementia, personal care and movement are exactly when osteoarthritic pain is provoked, and he receives no analgesia despite severe knee disease. A trial of regular simple analgesia is low risk and has good evidence for reducing agitation before any antipsychotic is considered. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Benzodiazepines increase falls, confusion and paradoxical agitation in this population and do not address the daytime trigger. They are reserved for short term use in acute severe distress where other measures have failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

These agents produce modest cognitive benefit but have little effect on established agitation and take months to show any change. They are indicated for cognitive symptoms rather than as a behavioural intervention. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Depression is worth considering in dementia but his distress is confined to personal care and movement rather than being pervasive, which points to a pain trigger. An antidepressant trial would be reasonable if there were persistent low mood, tearfulness or withdrawal across the day. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Shift work disorder is a circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder in which the work schedule conflicts with the endogenous circadian drive, producing insomnia during the designated sleep period, excessive sleepiness during work, and consequent mood and cognitive symptoms. Around one in five to one in three shift workers meet criteria, and the diagnosis is frequently mislabelled as depression because fatigue, irritability and poor concentration dominate the presentation. The discriminating feature is that symptoms track the roster and resolve when the worker can sleep according to their own rhythm, whereas a depressive episode persists across days off with anhedonia and negative cognitions. A sleep diary over two weeks is the key diagnostic tool and also exposes the inadequate sleep opportunity that patients often normalise. Management combines sleep hygiene adapted to shift work, strategic light exposure and avoidance, planned napping, careful caffeine timing and forward rotating rosters, with the occupational stakes real because drowsy driving after night shift is a major cause of vehicle crashes.
key_points: Symptoms that resolve completely on days off point to circadian misalignment, not depression
A two week sleep diary is the central diagnostic tool
Chronic insomnia requires adequate sleep opportunity, which shift workers often lack
Forward rotating rosters are better tolerated than backward rotating ones
Drowsy driving after night shift is a major occupational safety risk
explanation.pearls: Advise wearing dark sunglasses on the drive home after a night shift and blocking daylight in the bedroom, since morning light exposure resets the circadian clock in the wrong direction and undoes the day sleep he is trying to obtain.

sources.label: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift Work and Sleep

options.rationale: Sleepiness and mood symptoms that track his roster and resolve completely on days off, with normal restorative sleep when he can follow his own rhythm, define a circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder rather than a primary psychiatric or medical illness. The complete recovery within days off is the finding that separates it from a depressive episode. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift Work and Sleep)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift Work and Sleep

options.rationale: A depressive episode requires persistently low mood or anhedonia for most of the day nearly every day, and his symptoms remit entirely on days off with preserved enjoyment and no guilt or hopelessness. Fatigue alone is insufficient for the diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

He has no snoring, no witnessed apnoeas and a normal body mass index, and his sleep on days off is restorative, which argues against a breathing related disorder. Sleep study referral would be indicated if any of those features were present. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift Work and Sleep)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift Work and Sleep

options.rationale: Chronic insomnia requires difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep despite adequate opportunity, and his problem is inadequate opportunity because he is trying to sleep in daylight against his circadian drive. He sleeps normally when the opportunity aligns with his rhythm. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift Work and Sleep)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift Work and Sleep

options.rationale: His intake is substantial and worth addressing, particularly its timing late in a night shift, but caffeine does not account for eight months of sleepiness that resolves entirely on days off. Withdrawal symptoms would be expected on days off when intake falls, which is when he feels best. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift Work and Sleep)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift Work and Sleep

explanation.summary: The menopausal transition carries a genuinely increased risk of depressive symptoms and of a first depressive episode, with the vulnerability concentrated in the perimenopause rather than after the final menstrual period, and it is greatest in women with a history of premenstrual mood change, postnatal depression or previous depression. Distinguishing a depressive episode arising in this context from one occurring independently matters because the treatment differs: where prominent vasomotor symptoms are disrupting sleep and driving the mood change, hormone therapy improves both, whereas an established major depressive episode with prior history is treated with standard antidepressant and psychological therapy. Diagnosis of the transition itself is clinical in women over 45, and hormone measurement is explicitly not recommended because levels fluctuate unpredictably. Hormone therapy also requires assessment of contraindications including hormone sensitive cancer, unexplained vaginal bleeding, active liver disease and prior venous thromboembolism, and transdermal preparations carry lower thrombotic risk than oral ones. Where mood does not improve as flushes settle, an antidepressant is added rather than substituted.
key_points: Perimenopause carries greater depressive risk than the postmenopausal years
Prior premenstrual, postnatal or major depression identifies the highest risk group
Hormone measurement is not recommended for diagnosis in women over 45 with typical symptoms
Hormone therapy treats both vasomotor symptoms and associated mood disturbance
Add an antidepressant if mood fails to improve once vasomotor symptoms are controlled
explanation.pearls: Transdermal oestrogen avoids first pass hepatic metabolism and does not carry the increased venous thromboembolism risk seen with oral preparations, making it the preferred route in women with raised body mass index or other thrombotic risk factors.

sources.label: Australasian Menopause Society: Menopause and Mood

options.rationale: Antidepressants are first line for a major depressive episode but treat the vasomotor symptoms less effectively than hormonal therapy, and here the flushes and night sweats are driving the sleep disruption that sustains the mood disturbance. They become the preferred choice when hormone therapy is contraindicated or declined. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Menopause and Mood)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Menopause and Mood

options.rationale: Hormone levels fluctuate widely during the transition and are not recommended for diagnosis in a woman over 45 with typical symptoms and menstrual change. Testing would delay treatment without changing the management decision. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Menopause and Mood)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Menopause and Mood

options.rationale: Where new depressive symptoms arise in the perimenopause alongside prominent vasomotor symptoms and no prior mood history, hormone therapy improves both the flushes and the mood and is the appropriate first recommendation in a woman with no contraindications. Reviewing at six weeks allows an antidepressant to be added if mood does not follow the vasomotor response. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Menopause and Mood)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Menopause and Mood

options.rationale: Psychological therapy is a valuable component and helps the distress associated with flushes, but used alone it leaves the nightly vasomotor sleep disruption untreated. It is a reasonable primary choice when a woman declines or cannot take pharmacological treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Complementary preparations have inconsistent evidence and do not reliably control moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms or depressive symptoms, so three months of waiting has a substantial opportunity cost. They may suit women with mild symptoms who prefer non-prescription options. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Menopause and Mood)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Menopause and Mood

explanation.summary: Hair pulling disorder is classified among the obsessive compulsive and related disorders and is characterised by recurrent pulling with repeated attempts to stop, often preceded by tension and followed by relief. The examination findings of irregular patches containing hairs of varying lengths, with a normal non-scarred scalp, distinguish it from alopecia areata and from fungal infection. First line treatment is habit reversal training, a behavioural package of awareness training, a competing response and stimulus control, which outperforms medication in this condition. Asking specifically about swallowing hair matters because trichobezoar can cause obstruction, and screening for depression and anxiety is routine since comorbidity is common.
key_points: Hairs of varying length in irregular patches with a normal scalp point to pulling rather than alopecia areata
Habit reversal training is first line and outperforms serotonin reuptake inhibitors
Serotonin reuptake inhibitors are reserved for comorbid disorders or failed behavioural therapy
Ask about swallowing hair, since trichobezoar can cause gastrointestinal obstruction
explanation.pearls: Ask two questions when you see patchy hair loss with intact scalp skin: does the tension build before and ease after, and does she swallow the hair? A yes to the first makes habit reversal training the treatment, and a yes to the second makes an abdominal examination for a trichobezoar urgent.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.rationale: N-acetylcysteine has shown benefit for hair pulling in some adult trials and is sometimes used as an adjunct, but the adolescent evidence is weak and it has not displaced behavioural therapy as first line. Offering a supplement first also implies that the behaviour cannot be modified directly, which is the opposite of the message that helps. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.rationale: Habit reversal training, in which awareness training, a competing physical response and stimulus control are taught together, is the first line treatment for hair pulling disorder at every age and outperforms medication. Starting a record of when and where pulling happens gives the therapist the pattern to work with and begins the awareness training component immediately. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.rationale: Serotonin reuptake inhibitors are effective for obsessive compulsive disorder itself but have not shown consistent benefit for hair pulling, which is a body focused repetitive behaviour rather than a compulsion driven by an obsession. Medication is considered when behavioural therapy has failed or when a comorbid disorder such as depression is present, and she has neither. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.rationale: Topical minoxidil treats androgenetic hair loss, which produces diffuse thinning rather than irregular patches with hairs of different lengths. Regrowth here depends on stopping the pulling, and prescribing a topical agent implies that the scalp rather than the behaviour is the problem. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology, Hair disorders)

Biopsy is useful when the cause of patchy alopecia is uncertain, particularly to identify scarring processes, but here the girl has described the mechanism directly and the scalp shows no scarring or inflammation. Investigating further risks conveying disbelief at the moment she has disclosed something difficult. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology, Hair disorders)

explanation.summary: Deliberate insulin restriction for weight control is a disordered eating behaviour unique to type 1 diabetes and is easily missed because body weight is normal and the classic purging signs are absent. The clues are a rising glycated haemoglobin, repeated admissions with ketoacidosis, clinic non-attendance, and body checking with weight-related reasoning about insulin. It carries a substantially increased risk of retinopathy, nephropathy and early death, which makes it more dangerous than the numbers alone suggest. Effective management is joint: an eating disorder service for the body image and behavioural work, and the diabetes team to restart insulin gradually, since rapid normalisation of glucose can cause oedema, worsening retinopathy and neuropathic pain that reinforces avoidance.
key_points: Normal body weight does not exclude an eating disorder in type 1 diabetes
Rising glycated haemoglobin with repeated ketoacidosis and clinic avoidance is the pattern to recognise
Ask directly about omitting insulin to control weight, since it is rarely volunteered
Reintroduce insulin gradually within a joint eating disorder and diabetes plan
explanation.pearls: Ask every young person with type 1 diabetes and recurrent ketoacidosis whether they ever take less insulin than prescribed to influence their weight. A yes reframes the admission from poor adherence to an eating disorder, and the treatment becomes joint eating disorder and diabetes care with deliberately gradual insulin reintroduction.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders
InsideOut Institute: Eating disorders and diabetes

options.rationale: Insulin restriction for weight control is an eating disorder expressed through diabetes, so treatment has to be delivered jointly by a service able to address body image and by the diabetes team able to reintroduce insulin at a pace that limits the fluid shift, oedema and neuropathic pain that rapid normalisation causes. Addressing either side alone reproduces the pattern of escalating glycated haemoglobin and repeated admissions. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders
