Charcoal can be considered within 1 to 2 hours in an intubated protected airway but does not replace sodium bicarbonate for cardiotoxicity; delaying bicarbonate risks arrhythmia. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)
Magnesium is used for torsades not for sodium channel blockade; delaying bicarbonate until QRS above 160 misses the AU threshold of 100 milliseconds. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

Lipid emulsion is a rescue for local anaesthetic and severe lipophilic drug toxicity refractory to standard care; not first line for tricyclic cardiotoxicity ahead of sodium bicarbonate. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

explanation.summary: Lithium remains the first line maintenance mood stabiliser for bipolar I disorder after a manic episode and has the strongest evidence for reduced suicide. Baseline investigations before starting lithium are urea and electrolytes with estimated glomerular filtration rate, thyroid stimulating hormone, calcium, weight, pregnancy test in women of reproductive age and electrocardiogram in patients over 40 or with cardiac risk. Start at 250 to 500 mg at night and check a 12 hour post dose serum lithium level 5 to 7 days later. Maintenance target is 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L (0.8 to 1.0 in acute mania). Regular monitoring includes serum lithium every 3 months, urea and electrolytes and thyroid stimulating hormone every 6 months, and calcium annually. Warn about nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors, dehydration and salt restriction which raise lithium levels. Signs of toxicity include tremor, ataxia, drowsiness, and diarrhoea.
key_points: AU baseline: urea and electrolytes, estimated glomerular filtration rate, TSH, calcium, weight, pregnancy test, electrocardiogram if indicated.
Starting dose: lithium 250 to 500 mg nocte; check 12 hour post dose level in 5 to 7 days.
Maintenance level target: 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L; check every 3 months plus renal and thyroid every 6 months.
explanation.pearls: Lithium maintenance target is a 12 hour post dose serum level of 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L in bipolar I; monitor every 3 months, with urea/electrolytes and thyroid stimulating hormone every 6 months and calcium annually.

options.rationale: Baseline renal function, thyroid function, calcium, electrocardiogram and pregnancy test are mandatory before lithium; maintenance target is 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L not 1.2 to 1.6. (Source: RANZCP: Bipolar Disorder)

Baseline renal, thyroid, calcium, pregnancy test and electrocardiogram then start lithium 250 to 500 mg nocte, titrated to a maintenance serum level of 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L (12 hours post dose) is the AU standard. (Source: RANZCP: Bipolar Disorder)

Sodium valproate is teratogenic and specifically avoided in women of childbearing potential; lithium has the strongest antisuicidal and maintenance evidence in bipolar I. (Source: RANZCP: Bipolar Disorder)

AU guidance recommends adding a mood stabiliser (lithium first line) rather than antipsychotic monotherapy for maintenance in bipolar I disorder given superior relapse prevention. (Source: RANZCP: Bipolar Disorder)
Lamotrigine is first line for bipolar depression prevention rather than mania; lithium is preferred after a first manic episode. (Source: RANZCP: Bipolar Disorder)

explanation.summary: Clozapine causes greater metabolic morbidity than any other antipsychotic (weight gain, insulin resistance, dyslipidaemia). RANZCP and Therapeutic Guidelines set a monitoring schedule: baseline fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipids, weight, waist, blood pressure; repeat at 3, 6 and 12 months, then annually. Weekly white cell counts continue for 18 weeks, then fortnightly to 12 months, then monthly. Weight gain is common in the first 6 months and is managed with dietitian, exercise, and metformin if BMI or waist trend continues to rise. Do not stop or dose-reduce an effective clozapine trial for early weight gain alone.
key_points: Baseline plus 3, 6, 12 months then annual metabolic monitoring
Weekly WCC for 18 weeks, fortnightly to 12 months, then monthly
Manage weight with lifestyle then metformin, not dose reduction
Waist over 94 cm (male) or 80 cm (female) signals metabolic risk
Do not cease effective clozapine trial for early weight gain
explanation.pearls: Metformin 500 mg orally titrated to 1 g twice daily is the evidence-based adjunct that limits antipsychotic weight gain; consider it when BMI increase exceeds 5 percent from baseline.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: Ceasing an effective clozapine trial after 4 weeks of response is not indicated for early weight gain; the switch back removes treatment resistant response (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: 3 months from initiation is the recommended interval; a 3 kg gain in 4 weeks warrants dietitian and exercise input but not immediate biochemistry (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: Dose reduction risks losing symptomatic benefit; weight gain is managed with lifestyle first and metformin as adjunct rather than dose reduction (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: RANZCP metabolic monitoring for clozapine repeats fasting glucose and lipids at 3 months from initiation, then 6 months, then annually; HbA1c at 3 months provides an early signal of insulin resistance (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: Polypharmacy adds side effects and pharmacokinetic interactions without evidence of metabolic benefit in clozapine users; the answer is lifestyle intervention plus scheduled monitoring (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

explanation.summary: Lithium remains a first line mood stabiliser in bipolar I disorder with clear anti-suicide effect. Long-term monitoring requires attention to the renal (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, chronic tubular disease, eGFR trend), thyroid (up to 15 percent develop hypothyroidism), and parathyroid (10 percent develop hyperparathyroidism) systems. Australian guidance repeats lithium level, U&E, creatinine and TSH every 6 months and adjusted calcium every 6 to 12 months once stable. Target lithium is typically 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L for maintenance; higher (0.8 to 1.0) for acute mania under supervision. Toxicity presents with coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion, and vomiting; level above 1.5 mmol/L is toxic.
key_points: 6 monthly: lithium level, U&E, creatinine, TSH
6 to 12 monthly: adjusted calcium for hyperparathyroidism
Target maintenance level 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L
Toxicity: coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion, vomiting
Level above 1.5 mmol/L is toxic and needs intervention
explanation.pearls: Lithium associated hyperparathyroidism raises PTH and calcium but the patient is often asymptomatic; screen adjusted calcium routinely because early detection allows medication review before parathyroidectomy is needed.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder

options.rationale: Long-term lithium monitoring requires thyroid function testing every 6 to 12 months because of the risk of hypothyroidism; omitting TSH misses a common preventable morbidity (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder

options.rationale: A 24 hour collection is reserved for evaluation of polyuria or suspected nephrogenic diabetes insipidus rather than routine monitoring in an asymptomatic patient (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder

options.rationale: Liver function testing is not part of routine lithium monitoring (lithium is renally excreted); this set misses TSH, calcium and renal indices (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder

options.rationale: Renal monitoring (U&E, creatinine, eGFR) is central because lithium causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathy; adjusted calcium screens for parathyroid effect (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder

options.rationale: Australian bipolar guidance recommends 6-monthly lithium level, U&E, creatinine and TSH, with adjusted calcium every 6 to 12 months to detect lithium associated hyperparathyroidism (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndrome of psychomotor disturbance defined by 3 of 12 DSM-5 features including stupor, catalepsy, waxy flexibility, mutism, negativism, posturing, mannerism, stereotypy, agitation, grimacing, echolalia, or echopraxia. Half of cases occur in mood disorders (especially mania and depression), a quarter in psychotic disorders, and the remainder in medical or neurological illness. First line treatment is benzodiazepines (lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IM or IV, repeated 3 to 6 hourly to a total 8 to 16 mg/day); response is often dramatic within hours. Malignant catatonia (fever, autonomic instability, rhabdomyolysis) requires ECT. Avoid antipsychotics until catatonia has resolved.
key_points: Catatonia: 3 of 12 DSM-5 features including waxy flexibility, mutism
Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IM as diagnostic and therapeutic challenge
Avoid antipsychotics until catatonia resolves
Malignant catatonia (fever, autonomic instability) needs ECT
Screen for medical causes: encephalitis, metabolic, autoimmune
explanation.pearls: The Bush Francis Catatonia Rating Scale is the AU-used screen; 2 of the first 14 items or a total score at least 6 supports diagnosis and quantifies severity for treatment response.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder

options.rationale: Antipsychotics can precipitate or worsen catatonia and risk neuroleptic malignant syndrome; catatonia is treated first before restarting antipsychotic (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Catatonia (waxy flexibility, mutism, gegenhalten, staring) responds to benzodiazepines; a lorazepam 2 mg IM challenge produces observable improvement in most catatonia and confirms the diagnosis while treating it (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder

options.rationale: NMS is unlikely because she is afebrile with normal CK and stable haemodynamics; the presentation is catatonia and dantrolene is not first-line (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

There is no EEG or clinical evidence of ongoing seizure and the clinical picture (waxy flexibility, gegenhalten) is catatonia rather than non-convulsive status (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

First-generation antipsychotics carry a high risk of precipitating malignant catatonia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome in this setting; the priority is benzodiazepine challenge not chemical restraint (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: TCA overdose is a leading cause of drug related death from prescribed medications. Amitriptyline and dosulepin have the highest cardiotoxicity because of sodium channel blockade in ventricular myocardium, which widens QRS, produces R wave in aVR, and predisposes to broad complex tachyarrhythmia. Central effects include coma, seizures, and anticholinergic delirium. QRS over 100 ms indicates significant sodium channel blockade and the threshold for hypertonic sodium bicarbonate to keep pH 7.45 to 7.55 and QRS under 120. Class I antiarrhythmics and physostigmine are contraindicated; seizures are treated with benzodiazepines rather than phenytoin.
key_points: QRS over 100 ms is threshold for sodium bicarbonate
R wave in aVR over 3 mm confirms significant Na channel block
Alkalinise to pH 7.45 to 7.55 and QRS under 120 ms
Class I antiarrhythmics and physostigmine are contraindicated
Benzodiazepines first-line for seizures; avoid phenytoin
explanation.pearls: The R wave in aVR sign is more specific than QRS width: R at least 3 mm or R:S ratio at least 0.7 predicts seizure and arrhythmia risk and may justify treatment even with a borderline QRS.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Toxinology Consensus

options.rationale: TCA cardiotoxicity is driven by sodium channel blockade; QRS over 100 ms is the threshold to give hypertonic sodium bicarbonate and R in aVR over 3 mm confirms significant blockade (Source: Australian and New Zealand Toxinology Consensus; Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Toxinology Consensus

options.rationale: At 2 hours post ingestion charcoal has limited efficacy, and giving oral charcoal in a drowsy patient without airway protection risks aspiration; treat the toxicity first (Source: Australian and New Zealand Toxinology Consensus).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Toxinology Consensus

options.rationale: Lipid emulsion is reserved for refractory cardiotoxicity where sodium bicarbonate has failed; first-line intervention for QRS widening is sodium bicarbonate (Source: Australian and New Zealand Toxinology Consensus).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Toxinology Consensus

options.rationale: Flecainide is a class Ic sodium channel blocker and worsens TCA cardiotoxicity; class I antiarrhythmics are contraindicated in TCA overdose (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology).

Physostigmine is contraindicated in TCA overdose because it can precipitate asystole and seizure by unopposed cholinergic effect combined with sodium channel blockade (Source: Australian and New Zealand Toxinology Consensus).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Toxinology Consensus

explanation.summary: Smoking cessation pharmacotherapy in Australia offers three first line options: combination NRT (long-acting patch plus rapid acting gum or lozenge), varenicline, or bupropion. Varenicline (alpha4 beta2 partial nicotinic agonist) has the highest single agent efficacy but requires review of cardiovascular history and any serious psychiatric illness. Bupropion (noradrenergic and dopaminergic reuptake inhibitor) is effective but contraindicated with seizure disorder, eating disorder, or MAOI use. Combination NRT is the recommended NRT approach for moderate to heavy dependence, and behavioural support doubles quit rates alongside pharmacotherapy.
key_points: First line: combination NRT, varenicline, or bupropion
Bupropion contraindicated in seizure disorder or eating disorder
Varenicline is the most effective single agent
Combination NRT for Fagerstrom over 5
Behavioural support doubles quit rate
explanation.pearls: The EAGLES trial (2016) showed varenicline is safe in stable psychiatric illness with no significant increase in neuropsychiatric adverse events compared with placebo, patch, or bupropion; the FDA black box warning was removed.

options.rationale: Bupropion lowers seizure threshold and is contraindicated with any history of seizure disorder including alcohol withdrawal seizure; varenicline is safer here (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

Varenicline is the most effective single agent for smoking cessation and preferred over bupropion here because bupropion lowers seizure threshold and he has a prior withdrawal seizure; RACGP endorses varenicline in patients without recent cardiovascular event or serious mental illness (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).
Monotherapy nicotine replacement has already failed him; combination NRT (patch plus rapid rescue) or varenicline is more effective for heavy dependence (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation).

Nortriptyline is second line for smoking cessation and carries anticholinergic and cardiotoxic risks; it is not preferred where varenicline is safe and effective (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation).
Clonidine is a third line agent with adverse effect burden (sedation, hypotension, rebound hypertension); it is not appropriate as first choice (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation).

explanation.summary: Valproate is the most teratogenic anti-seizure medication in current AU use: 10 percent major congenital malformation rate (neural tube, cardiac, orofacial, hypospadias), and up to 30 to 40 percent risk of neurodevelopmental impairment including autism and lower IQ. The TGA restricts valproate in women and girls of reproductive potential to those in whom other options have failed AND with effective contraception (pregnancy prevention program). Lamotrigine, lithium (with fetal cardiac surveillance), and second generation antipsychotics (olanzapine, quetiapine) are safer bipolar mood stabilisers in reproductive age women. Switching is planned with pharmacist input to avoid relapse.
key_points: Valproate causes 10 percent major malformation and 30-40 percent NDD risk
Not for reproductive age women unless other options have failed
Effective contraception required during use
Lamotrigine, lithium, quetiapine are safer bipolar options
Switch is planned, not abrupt
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine cross-titration to valproate requires very slow titration (starting 25 mg every other day) because valproate inhibits lamotrigine metabolism, doubling risk of severe rash including Stevens Johnson syndrome.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder

options.rationale: Continuing valproate exposes any future pregnancy to a 10 percent major malformation risk and dose-dependent neurodevelopmental impairment; folic acid does not mitigate this risk (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder; TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder

options.rationale: Effective contraception is necessary during valproate use but the plan is to switch away from valproate before conception; contraception alone does not address the desired pregnancy timeline (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program).

Abrupt cessation of a mood stabiliser in bipolar I risks rapid relapse into mania or depression; a planned taper with alternative mood stabiliser and effective contraception is required (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder

options.rationale: There is no safe dose of valproate in pregnancy; even under 500 mg/day the malformation risk exceeds background and neurodevelopmental risk is present; the AU program is switch, not reduce (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program).

AU TGA and RANZCP guidance are that valproate should not be prescribed to women of reproductive potential unless other options have failed and effective contraception is in place; here lamotrigine is a first line alternative and switch with effective contraception is required (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder; TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder

explanation.summary: Panic disorder is the DSM-5 diagnosis when recurrent unexpected panic attacks are followed by at least one month of anticipatory worry or maladaptive behavioural change. First-line pharmacotherapy in Australian practice is a low-dose SSRI titrated slowly over 1 to 2 weeks to a standard depression-range dose, because full-dose initiation commonly precipitates transient jitteriness that undermines adherence. Sertraline, escitalopram, and paroxetine all have TGA registration for panic disorder. Cognitive behavioural therapy with interoceptive exposure is at least equally effective and can be run in parallel. Benzodiazepines have a limited bridging role.
key_points: SSRI titrated from low start over 1 to 2 weeks is first-line
Sertraline 25 mg then 50 mg is the eTG initiation pattern
Standard-dose SSRI start commonly precipitates activation
Benzodiazepines are not first-line monotherapy
CBT with interoceptive exposure runs alongside SSRI
explanation.pearls: Warning the patient that panic-like symptoms may transiently worsen for 1 to 2 weeks on any SSRI, and pre-prescribing 5 diazepam 5 mg tablets as a rescue, improves 12 week adherence in RANZCP audit data.

options.rationale: Mirtazapine has evidence in depression with anxious features but is not first-line for panic disorder in eTG or RANZCP guidance; sedation and weight gain are relevant for a physically well working adult (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Regular benzodiazepine monotherapy for panic disorder carries dependence risk and blunts the exposure-based learning that resolves avoidance; short-term use is at most a bridge, not the initiating agent (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Beta blockers reduce sympathetic somatic symptoms in performance anxiety but do not treat the cognitive and avoidance features of panic disorder and are not recommended as monotherapy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Fluoxetine is effective for panic disorder but starting at the standard depression dose commonly precipitates activation and worsening panic in the first fortnight; the recommendation is a lower start (5 to 10 mg) then titrate (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

SSRIs at low starting doses titrated up over 1 to 2 weeks are first-line pharmacotherapy for panic disorder; sertraline 25 mg titrated to 50 mg is the recommended eTG initiation regimen because full dose introduction commonly precipitates a transient jitteriness that undermines adherence (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; RANZCP Panic Disorder CPG).

explanation.summary: Postnatal depression is common and treatable, and the choice of antidepressant in breastfeeding is guided by the relative infant dose (RID) of the drug in breastmilk. Sertraline consistently has the lowest RID and undetectable infant plasma levels in most studies, which is why RANZCP places it first for perinatal antidepressant initiation. Fluoxetine and citalopram have higher RID and their long-acting metabolites can accumulate in neonates; they are still reasonable if the mother was already responding to them prior to conception. Psychological therapy (CBT or interpersonal therapy) should be offered in parallel, and thyroid, ferritin, and B12 should be excluded as contributors before ascribing symptoms to postnatal depression.
key_points: Sertraline is first-line SSRI in breastfeeding
RID under 2 percent with undetectable infant plasma levels
Fluoxetine is not first-line new due to long half-life metabolite
Do not wean breastfeeding to start an antidepressant
Screen with EPDS and check item 10 for suicidal thoughts
explanation.pearls: The EPDS item 10 asks about thoughts of self-harm and any positive score requires same-day risk assessment even when the total score is modest; a score of 2 or 3 on item 10 with a total of 12 outweighs a total of 17 with item 10 zero.

options.rationale: Weaning is not required to treat postnatal depression pharmacologically; several SSRIs are considered safe in lactation and abrupt weaning itself worsens maternal mood (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health CPG).

Fluoxetine has a long half-life active metabolite that accumulates in neonates and gives the highest relative infant dose of the SSRIs; it is a second-line perinatal choice when the mother is already established on it, not for a new start (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health CPG).

Venlafaxine has an infant relative dose higher than sertraline and lacks the same reassuring evidence base for perinatal initiation; it is reasonable if the mother was already responding to it, not first-line new (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health CPG).

Mirtazapine has limited perinatal safety data and its sedation and weight gain profile are unfavourable when the mother needs to be responsive to a young infant; it is not first-line (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health CPG).

Sertraline is the preferred SSRI in breastfeeding because relative infant dose is under 2 percent and infant plasma levels are usually undetectable; it is the first-line perinatal antidepressant in RANZCP and eTG guidance (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health CPG; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Alcohol withdrawal management in the ED runs on three parallel tracks: prevent Wernicke encephalopathy with parenteral thiamine before any glucose, control autonomic and neurological features with a symptom-triggered benzodiazepine schedule (usually diazepam) titrated to CIWA-Ar, and treat the metabolic and electrolyte disturbances of chronic heavy drinking. The AU thiamine dose is 300 mg IV or IM daily for at least 3 days when Wernicke risk is present, followed by oral maintenance. Giving glucose before thiamine to a thiamine-deplete patient precipitates the classic triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and confusion. Haloperidol should be avoided as it lowers the seizure threshold in withdrawal.
key_points: Thiamine 300 mg IV or IM before any glucose load
Continue parenteral thiamine daily for at least 3 days
Symptom-triggered diazepam titrated to CIWA-Ar for withdrawal
Avoid haloperidol which lowers seizure threshold
Monitor magnesium, phosphate, and potassium
explanation.pearls: Point-of-care glucose is the trigger that catches the pre-Wernicke deteriorating patient in the ED: a value below 4 mmol/L in a heavy drinker mandates thiamine before you touch the glucose vial.

options.rationale: Parenteral thiamine before any glucose load is standard because glucose given to a thiamine deplete patient precipitates Wernicke encephalopathy; the AU eTG dose is 300 mg IV or IM followed by ongoing daily dosing for at least 3 days (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction; RACP Alcohol Withdrawal Guideline).

Giving concentrated glucose to a thiamine deplete patient precipitates Wernicke encephalopathy and oral thiamine has variable absorption in malnourished heavy drinkers; the order and route are wrong (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

Benzodiazepine loading is needed for a CIWA-Ar of 22 but thiamine must be given first when point-of-care glucose is low and the patient is at high Wernicke risk; benzodiazepines alone leave the metabolic emergency unaddressed (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

Haloperidol lowers seizure threshold and is not first-line for alcohol withdrawal agitation; benzodiazepines are the class of choice and thiamine and glucose remain the immediate priority (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

A symptom-triggered regimen is preferred over a fixed schedule for uncomplicated withdrawal, and thiamine is a non-negotiable safety step in a malnourished heavy drinker regardless of the benzodiazepine strategy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome is a shift of phosphate, potassium, magnesium and glucose into cells triggered by the insulin surge of reintroduced carbohydrate. It typically peaks between 24 and 72 hours of refeeding and can precipitate arrhythmia, respiratory failure and cardiac failure. The RCH and MARSIPAN paediatric pathways define high-risk anorexia nervosa by BMI under 14, rapid weight loss, bradycardia under 50, QTc prolongation, or baseline low phosphate or potassium. High-risk patients require 12-hourly biochemistry for the first 72 hours, continuous cardiac monitoring, prophylactic oral phosphate replacement, and a slow calorie ladder starting around 1000 kcal per day.
key_points: Refeeding shifts peak between 24 and 72 hours
12-hourly phosphate, magnesium, potassium and glucose in high-risk
Continuous cardiac monitoring for BMI under 14 or QTc over 460 ms
Prophylactic oral phosphate and thiamine at admission
Slow calorie ladder starting around 1000 kcal per day
explanation.pearls: The RCH threshold for continuous cardiac monitoring in adolescent anorexia is a resting pulse under 50, QTc over 460 ms, or any postural drop over 20 mmHg systolic; meeting any one of these commits the patient to a HDU-level of surveillance during refeeding.

options.rationale: Daily bloods miss the early refeeding shift which typically peaks at 24 to 72 hours; the AU standard is 12-hourly monitoring for the first 72 hours in high-risk cases (Source: RCH CPG: Eating Disorders).

RCH and MARSIPAN adolescent pathways mandate 12-hourly electrolyte monitoring including phosphate for the first 72 hours of refeeding in high-risk anorexia nervosa (BMI under 14, rapid loss, bradycardia, QTc prolongation) with continuous cardiac monitoring on a paediatric ward (Source: RCH CPG: Eating Disorders; RANZCP Eating Disorders CPG).

Refeeding hypophosphataemia is a laboratory diagnosis that often precedes clinical features and can precipitate arrhythmia and respiratory failure; symptom-triggered testing is unsafe in a patient with baseline low phosphate (Source: RCH CPG: Eating Disorders).
Empirical phosphate replacement is reasonable but does not remove the need for close monitoring; the pathway is both prophylactic replacement and 12-hourly checks (Source: RCH CPG: Eating Disorders).

Continuous cardiac monitoring rather than symptom-triggered ECG is the RCH standard for the first 72 hours in a patient with baseline bradycardia and QTc 470 ms; intermittent ECG misses developing arrhythmia (Source: RCH CPG: Eating Disorders).

explanation.summary: Lithium remains a first-line mood stabiliser for acute mania in adults with preserved renal function, especially when there is a documented prior good response. Australian practice is to initiate at 750 to 1000 mg nocte as a single dose and re-check the 12-hour trough level after 5 to 7 days, aiming for 0.8 to 1.2 mmol/L for acute mania and 0.4 to 0.8 mmol/L for maintenance. Once-daily nocte dosing gives lower renal peak exposure than divided dosing and is now standard. Baseline workup includes urea electrolytes creatinine, eGFR, TSH, calcium, and ECG, all repeated at 3 to 6 monthly intervals during maintenance.
key_points: Target-directed dose 750 to 1000 mg nocte in normal renal function
12-hour trough drawn at 5 to 7 days to guide titration
Acute mania target 0.8 to 1.2 mmol/L
Once nightly dosing lowers long-term nephrotoxicity risk
Baseline TSH, calcium, eGFR, ECG before initiation
explanation.pearls: The steady-state assumption behind a 12-hour trough is only valid after 5 half-lives, which for lithium in normal renal function is 5 to 7 days; a level drawn at 48 hours will systematically underestimate the eventual steady state and drives inappropriate over-titration.

options.rationale: Lithium loading doses risk supratherapeutic levels and are not recommended; steady state is reached over 5 to 7 days and titration relies on 12-hour troughs (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

A subtherapeutic starting dose delays symptom control in acute mania and a 24 hour post-dose level does not represent the 12-hour trough that guides titration; this delays effective treatment (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

In acute mania with normal renal function the AU practice is to initiate lithium at a target-directed dose of around 750 to 1000 mg nocte titrated by a 12-hour trough drawn 5 to 7 days after each dose change, aiming for a level of 0.8 to 1.2 mmol/L (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; RANZCP Bipolar CPG).

Once nightly dosing is preferred to divided dosing because it reduces peak renal exposure and long-term nephrotoxicity risk without loss of efficacy; three times daily dosing is outdated (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Sodium valproate is a reasonable alternative but the patient has a prior good response to lithium and preserved renal function; that history makes lithium first-line rather than a switch to valproate (Source: RANZCP Bipolar CPG).

explanation.summary: Post-traumatic stress disorder is a DSM-5 diagnosis after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence, with re-experiencing, avoidance, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and hyperarousal persisting more than one month. The Phoenix Australia guideline places structured trauma-focused psychological therapies (TF-CBT, cognitive processing therapy, EMDR) as first-line treatment ahead of pharmacotherapy in both civilian and veteran populations. Sertraline, paroxetine, and venlafaxine are second-line when trauma-focused therapy is unavailable or has failed. Benzodiazepines are contraindicated because they worsen long-term outcomes.
key_points: TF-CBT, CPT and EMDR are first-line for PTSD
Sertraline is second-line when psychological therapy fails
Benzodiazepines worsen outcomes and are contraindicated
Prazosin has an adjunctive role for nightmares only
Screen with PCL-5 and monitor for comorbid depression
explanation.pearls: Trauma-focused psychological therapies deliver an effect size of around 1.4 for PTSD symptoms in the Phoenix Australia meta-analysis, roughly twice that of pharmacotherapy alone, which is why they lead the algorithm even in veteran cohorts where medication adherence is often better than therapy attendance.

options.rationale: Sertraline is second-line for PTSD when trauma-focused therapy is unavailable, refused or has failed; monotherapy pharmacotherapy first-line is not the AU standard (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines).

AU and international guidelines place trauma-focused psychological therapies (TF-CBT, cognitive processing therapy, EMDR) as first-line treatment for PTSD ahead of pharmacotherapy because effect sizes are larger and gains are more durable (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines; RANZCP PTSD CPG).
Prazosin is adjunctive for PTSD nightmares but does not treat re-experiencing, avoidance, or hyperarousal broadly; it is not first-line monotherapy (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines).

Second-generation antipsychotics as PTSD monotherapy are not supported by the AU guideline and carry metabolic and sedation risks unlikely to be justified before trauma-focused therapy has been offered (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines).

Benzodiazepines are contraindicated in PTSD as they worsen long-term outcomes, blunt exposure-based recovery, and carry dependence risk in a veteran population with elevated substance use rates (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Obsessive-compulsive disorder responds to SSRIs at doses higher than those used for depression and requires longer trials before non-response is declared. The AU recommendation is to titrate to the maximum tolerated dose (fluoxetine up to 80 mg, sertraline up to 200 mg, escitalopram up to 40 mg with ECG surveillance) and continue for at least 12 weeks at that dose before switching or augmenting. Exposure and response prevention therapy is the psychological treatment of choice and runs in parallel with pharmacotherapy. Augmentation with a low-dose antipsychotic is reserved for confirmed SSRI failure after adequate dose and duration.
key_points: OCD SSRI doses run higher than depression doses
Fluoxetine target up to 80 mg orally daily
12 weeks at maximum tolerated dose before failure declared
ERP therapy runs in parallel with SSRI
Antipsychotic augmentation only after true SSRI failure
explanation.pearls: A common OCD pitfall is switching SSRIs at 12 weeks on a sub-therapeutic dose because clinicians extrapolate from depression trials; the trial clock only starts once the OCD-target dose is reached, so a 12 week trial at 20 mg fluoxetine is a 0 week OCD trial.

options.rationale: OCD often requires SSRI doses above the standard depression range, with fluoxetine up to 80 mg the AU-recommended target, and a 12 week trial at the maximum tolerated dose is required before declaring a treatment failure (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; RANZCP OCD CPG).

Switching SSRIs before a full 12 week trial at maximum tolerated dose is premature; OCD needs both higher doses and longer trials than depression before an SSRI is deemed to have failed (Source: RANZCP OCD CPG).

Antipsychotic augmentation is reserved for SSRI non-response after full-dose full-duration trial, particularly for OCD with tic-related features; augmentation before dose optimisation is not first-line (Source: RANZCP OCD CPG).

TMS for OCD is a last-line intervention reserved for treatment-resistant disease after multiple failed SSRI trials and augmentation; discontinuing pharmacotherapy before dose optimisation is not indicated (Source: RANZCP OCD CPG).

Clomipramine is effective in OCD but carries greater anticholinergic, cardiac and seizure risks than SSRIs, and is reserved for failure of two SSRIs at optimised dose and duration (Source: RANZCP OCD CPG).

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD requires DSM-5 criteria that includes onset of symptoms in the developmental period, corroborated by collateral or school reports, and pervasive dysfunction across multiple settings. First-line pharmacotherapy in the AADPA Australian guideline is a long-acting stimulant (lisdexamfetamine or extended-release methylphenidate) titrated over 4 to 6 weeks with cardiac and mental state monitoring. Non-stimulants (atomoxetine, guanfacine in paediatrics, clonidine) are second-line for stimulant intolerance, contraindication, or when there is a concurrent substance use disorder. Contraindications to stimulants include untreated hypertension, arrhythmia, structural heart disease, glaucoma, and current stimulant misuse.
key_points: Long-acting stimulant is first-line for adult ADHD
Lisdexamfetamine 30 mg or methylphenidate XR standard starts
Atomoxetine is second-line for stimulant intolerance
Cardiac screen with pulse, BP, and personal or family history before starting
Review at 4 weeks then titrate to symptom control
explanation.pearls: Lisdexamfetamine is a prodrug requiring gut activation and gives a smoother release curve than dexamfetamine, which reduces afternoon rebound irritability and lowers diversion potential; this profile is why it is the AU authority-approved default first-choice stimulant in adult ADHD.

sources.label: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Bupropion has modest evidence for adult ADHD and is not first-line; it is reserved for stimulant failure or when a comorbid tobacco use disorder or depression steers the choice (Source: AADPA ADHD Guideline).
source_refs: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Atomoxetine is a second-line non-stimulant option reserved for stimulant intolerance, contraindication, or substance use disorder concerns; effect size is lower than stimulants (Source: AADPA ADHD Guideline).
source_refs: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Long-acting stimulants (lisdexamfetamine or extended-release methylphenidate) are first-line pharmacotherapy in adult ADHD with no substance use disorder or cardiac contraindication; lisdexamfetamine 30 mg is a standard starting dose per AU authority prescribing guidance (Source: RANZCP ADHD CPG; AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD).
source_refs: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Guanfacine is TGA-registered for paediatric ADHD only and is not first-line for adult ADHD; it is used as an adjunct in select paediatric cases with tic disorder or oppositional features (Source: AADPA ADHD Guideline).
source_refs: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Psychological therapy alone has smaller effect sizes than stimulant pharmacotherapy in adult ADHD; the AU algorithm places stimulant pharmacotherapy first with psychological therapy as an adjunct once symptom control is achieved (Source: AADPA ADHD Guideline).
source_refs: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

explanation.summary: Generalised anxiety disorder is a DSM-5 diagnosis when excessive worry that is difficult to control persists for at least 6 months and is accompanied by at least 3 of muscle tension, restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, and sleep disturbance. AU guidelines recommend CBT as first-line for moderate GAD given comparable acute efficacy to pharmacotherapy and greater durability of gains after treatment. SSRIs (escitalopram, sertraline) or SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine) are first-line pharmacotherapy when CBT is unavailable, refused, or insufficient. Benzodiazepines are reserved for short-term bridging, and pregabalin is second-line.
key_points: CBT is first-line for moderate GAD
SSRIs and SNRIs are first-line pharmacotherapy when CBT unavailable
Benzodiazepines are short-term bridging only
Pregabalin is second-line
GAD-7 of 15 or above indicates severe anxiety
explanation.pearls: CBT gains in GAD are more durable than SSRI gains once treatment ends: 12 month post-treatment remission rates are around 60 percent for CBT versus 40 percent for SSRI-only, which is why the AU algorithm favours the psychological arm even in patients willing to take medication.

options.rationale: Regular benzodiazepine use in GAD carries dependence risk, blunts cognitive engagement in therapy, and is not first-line; short courses can bridge acute distress but not as an initial monotherapy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

AU and international guidelines recommend CBT as first-line for adult GAD given its effect size comparable to SSRIs and superior durability of gains after treatment ends; pharmacotherapy is added if CBT is unavailable, refused, or gives partial response (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; RANZCP Generalised Anxiety CPG).

Pregabalin is second-line for GAD with dependence potential and PBS restrictions in AU; it is reserved for SSRI or SNRI failure or intolerance rather than initial monotherapy (Source: RANZCP Generalised Anxiety CPG).

Second-generation antipsychotic monotherapy for GAD is not first-line and carries metabolic and sedation risks not justified before evidence-based first-line options are tried (Source: RANZCP Generalised Anxiety CPG).

Watchful waiting is only appropriate for mild anxiety with recent onset and mild functional impact; this patient has 14 months of symptoms, a GAD-7 of 16, and significant impairment (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Chronic insomnia disorder is a DSM-5 diagnosis when dissatisfaction with sleep quality or quantity persists at least 3 nights per week for at least 3 months with daytime consequences. AU and international guidelines place CBT for insomnia (CBT-I) as first-line treatment for adults of all ages, delivered over 6 to 8 sessions covering sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive restructuring, and sleep hygiene. Pharmacological options are second-line and in older adults carry an especially unfavourable balance because of fall, fracture, and cognitive impairment risk. Prolonged-release melatonin has modest evidence in over-55s; benzodiazepine and Z-drug hypnotics are Beers-listed as generally avoid in older adults.
key_points: CBT-I is first-line for chronic insomnia at any age
Sessions cover sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive work
Benzodiazepines and Z-drugs are Beers-listed avoid in older adults
Prolonged-release melatonin is second-line in over-55s
Exclude sleep apnoea, restless legs, and depression
explanation.pearls: Sleep restriction paradoxically improves total sleep time by consolidating fragmented sleep: an older adult sleeping 4.5 hours across 8 hours in bed is prescribed a 5 hour time-in-bed window that shifts homeostatic sleep drive back to their favour, with the window widened only as sleep efficiency exceeds 85 percent.

options.rationale: CBT for insomnia (CBT-I) is first-line for chronic insomnia in adults of any age, has larger durable effect sizes than pharmacotherapy, and specifically avoids the fall, cognition, and dependence risks that make hypnotic use hazardous in older adults (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Sleep Health Foundation Australia).

Benzodiazepine hypnotics in older adults increase falls, hip fracture, and cognitive impairment; ongoing use is not first-line and violates the Beers Criteria age-related deprescribing recommendations (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Non-benzodiazepine Z-drugs carry the same falls and cognitive risks as benzodiazepines in older adults and are not first-line for chronic insomnia when CBT-I is available (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Mirtazapine is not first-line for insomnia in the absence of a mood disorder; it carries weight gain, dry mouth, and daytime somnolence, and is off-label for primary insomnia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Prolonged-release melatonin is a reasonable pharmacological option in adults over 55 with primary insomnia but is second-line to CBT-I when CBT-I is available; effect size is modest (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Benign ethnic neutropenia is a genetically determined lower baseline neutrophil count seen in around 25 to 50 percent of people of African, Middle Eastern, and West Indian ancestry, associated with the Duffy-null (DARC) phenotype. It reflects reduced peripheral neutrophil pool with preserved marrow reserve and no increased infection risk. The Australian Clozapine Patient Monitoring Service maintains a specific BEN pathway with lower amber (1.0 x10^9/L) and red (0.5 x10^9/L) thresholds, activated after formal haematology confirmation. Rechallenge is appropriate when a prior discontinuation was on standard thresholds but the neutropenia is attributable to BEN and treatment resistance to two adequate non-clozapine trials is established.
key_points: BEN affects 25 to 50 percent of African-ancestry individuals
Duffy-null phenotype with reduced peripheral neutrophil pool
CPMS BEN pathway: amber 1.0, red 0.5 x10^9/L
Rechallenge appropriate after haematology confirmation of BEN
Preserved marrow reserve with no increased infection risk
explanation.pearls: The Duffy-null phenotype confers relative resistance to Plasmodium vivax malaria, which is the selective pressure driving its high prevalence in West African populations; the associated neutropenia is a benign incidental phenotype, not a haematological pathology, and the CPMS BEN pathway exists so that this evolutionary quirk does not deny effective psychiatric treatment.

options.rationale: Permanent ineligibility applies to a red result of true drug-induced neutropenia, not to a haematologist-confirmed BEN diagnosis; excluding rechallenge denies effective therapy for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (Source: Clozapine Patient Monitoring Service Protocol).

Lithium can raise the neutrophil count but does not address the underlying treatment resistance and is not a substitute for clozapine in genuine treatment-resistant schizophrenia (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic CPG).

Antipsychotic polypharmacy carries higher metabolic and extrapyramidal burden without evidence of superiority to clozapine monotherapy in treatment resistance; it is not a substitute for clozapine when BEN pathway is available (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic CPG).

ECT is an adjunct for clozapine-augmentation in schizophrenia, not a first-choice monotherapy when clozapine has not yet had an adequate trial under an appropriate monitoring pathway (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic CPG).

Australian CPMS has a specific BEN pathway with a lower ANC threshold (1.0 x10^9/L amber, 0.5 x10^9/L red) confirmed by haematology; rechallenge is standard when prior neutropenia is attributable to BEN and treatment resistance is established (Source: Clozapine Patient Monitoring Service Protocol; RANZCP Antipsychotic CPG).

explanation.summary: Treatment-resistant depression is conventionally defined as failure to respond to two adequate trials of antidepressants from different classes at optimal dose and duration. AU RANZCP guidelines place lithium augmentation and second-generation antipsychotic augmentation (aripiprazole, quetiapine XR, olanzapine) at the top of the third-line pharmacotherapy algorithm, with lithium having the largest evidence base and a number needed to treat of around 4 for response. Baseline renal function, TSH, calcium, and ECG are checked before initiation and a 12 hour trough level is drawn 5 to 7 days after each dose change targeting 0.4 to 0.8 mmol/L for augmentation. ECT is reserved for further failure or when acute severity demands rapid response.
key_points: Treatment-resistant depression: failure of 2 adequate trials from different classes
Lithium augmentation is the most evidence-supported strategy
Target lithium level 0.4 to 0.8 mmol/L for augmentation
Aripiprazole, quetiapine XR are alternative augmenting agents
ECT reserved for further failure or severe presentations
explanation.pearls: The lithium augmentation trial rule is that non-response at 4 weeks of a therapeutic level (over 0.4 mmol/L) predicts non-response overall, so serial 12 hour trough measurement matters more for augmentation adherence checks than for chasing a specific target within the lower range.

options.rationale: Deep brain stimulation is an investigational last-line intervention for depression that has failed multiple pharmacological, psychological, and neuromodulation options including ECT; it is not appropriate as third-line therapy (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorder CPG).

SSRI plus SNRI combination has additive serotonergic risk without robust efficacy evidence; it is not a recognised augmentation strategy and increases serotonin syndrome risk (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorder CPG).

A third serotonergic monotherapy trial after adequate SSRI and SNRI trials has diminishing yield; augmentation strategies have higher response rates than a further switch in this scenario (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorder CPG).

Benzodiazepine augmentation is not an evidence-based strategy for depression treatment resistance and carries dependence risk; it addresses insomnia not depressive core symptoms (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorder CPG).

Lithium augmentation is the most evidence-supported strategy for antidepressant-resistant unipolar depression with a number needed to treat of around 4 for response, and remains AU first-line augmentation ahead of antipsychotic augmentation in the RANZCP algorithm (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorder CPG; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Antipsychotic-induced weight gain and metabolic syndrome are common with olanzapine and clozapine because of histamine H1 and 5HT2C antagonism driving appetite and adiposity. When lifestyle measures fail and the psychiatric picture is stable, the most effective single intervention is switching to a metabolically favourable agent such as aripiprazole, ziprasidone, or lurasidone. Cross-titration over 4 weeks preserves psychiatric stability. Metformin adjunct produces modest weight attenuation but is less effective than switching. Bariatric surgery and orlistat are reserved for the setting where switching is not clinically feasible.
key_points: Olanzapine has the highest metabolic burden after clozapine
Switching to aripiprazole is the most effective single intervention
Cross-titration over 4 weeks preserves psychiatric stability
Metformin adjunct produces 2 to 3 kg weight attenuation
Screen fasting glucose, lipids, waist quarterly on olanzapine
explanation.pearls: The olanzapine to aripiprazole switch typically produces 5 to 8 kg of weight loss and reversal of insulin resistance markers over 6 months, an effect size several times greater than metformin augmentation, which is why AU early psychosis programs favour it once metabolic drift is established despite lifestyle intervention.

sources.label: Orygen Australian Clinical Guidelines for Early Psychosis

options.rationale: Metformin adjunct has modest weight-attenuating effect (2 to 3 kg over 3 months) but does not match the effect of an olanzapine to aripiprazole switch and does not address the underlying receptor pharmacology driving the weight gain (Source: Orygen Early Psychosis Guidelines).
source_refs: Orygen Australian Clinical Guidelines for Early Psychosis

options.rationale: Switching to a metabolically favourable antipsychotic (aripiprazole, ziprasidone or lurasidone) is the most effective single intervention for antipsychotic-induced weight gain when lifestyle measures have failed and psychiatric stability allows switching; the RANZCP EPPIC algorithm places switching ahead of pharmacological adjuncts (Source: RANZCP Psychosis CPG; Orygen Australian Clinical Guidelines for Early Psychosis).
source_refs: Orygen Australian Clinical Guidelines for Early Psychosis

options.rationale: Dose reduction of olanzapine has weak dose-response for weight gain and risks psychiatric relapse in a stable first-episode patient; a switch to a metabolically favourable agent is more effective (Source: Orygen Early Psychosis Guidelines).
source_refs: Orygen Australian Clinical Guidelines for Early Psychosis

options.rationale: Bariatric surgery is not indicated for a BMI in the mid-30s where a reversible pharmacological cause is present and untried; addressing the pharmacological driver is the correct sequence (Source: Orygen Early Psychosis Guidelines).
source_refs: Orygen Australian Clinical Guidelines for Early Psychosis

options.rationale: Orlistat has a small weight effect and gastrointestinal adverse profile that further undermines adherence; it does not match the effect of a switch to a metabolically favourable agent (Source: Orygen Early Psychosis Guidelines).
source_refs: Orygen Australian Clinical Guidelines for Early Psychosis

explanation.summary: Lithium baseline in Australia includes renal (UEC), thyroid (TFT), parathyroid (calcium and PTH), full blood count, ECG, urinalysis, and beta hCG in women of reproductive potential. Ongoing monitoring includes 12 hour post dose lithium levels every 3 months and TFT, UEC, calcium every 6 months long term. HbA1c and lipid panels drive antipsychotic metabolic monitoring rather than the lithium baseline.
key_points: Include calcium and PTH at baseline for lithium.
ECG is part of the baseline lithium panel.
Serum beta hCG matters in women of reproductive potential before initiation.
explanation.pearls: Lithium baseline in Australian practice includes calcium and PTH alongside UEC, TFT, FBC, ECG, and urinalysis, plus a serum beta hCG in women of reproductive potential.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: HLA-B*1502 is relevant to carbamazepine and phenytoin in Han Chinese and related ancestries, not to lithium (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Baseline monitoring must also cover calcium and PTH given hyperparathyroidism risk, an ECG for conduction, and a pregnancy test in women of reproductive potential; monthly lithium levels alone are insufficient early in titration (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

eTG and RANZCP recommend baseline UEC, TFTs, calcium and PTH, FBC, ECG, and urinalysis before lithium, with a serum beta hCG in women of reproductive potential because of first trimester Ebstein anomaly risk (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

A 24 hour urine collection is not required routinely; eGFR from serum creatinine is adequate at baseline and liver function tests are not part of the lithium panel (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
Metabolic monitoring is a priority for second generation antipsychotics rather than lithium; HbA1c and lipids are not the required baseline for lithium (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: First line adult ADHD pharmacotherapy in Australia is a stimulant such as lisdexamfetamine or methylphenidate. Atomoxetine is a second line non stimulant option and modafinil is not TGA approved for ADHD. Treated ADHD is notifiable to the driver licensing authority under Assessing Fitness to Drive for review of a conditional licence, irrespective of drug class.
key_points: Lisdexamfetamine or methylphenidate is first line adult ADHD pharmacotherapy.
Atomoxetine is second line non stimulant.
AFTD requires driver licence authority notification for treated ADHD.
explanation.pearls: Adult ADHD treated with pharmacotherapy is notifiable under Assessing Fitness to Drive regardless of whether the drug is a stimulant or atomoxetine.

options.rationale: Modafinil is not TGA approved for ADHD and is not first line under RANZCP guidance (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline).

Atomoxetine is a second line non stimulant option rather than first line for typical adult ADHD; licence notification is still required for treated ADHD irrespective of drug class (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline).
SSRIs are not a treatment for core ADHD inattention and hyperactivity, though they treat comorbid anxiety or depression (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline).

Australian guidance supports methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine as first line for adult ADHD; Assessing Fitness to Drive requires reporting to the licensing authority for a conditional licence review when treated ADHD is medically managed (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline; Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022).
CBT for ADHD is a valuable adjunct but delaying pharmacotherapy 12 months in a functionally impaired adult is not aligned with Australian guidance (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline).

explanation.summary: An EPDS of 16 with a positive item 10 requires immediate structured suicide risk assessment before treatment decisions. Treatment options and referral pathways follow that assessment. Weaning breastfeeding is not required to start compatible antidepressants.
key_points: EPDS 13 or above suggests probable depression.
Any positive item 10 mandates immediate risk assessment.
Sertraline is compatible with breastfeeding when treatment is warranted.
explanation.pearls: A positive EPDS item 10 answered other than 'never' triggers same day structured suicide risk assessment before pharmacotherapy or referral is decided.

sources.label: COPE Perinatal Mental Health National Guideline

options.rationale: Weaning is not required to commence psychological or pharmacological treatment; several antidepressants including sertraline are compatible with breastfeeding (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health National Guideline).
source_refs: COPE Perinatal Mental Health National Guideline

options.rationale: SSRI initiation may be appropriate later but does not replace risk assessment; medication should not be started before quantifying suicidal thoughts and safety planning (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health National Guideline).
source_refs: COPE Perinatal Mental Health National Guideline

options.rationale: An EPDS of 13 or above suggests probable depression and a positive item 10 requires immediate risk assessment, not deferred rescreening (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health National Guideline).
source_refs: COPE Perinatal Mental Health National Guideline

options.rationale: A 4 week wait without present day risk assessment leaves an at risk mother without immediate safety planning (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health National Guideline).
source_refs: COPE Perinatal Mental Health National Guideline

options.rationale: Any positive answer on EPDS item 10 mandates a face to face risk assessment with detail of frequency, intent, plan, and access to means before any prescription or referral decision (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health National Guideline).
source_refs: COPE Perinatal Mental Health National Guideline

explanation.summary: Recent antipsychotic dose escalation with hyperthermia, lead-pipe rigidity, dysautonomia, and a creatine kinase in the thousands is classic NMS. Serotonin syndrome features hyperreflexia and clonus, not lead-pipe rigidity, and requires a serotonergic precipitant. Anticholinergic delirium has mydriasis and absent bowel sounds. Cease antipsychotics and support in ICU; consider dantrolene or bromocriptine in severe or refractory cases.
key_points: NMS lead-pipe rigidity contrasts with serotonin syndrome hyperreflexia and clonus.
CK is grossly elevated in NMS.
First step is cessation of the offending drug and supportive intensive care.
explanation.pearls: Lead-pipe rigidity plus hyperthermia plus CK in the thousands after antipsychotic escalation is NMS, not serotonin syndrome; the latter demands a serotonergic precipitant and hyperreflexia.

options.rationale: The clinical picture, hyperthermia, lead-pipe rigidity, dysautonomia, and grossly elevated creatine kinase after recent antipsychotic escalation is NMS; first line is cessation of the offending drug and supportive care in a high acuity setting (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; RANZCP Antipsychotic use in schizophrenia).

Serotonin syndrome features hyperreflexia and inducible clonus rather than lead-pipe rigidity, and there is no serotonergic drug in the history to precipitate it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
Anticholinergic delirium presents with mydriasis, absent bowel sounds, and dry skin; his diaphoresis and normal pupils argue against it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
Malignant hyperthermia is triggered by volatile anaesthetic or succinylcholine, neither of which he has received (Source: ANZCA Malignant Hyperthermia Resource Kit).
Acute dystonia produces focal muscle spasm rather than generalised rigidity with hyperthermia and dysautonomia; benzatropine does not treat NMS (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Australian clozapine monitoring uses a three zone system: green (neutrophils 1.5 x10^9/L or above), amber (1.0 to 1.5 x10^9/L), and red (below 1.0 x10^9/L). In the amber zone the drug is continued but the count is repeated twice weekly until recovery. Dose reduction and colony stimulating factor are not part of the amber zone response.
key_points: Amber zone: neutrophils 1.0 to 1.5 x10^9/L; continue drug; twice weekly counts.
Red zone: neutrophils below 1.0 x10^9/L; cease clozapine and refer.
Filgrastim is reserved for red zone or specialist rechallenge.
explanation.pearls: The Australian clozapine amber zone (neutrophils 1.0 to 1.5 x10^9/L) is managed by continuing clozapine and repeating full blood count twice weekly until neutrophils recover above 1.5 x10^9/L.

sources.label: Clopine and Clozaril Australian Monitoring Protocols

options.rationale: The Australian red zone is neutrophils below 1.0 x10^9/L; 1.2 x10^9/L is amber, in which the drug is continued with intensified monitoring (Source: Clopine and Clozaril Australian Monitoring Protocols).
source_refs: Clopine and Clozaril Australian Monitoring Protocols

options.rationale: The Australian clozapine amber zone is neutrophils 1.0 to 1.5 x10^9/L, in which clozapine continues with twice weekly full blood counts until recovery above 1.5 x10^9/L (Source: Clopine and Clozaril Australian Monitoring Protocols; TGA clozapine product information).
source_refs: Clopine and Clozaril Australian Monitoring Protocols

options.rationale: Dose reduction is not part of the amber zone protocol; monitoring is intensified rather than the dose changed (Source: Clopine and Clozaril Australian Monitoring Protocols).
source_refs: Clopine and Clozaril Australian Monitoring Protocols

options.rationale: Being asymptomatic does not remove the amber zone requirement to intensify monitoring; monthly counts are inadequate at this neutrophil level (Source: Clopine and Clozaril Australian Monitoring Protocols).
source_refs: Clopine and Clozaril Australian Monitoring Protocols

options.rationale: Granulocyte colony stimulating factor is reserved for red zone counts and clozapine rechallenge decisions in specialist settings rather than routine amber zone management (Source: Clopine and Clozaril Australian Monitoring Protocols).
source_refs: Clopine and Clozaril Australian Monitoring Protocols

explanation.summary: Delusional infestation is a monosymptomatic delusional disorder in which the patient holds an unshakeable belief that they are infested by organisms, most often presenting to dermatology or general practice rather than to psychiatry. It occurs most commonly in middle aged and older women, and the presentation of collected material for analysis is so characteristic that it has its own name in the literature. The essential differential includes true infestation, which must be excluded with proper examination and scrapings, substance induced psychosis particularly with stimulants, secondary causes such as cognitive impairment, thyroid disease and vitamin B12 deficiency, and excoriation disorder in which insight is preserved. The distinction from excoriation disorder is decisive because that condition responds to behavioural therapy while delusional infestation requires an antipsychotic. Engagement is the central clinical challenge, since the patient rejects a psychiatric framing, and it is generally achieved by acknowledging the distress and the skin damage and offering treatment for those rather than by direct confrontation of the belief.
key_points: Conviction unmoved by negative testing separates delusion from health anxiety
Presenting collected specimens for analysis is close to characteristic
Exclude true infestation, stimulant use, cognitive impairment and metabolic causes
Excoriation disorder involves preserved insight and no belief in organisms
Treatment is antipsychotic medication delivered through a carefully built alliance
explanation.pearls: Note the distribution of the excoriations, because lesions confined to skin the patient can reach with sparing of the mid upper back is a strong physical sign that the lesions are self inflicted, and it can be recorded in the notes without being used to confront the patient in a way that would end the therapeutic relationship.

options.rationale: An unshakeable belief in infestation held with full conviction despite two negative scrapings, an unaffected household contact and repeated professional reassurance, in a woman with otherwise intact cognition and no other psychotic features, is a monosymptomatic delusional disorder. Bringing collected specimens for analysis is close to characteristic of this presentation. (Source: RANZCP: Psychotic disorders)

In excoriation disorder the person picks at perceived skin irregularities and recognises the behaviour as their own compulsion, without a conviction that organisms are present. Her picking is secondary to a fixed belief and would stop, in her account, if the belief were resolved. (Source: RANZCP: Psychotic disorders)

Somatic symptom disorder involves distressing symptoms with excessive thoughts and health anxiety, but the belief remains open to doubt and the patient can entertain alternative explanations. Complete conviction unmoved by negative testing places this beyond that threshold. (Source: RANZCP: Psychotic disorders)

Secondary psychosis in cognitive decline is an important consideration in this age group and would justify cognitive assessment and imaging. Fully intact orientation and memory with a single circumscribed delusion argues against it as the explanation. (Source: RANZCP: Psychotic disorders)

Stimulants classically produce tactile sensations of insects on the skin and this must always be considered, but her urine drug screen is negative and the course has run for eight months without intoxication or withdrawal. The temporal pattern does not fit substance use. (Source: RANZCP: Psychotic disorders)

explanation.summary: Seasonal pattern is a specifier applied to recurrent major depressive episodes that begin and remit at characteristic times of year, most often with winter onset, and requires that seasonal episodes substantially outnumber non seasonal ones over a lifetime. The winter pattern is typically atypical in character, with hypersomnia, increased appetite with carbohydrate craving, weight gain and leaden fatigue, in contrast to the insomnia and anorexia of melancholic depression. Prevalence rises with latitude, which in Australia makes it more relevant in Tasmania and southern Victoria than in the tropics, and relocation to a higher latitude is a recognised trigger. Bright light therapy delivered in the morning is first line, with response usually within one to two weeks and treatment continued through the season, and adapted cognitive behavioural therapy and antidepressants are the main alternatives. Screening for bipolar disorder is essential before starting any treatment, since light therapy as well as antidepressants can precipitate a switch into mania.
key_points: Winter episodes are typically atypical with hypersomnia, overeating and weight gain
Prevalence rises with latitude, so it is more relevant in Tasmania than in the tropics
Morning timing is essential; evening light does not produce the same benefit
Bright light therapy is first line with response usually within one to two weeks
Screen for bipolarity because light therapy can precipitate a manic switch
explanation.pearls: Ask about eye disease and photosensitising medication before recommending bright light therapy, because retinal pathology and drugs such as lithium, some antipsychotics and certain antibiotics increase the risk of retinal injury, and an ophthalmological opinion is warranted before starting daily high intensity exposure.

options.rationale: Adapted cognitive behavioural therapy performs comparably to light therapy over a single season and may reduce recurrence more in subsequent winters, making it a strong option. Availability of a trained therapist is limited and onset is slower, so it is generally combined with or follows light therapy rather than replacing it as the immediate step. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders)

Recurrent depressive episodes confined to winter with hypersomnia, carbohydrate craving and weight gain, remitting each spring, is a seasonal pattern for which bright light therapy is first line and typically produces response within one to two weeks. Morning timing is what advances the delayed circadian phase thought to underlie the syndrome, and the effect is lost if the light is used in the evening. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders)

Low vitamin D has been proposed as a mechanism but supplementation has not demonstrated antidepressant benefit in trials, and her level is already adequate. Correcting a value that is not deficient offers no plausible route to improvement. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders)

Antidepressants are effective in seasonal depression and are a legitimate option, particularly for severe episodes or when light therapy fails or is impractical. Continuous year round treatment for a condition that reliably remits each spring commits her to medication through months when she is well. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders)

Evening melatonin does advance circadian phase and has been studied in this condition, but the evidence base is far smaller than for morning bright light and it is not established as a first line treatment. It remains a reasonable adjunct in specialist hands. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia typically presents between the ages of forty five and sixty five with early and progressive change in personality and social conduct, including disinhibition, loss of empathy, apathy, compulsive and ritualistic behaviours, and hyperorality with a marked preference for sweet foods. Memory and orientation are relatively preserved early, so bedside cognitive screens are frequently normal and provide false reassurance, while executive deficits such as reduced verbal fluency and impaired set shifting are apparent on more detailed testing. Absent insight is close to universal and means the history must come from family. New criminal behaviour in middle age, particularly theft and socially inappropriate conduct in a person with no previous history, is a recognised presentation and carries substantial forensic consequences if the diagnosis is missed. Assessment requires structural and often functional neuroimaging, formal neuropsychological testing and specialist referral, with genetic counselling considered because a significant proportion of cases are familial.
key_points: Onset is typically between forty five and sixty five with personality change preceding memory loss
A normal bedside cognitive screen is expected and is not reassuring
Reduced verbal fluency and impaired set shifting reveal the executive deficit
Absent insight means collateral history from family is essential
New offending in middle age without prior history warrants cognitive assessment
explanation.pearls: Ask the family specifically about a new sweet tooth and about rigid daily routines, because hyperorality with carbohydrate preference and compulsive ritualistic behaviour are among the most discriminating early features and are almost never volunteered as medical symptoms, being reported instead as the person simply having become difficult.

options.rationale: Mania is an important differential for late onset disinhibition but runs an episodic course with elevated or irritable mood and reduced need for sleep, none of which are present. A steady two year decline without mood elevation does not fit. (Source: RANZCP: Dementia)

A report framing the offence as situational without investigating the underlying cause would mislead the court and deny him a diagnosis with major implications. The forensic opinion should follow the clinical assessment rather than precede it. (Source: RANZCP: Dementia)

Progressive disinhibition, loss of empathy, dietary change with carbohydrate craving, compulsive rituals and absent insight in late middle age, with preserved memory and orientation but impaired fluency and set shifting, is the behavioural variant frontotemporal syndrome. Structural and functional imaging with formal neuropsychological testing is what establishes it, and a normal bedside screen is expected and must not be taken as reassurance. (Source: RANZCP: Dementia)

Kleptomania involves rising tension before the theft and relief afterwards, with items that are not needed and a person who recognises the behaviour as wrong. He took what he wanted openly and without concern, and the theft sits within a broader two year change in personality. (Source: RANZCP: Dementia)

Late onset depression is a genuine mimic and often coexists, but he describes no low mood and his presentation is disinhibited and facetious rather than withdrawn. Serotonergic agents may help specific behaviours later but do not substitute for making the diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP: Dementia)

explanation.summary: Vascular depression describes late onset depression occurring with significant cerebrovascular disease, characterised clinically by psychomotor slowing, apathy, prominent executive dysfunction and comparatively little guilt or self reproach. The imaging correlate is confluent deep and periventricular white matter hyperintensity with lacunes, reflecting disruption of frontostriatal circuits, and this burden predicts poorer and slower response to antidepressant monotherapy as well as higher relapse rates. Management is therefore broader than sequential drug switching and includes aggressive secondary prevention with blood pressure, glycaemic and lipid control, since progression of white matter disease worsens both mood and cognition. Psychological approaches that compensate directly for impaired initiation and planning, such as behavioural activation and problem solving therapy, have specific evidence in executive dysfunction and outperform insight oriented approaches. Electroconvulsive therapy and pharmacological augmentation remain available for those who do not respond to this combined approach.
key_points: Apathy and slowing with little guilt characterise the vascular depression phenotype
Confluent white matter change predicts poor antidepressant monotherapy response
Executive deficits with preserved recognition memory point to frontostriatal disruption
Vascular risk factor control is part of psychiatric management, not separate from it
Behavioural activation and problem solving therapy target the initiation deficit directly
explanation.pearls: Treat blood pressure of 158/92 mmHg in this man as a psychiatric intervention rather than a matter for his general practitioner alone, because progression of the white matter burden is what drives both the persistence of the mood disorder and the conversion to vascular cognitive impairment over the following years.

options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors are licensed for Alzheimer disease and dementia with Lewy bodies and have not shown benefit in pure vascular cognitive impairment. His memory is relatively preserved and the deficit is executive, so the drug target does not match. (Source: RANZCP: Dementia)

Electroconvulsive therapy is effective in older people and is the right answer for severe, psychotic, catatonic or life threatening depression, and it remains an option later. Proceeding to it before the vascular contribution and the behavioural deficit have been addressed skips reversible ground. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders)

Antipsychotic augmentation is an evidence-based strategy in treatment resistant depression including in older adults, but it carries movement, metabolic and cerebrovascular risks in this population. It is a reasonable later step once vascular optimisation and behavioural treatment are in place. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Late onset depression with executive slowing, poor antidepressant response and confluent white matter disease is a vascular depression, in which cerebrovascular burden both contributes to the syndrome and predicts continued poor response to monotherapy escalation. Aggressive treatment of blood pressure, glycaemia and lipids addresses the substrate while a structured behavioural activation or problem solving program compensates directly for the initiation deficit. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders)

Tricyclics remain effective in severe depression and levels can be monitored, but anticholinergic burden, orthostatic hypotension and falls make them a poor choice in a 74-year-old with cerebrovascular disease. A third sequential monotherapy also ignores what the imaging and cognitive profile are indicating. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Delayed sleep wake phase disorder is the commonest circadian rhythm disorder of adolescence and is frequently misdiagnosed as depression or school refusal, because the daytime consequences of chronic sleep restriction closely resemble a depressive syndrome. The discriminating feature is that sleep is normal in duration, quality and refreshment when the person is free to choose their own timing, so wellbeing during holidays with an unchanged late schedule effectively excludes a primary mood disorder. A sleep diary with actigraphy over at least a week documents the pattern and is the practical diagnostic tool.
