Twelve hours of observation risks progression to rigidity and rhabdomyolysis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

That syndrome develops over days rather than hours, produces lead-pipe rigidity with hyporeflexia, and requires exposure to a dopamine antagonist which he has never had. Bromocriptine is the wrong mechanism for this presentation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

Lower limb predominant hyperreflexia with spontaneous and ocular clonus developing over hours after a second serotonergic drug is serotonin toxicity, and removal of both agents with benzodiazepine sedation is the treatment. Cyproheptadine is a serotonin antagonist reserved for moderate cases that do not settle. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

Sepsis does not cause clonus, ocular clonus or a lower limb reflex gradient, and his wound is clean with a barely raised white cell count. Cultures are reasonable but continuing both serotonergic drugs allows the toxicity to progress. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

Dantrolene treats the sustained muscle contraction of malignant hyperthermia and is used in severe neuroleptic malignant syndrome, neither of which produces clonus or hyperreflexia. It does not address serotonin receptor overstimulation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

explanation.summary: Prolonged grief disorder entered formal diagnostic classification to describe a minority of bereaved people whose grief does not attenuate and remains disabling long after the loss. The adult duration criterion is at least 12 months from the death, with the core features being persistent intense yearning or preoccupation with the deceased alongside identity disruption, disbelief, avoidance of reminders, emotional numbness, a sense of meaninglessness and difficulty re-engaging with life. The distinction from major depression matters because the sadness in grief is focused on the lost person and comes in waves triggered by reminders, while depressive mood is pervasive and accompanied by global worthlessness and anhedonia. Treatment is psychological first, with grief focused cognitive behavioural approaches producing the largest effects, and medication reserved for comorbid depression or anxiety.
key_points: The adult duration criterion for prolonged grief disorder is at least 12 months after the death
Core features are intense yearning or preoccupation with identity disruption and avoidance
Grief sadness is focused on the deceased and comes in waves; depressive mood is pervasive
Grief focused psychotherapy outperforms antidepressants for core grief symptoms
Treat comorbid major depression or post-traumatic stress disorder on their own merits
explanation.pearls: The duration criterion is 12 months in adults but only 6 months in children and adolescents, so a bereaved teenager with disabling grief at 8 months meets the diagnosis while an adult with the same picture at the same interval does not yet.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Grief that remains this intense and disabling beyond 12 months has crossed from an expected adaptation into a recognised disorder with its own treatment. Normalising it withholds an effective therapy and implies that continued suffering is simply to be endured. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Her symptoms have persisted beyond 12 months with identity disruption, avoidance of reminders and intense daily yearning causing functional impairment, which meets the threshold for prolonged grief disorder. Grief focused psychotherapy has the strongest evidence base for this condition and outperforms antidepressant monotherapy. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Peer support groups help many bereaved people and are a valuable adjunct, but they are not designed to treat a diagnosed disorder and have not shown efficacy for persistent grief of this severity. Offering only a group leaves the disorder untreated for another year. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Benzodiazepines suppress the emotional processing that grief work depends on and carry dependence risk with prolonged use in this age group. Evidence suggests early benzodiazepine use after bereavement does not reduce and may prolong grief symptoms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

She lacks the pervasive anhedonia, guilt, worthlessness and neurovegetative features that would indicate a depressive episode, and antidepressants have not been shown to reduce core grief symptoms. Medication has a place when major depression coexists, which it does not here. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia are best understood as communication rather than as symptoms requiring suppression, and the first task is always to look for an unmet need. Pain, constipation, urinary retention, infection, delirium, sensory impairment, boredom, fear and an over-stimulating environment account for a large share of behaviour that would otherwise be medicated. Pain is particularly easy to miss because the standard question cannot be answered, so assessment relies on observational tools and on the pattern of when the behaviour occurs, with resistance confined to handling being highly suggestive. Randomised evidence supports a stepwise protocol beginning with regular paracetamol, and antipsychotics carry a well-quantified increase in cerebrovascular events and mortality that makes them a last rather than a first resort.
key_points: Behaviour in dementia is communication; look for an unmet need before prescribing
Pain, constipation, retention, infection and delirium are the commonest reversible drivers
Behaviour confined to personal care or movement strongly suggests pain
A stepwise trial of regular paracetamol reduces agitation in randomised trials
Antipsychotics increase stroke and mortality risk in older people with dementia
explanation.pearls: When an antipsychotic is unavoidable in dementia, risperidone is the only agent with an Australian indication for persistent aggression, at a starting dose of 0.25 mg twice daily, and the approved duration is up to 12 weeks with review for withdrawal at that point.

sources.label: RANZCP: Antipsychotics in Dementia Position Statement

options.rationale: Antipsychotics are considered only after reversible causes and non-pharmacological approaches have failed, and they raise the risk of stroke and death in older people with dementia. Starting one before treating obvious untreated pain exposes her to that risk for a problem that has a safer remedy. (Source: RANZCP: Antipsychotics in Dementia Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Antipsychotics in Dementia Position Statement

options.rationale: Depression can present as agitation in dementia and citalopram has some evidence in this setting, but the behaviour here is tightly bound to physical handling rather than pervasive across the day. The pattern points to a nociceptive trigger rather than a mood disturbance. (Source: RACGP: Aged Care Clinical Guide)

A rotator cuff tear is plausible and imaging might confirm it, but scanning a woman with advanced dementia requires her to lie still for a prolonged period and rarely changes management at this stage. An empirical analgesic trial tests the same hypothesis without the burden. (Source: RACGP: Aged Care Clinical Guide)

Pre-medicating with a benzodiazepine sedates her through a painful experience rather than removing the pain, and increases falls, confusion and aspiration risk. As-required sedation before care is a form of chemical restraint when a treatable cause has not been addressed. (Source: RANZCP: Antipsychotics in Dementia Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Antipsychotics in Dementia Position Statement

options.rationale: Untreated pain is among the commonest reversible drivers of behavioural change in advanced dementia, and a person who cannot report it communicates through resistance during the movements that hurt. A stepwise trial of regular rather than as-required simple analgesia has been shown in randomised trials to reduce agitation substantially. (Source: RACGP: Aged Care Clinical Guide)

explanation.summary: Stimulant medication is the most effective treatment for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults, with effect sizes that exceed most interventions in psychiatry, and the safety framework around it is built on simple repeated clinical measurement rather than on investigation. The relevant physiological effects are a small rise in heart rate and blood pressure, appetite suppression with weight loss, and sleep disruption if dosing runs late in the day. Baseline pulse, blood pressure and weight are recorded so that change can be detected, and the cardiac history is taken to identify the small group with structural or electrical disease in whom a cardiology opinion is needed first. In Australia stimulant prescribing is regulated at state and territory level with authority requirements, and driving must be discussed because untreated symptoms themselves raise crash risk while treatment reduces it.
key_points: Baseline pulse, blood pressure and weight make later monitoring interpretable
Routine electrocardiography is not required in the absence of cardiac symptoms or family red flags
Red flags include exertional syncope, palpitations, structural disease and sudden death under 40 in a relative
Neuropsychological testing cannot confirm or exclude the diagnosis
Stimulant prescribing in Australia requires state or territory authority
explanation.pearls: Treating adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder reduces motor vehicle crash risk rather than increasing it, and long-acting preparations are preferred for drivers because the wearing-off period of short-acting formulations produces a rebound window of impaired attention in the late afternoon.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Stimulants raise heart rate and blood pressure modestly in most people, so a documented baseline is what makes subsequent monitoring interpretable, alongside a structured cardiac history to identify who needs further investigation. Australian guidance treats this clinical assessment rather than routine investigation as the required baseline. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Neuropsychological testing cannot diagnose or exclude this condition, which remains a clinical diagnosis based on history, developmental course and corroborative information. It is useful for characterising a suspected specific learning disorder alongside it. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Substance use history is an important part of the assessment and influences the choice of preparation, but universal repeated urine screening is not recommended and damages the therapeutic relationship. He reports alcohol within limits and no other substance use. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Routine electrocardiography for all patients is not recommended because the yield in people without cardiac symptoms or a concerning family history is very low. It is indicated when the history reveals structural disease, exertional syncope, palpitations or premature sudden death in a relative. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Acquired heart block in a woman in her sixties is age related and does not indicate an inherited cardiomyopathy or channelopathy in her son. Echocardiography is reserved for a murmur, symptoms or a family history of cardiomyopathy or premature sudden death. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

explanation.summary: Post-traumatic stress disorder requires exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence, followed by symptoms in four clusters: intrusion, avoidance, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and alterations in arousal and reactivity, persisting beyond one month with functional impairment. Occupational exposure is explicitly included, which is why emergency service workers carry elevated rates. The treatment hierarchy is unusually clear in this condition: trauma-focused psychological therapies, principally trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing, outperform pharmacotherapy and their benefits persist better after treatment stops. Medication is the second line option or an adjunct where comorbidity demands it, and benzodiazepines are specifically discouraged because they impair the extinction learning that therapy relies on.
key_points: Trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy and eye movement desensitisation are first line
Medication is second line or reserved for comorbid depression or when therapy is unavailable
Single session debriefing is not recommended and may cause harm
Benzodiazepines impair extinction learning and should be avoided
Prazosin is an adjunct for persistent trauma related nightmares
explanation.pearls: Symptoms lasting between 3 days and 1 month after the event constitute acute stress disorder rather than post-traumatic stress disorder, and the practical significance is that around half of people with acute stress disorder do not go on to develop the chronic condition.

options.rationale: Watchful waiting is appropriate in the first month after trauma when many people recover spontaneously, but symptoms established at seven months will not remit with rest alone. Extended avoidance of work can reinforce the avoidance that maintains the disorder. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

Medication is recommended when trauma-focused therapy is declined, unavailable or ineffective, or when there is significant comorbid depression, none of which applies. Starting with a drug when therapy is accessible inverts the recommended order. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

Single session debriefing is not recommended at any stage and evidence suggests it can worsen outcomes by reactivating distress without providing the structured processing that therapy offers. It is also seven months too late to be conceived of as an early intervention. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

Australian guidelines recommend trauma-focused psychological therapy as first line for adult post-traumatic stress disorder, with larger effect sizes and better maintenance of gains after treatment ends than medication. Eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing is an equally recommended alternative within this first line group. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

Prazosin has a genuine role as an adjunct for trauma related nightmares that persist despite first line treatment, and would be considered later. Using it alone leaves the intrusions, avoidance and hyperarousal that define the disorder untreated. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

explanation.summary: People with intellectual disability have substantially higher rates of untreated physical illness and a markedly lower life expectancy than the general population, and diagnostic overshadowing is a principal driver of that gap. The term describes the error of attributing new symptoms or behaviour to the disability itself rather than investigating them as one would in anyone else. Behaviour change is the presenting complaint for conditions that would otherwise be described verbally, so the differential begins with pain from teeth, ears, joints and abdomen, and includes constipation, reflux, urinary infection, epilepsy, sensory loss and medication adverse effects. Once physical causes are excluded, a functional behavioural assessment examines environmental triggers and communicative intent, and psychiatric diagnosis and medication follow only after those two steps.
key_points: Diagnostic overshadowing means wrongly attributing new symptoms to the intellectual disability
Behaviour change is often the only available expression of pain or illness
Dental disease, otitis, constipation, reflux and musculoskeletal pain are high yield
Functional behavioural assessment follows exclusion of physical causes
Psychotropic medication is overprescribed in this population and needs regular review
explanation.pearls: Annual comprehensive health assessment for adults with intellectual disability is supported by a dedicated Medicare item in Australia and reliably uncovers unrecognised problems such as untreated hearing loss, vision impairment and chronic constipation that commonly present first as behaviour change.

sources.label: RANZCP: Intellectual Disability Mental Health Position Statement
RACGP: Health Care of People with Intellectual Disability

options.rationale: Depression does present atypically in intellectual disability, with irritability, withdrawal and loss of skills rather than a verbal account of low mood, so it remains on the differential. Treating it empirically before excluding physical illness risks a months-long trial while a dental abscess goes untreated. (Source: RANZCP: Intellectual Disability Mental Health Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Intellectual Disability Mental Health Position Statement

options.rationale: Neuroimaging is indicated if there are new neurological signs, seizures or a fall with head injury, none of which is present. Jumping to a scan skips the far higher yield examinations of the teeth, ears and abdomen that the behaviour is pointing towards. (Source: RACGP: Health Care of People with Intellectual Disability)
source_refs: RACGP: Health Care of People with Intellectual Disability

options.rationale: New behaviour of this kind in a person with limited verbal communication is most often the expression of a physical problem, with dental disease, otitis, reflux, constipation and musculoskeletal pain heading the list. Attributing it to the intellectual disability itself is diagnostic overshadowing, the best documented source of avoidable harm in this population. (Source: RANZCP: Intellectual Disability Mental Health Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Intellectual Disability Mental Health Position Statement

options.rationale: A positive behaviour support plan is a legitimate and often essential intervention, but it must be built on a functional assessment that has first excluded pain and illness. Planned ignoring of head striking driven by ear or dental pain leaves the person in pain and unheard. (Source: RANZCP: Intellectual Disability Mental Health Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Intellectual Disability Mental Health Position Statement

options.rationale: Psychotropic medication is widely overprescribed in this population for behaviour that has an untreated physical or environmental cause, and it brings metabolic, extrapyramidal and sedative harms. A psychiatric referral may be warranted later but not before physical causes are excluded. (Source: RANZCP: Intellectual Disability Mental Health Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Intellectual Disability Mental Health Position Statement

explanation.summary: Autism is diagnosed considerably later in women and girls than in men and boys, and a substantial proportion receive a psychiatric label first, most often borderline personality disorder, an eating disorder or an anxiety disorder. The reason is camouflaging, the effortful learning and rehearsal of social behaviour that masks the underlying difficulty at enormous cognitive and emotional cost, which makes the presentation diverge from the male-derived stereotype that most clinicians pattern match against. Several features help discriminate the two diagnoses: in autism the distress is triggered by sensory overload and unpredictability rather than by perceived rejection, identity is stable rather than diffuse, relationships are few but not characterised by idealisation and devaluation, and the traits are lifelong and pervasive rather than emerging in adolescence. Getting this right changes everything downstream, because the useful interventions become sensory and environmental accommodation, predictability and communication support rather than emotion regulation therapy.
key_points: Autistic women are commonly misdiagnosed with borderline personality disorder
Camouflaging masks the presentation and delays diagnosis in women and girls
Autistic distress follows sensory overload and unexpected change rather than abandonment
Identity and relationship patterns are stable in autism and unstable in borderline personality disorder
Diagnosis requires developmental history and collateral information, not a screening score
explanation.pearls: Autistic burnout, presenting as profound exhaustion, loss of previously held skills and reduced tolerance of sensory input after a period of sustained camouflaging, is frequently mistaken for a depressive episode, and it responds to reduced demand and sensory recovery rather than to antidepressants.

sources.label: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia
RANZCP: Personality Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: The restructure is the precipitant that brought her back but not the reason two evidence-based treatment courses have failed over eight years. Treating only the trigger leaves the diagnostic question and the sensory environment that generates her distress unaddressed. (Source: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia)
source_refs: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia

options.rationale: Her distress is triggered by change and sensory input rather than by abandonment, her relationships and identity are stable, and the developmental history describes restricted interests and learned social camouflaging. Autistic women are frequently misdiagnosed with borderline personality disorder, and a formal reassessment reframes both the diagnosis and what support will actually help. (Source: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia)
source_refs: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia

options.rationale: Two adequate courses without benefit is evidence that the formulation rather than the therapist is wrong, and repeating a treatment aimed at abandonment sensitivity and identity disturbance will not address sensory and change intolerance. Some skills modules may still help, but as part of a revised formulation. (Source: RANZCP: Personality Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Personality Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy has a limited evidence base in borderline personality disorder and is recommended only for comorbid conditions or short term crisis management. Adding a drug to an unexamined diagnosis treats a symptom label rather than the underlying problem. (Source: RANZCP: Personality Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Personality Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Screening instruments have a useful role in deciding who to refer but cannot establish the diagnosis, which requires developmental history, collateral information and direct observation across domains. (Source: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia)
source_refs: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia

explanation.summary: Dementia with Lewy bodies is the second commonest neurodegenerative dementia and is defined by a core clinical triad of fluctuating cognition with pronounced variation in attention and alertness, recurrent well formed visual hallucinations, and spontaneous parkinsonism, with rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder as a fourth core feature that often precedes the others by years. The cognitive profile is distinguishable from Alzheimer disease by early attentional, executive and visuospatial impairment with relative preservation of memory. Autonomic dysfunction, particularly orthostatic hypotension, contributes heavily to the falls burden. The defining management constraint is neuroleptic sensitivity, a severe and sometimes fatal reaction to dopamine antagonists, which means that any antipsychotic is a last resort and that quetiapine or clozapine are the only agents contemplated when one is unavoidable.
key_points: Core features are fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and dream enactment
Cholinesterase inhibitors improve cognition and reduce hallucinations in this dementia
Neuroleptic sensitivity affects up to half of patients and can be fatal
Risperidone and haloperidol are both hazardous; quetiapine or clozapine only if unavoidable
Orthostatic hypotension is common and drives falls
explanation.pearls: The one year rule separates dementia with Lewy bodies from Parkinson disease dementia: cognitive decline beginning before or within 12 months of the onset of parkinsonism indicates the former, while dementia arising years after established Parkinson disease indicates the latter, though the treatment constraints are identical.

sources.label: RANZCP: Assessment and Management of Dementia

options.rationale: Fluctuating cognition, well formed visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and a history of dream enactment describe dementia with Lewy bodies, in which the cholinergic deficit is more profound than in Alzheimer disease. Cholinesterase inhibitors improve both cognition and the visual hallucinations in this condition and avoid the dopamine blockade that these patients tolerate so poorly. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and Management of Dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and Management of Dementia

options.rationale: Severe neuroleptic sensitivity reactions occur in up to half of these patients and can produce irreversible parkinsonism, autonomic instability and death, with high potency typical agents carrying the greatest risk. This is the single most dangerous prescription in this diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and Management of Dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and Management of Dementia

options.rationale: Levodopa is used cautiously for disabling parkinsonism in this condition but characteristically worsens hallucinations by increasing dopaminergic tone. Using it to treat the hallucinations targets the right patient with exactly the wrong direction of effect. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and Management of Dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and Management of Dementia

options.rationale: Clonazepam and melatonin are both used for rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder, but a benzodiazepine in a man with postural hypotension and two recent falls compounds his greatest immediate risk. It also does nothing for daytime visual hallucinations. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Risperidone has meaningful dopamine D2 blockade at therapeutic doses and carries the same neuroleptic sensitivity risk as a typical agent in this population. What makes an antipsychotic safer here is the degree of D2 antagonism rather than whether the drug is labelled atypical. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and Management of Dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and Management of Dementia

explanation.summary: Treatment resistant depression is conventionally defined as failure to respond to two or more adequate trials of antidepressants of adequate dose and duration in the current episode, and before escalating it is essential to confirm the diagnosis, adherence, dose adequacy and the absence of a bipolar diathesis or an unrecognised medical or substance contributor. Esketamine acts through N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antagonism and downstream glutamatergic and synaptogenic effects rather than through monoamine reuptake, which is why it can produce benefit within hours to days where conventional agents take weeks. That speed comes with a distinctive acute adverse effect profile of dissociation, sedation, dizziness, nausea and transient blood pressure elevation, all of which cluster in the first 90 minutes. The resulting requirement for supervised administration and post-dose observation shapes the entire service model, and the alternatives at this point in the treatment ladder remain electroconvulsive therapy, augmentation strategies and transcranial magnetic stimulation.
key_points: Esketamine is self administered under direct supervision in a healthcare setting, never at home
Blood pressure is measured before dosing and after, with observation for at least two hours
It is used in combination with an oral antidepressant rather than as monotherapy
Patients must not drive until the day after the dose following restful sleep
Dissociation, sedation and transient hypertension peak within the first 40 minutes
explanation.pearls: A history of aneurysmal vascular disease, arteriovenous malformation or intracerebral haemorrhage is a contraindication to esketamine because the transient blood pressure rise of around 10 to 15 mmHg systolic peaks at roughly 40 minutes after dosing and could precipitate rupture.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Esketamine is licensed for use in combination with an oral antidepressant rather than as monotherapy, and the pivotal trials were conducted with that combination. Stopping the antidepressant removes part of the treatment and risks discontinuation symptoms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Vascular imaging is not a routine requirement, and aneurysmal or arteriovenous disease is excluded by history and examination in the absence of red flags. She has already been screened clinically and found to have none. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Home administration is not permitted for this medicine in Australia precisely because dissociation and haemodynamic change occur predictably in the observation window. A telephone call cannot substitute for direct observation and blood pressure measurement. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Esketamine causes dissociation, sedation and a transient blood pressure rise peaking in the first 40 minutes, so every dose is self administered under direct supervision with blood pressure measured before and after and observation continuing for at least two hours until the patient is clinically stable. She must also be told not to drive until the following day after restful sleep. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Inpatient admission is required only when the clinical situation demands it, such as high suicide risk or significant comorbidity, and routine induction is delivered in a supervised outpatient clinic. Hospitalising every patient would be disproportionate and would limit access. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Trauma that is prolonged, repeated and inflicted in childhood by a caregiver produces a presentation that extends beyond the classical intrusion, avoidance and hyperarousal clusters to include difficulties with affect regulation, a persistently negative self concept and impaired relationships, described in the international classification as complex post-traumatic stress disorder. Dissociation sits at the centre of the clinical problem, ranging from depersonalisation and derealisation to amnesic gaps, and it both arises as a protective response and interferes with the processing that therapy requires. Australian guidance therefore recommends a phased model in which stabilisation precedes memory processing, which in turn precedes reintegration, with the length of the first phase determined by the person's regulation capacity rather than by a fixed schedule. The common error runs in both directions: processing too early destabilises, while stabilising indefinitely means the trauma is never addressed.
key_points: Complex presentations add affect dysregulation, negative self concept and relational difficulty
A phased approach places stabilisation before memory processing and then reintegration
Dissociation and active self-harm are indications to extend the stabilisation phase
Trauma-focused therapies remain the goal rather than being abandoned
Indefinite stabilisation without ever processing trauma is also a treatment failure
explanation.pearls: Dissociation during a therapy session is managed with grounding through the five senses rather than by continuing to process the memory, because material encoded while the person is dissociated is not integrated and the session reinforces avoidance instead of extinction.

sources.label: RANZCP: Personality Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: This modality is first line for post-traumatic stress disorder and will very likely form part of her later treatment, but its processing phases carry the same destabilisation risk as exposure in this context. The problem is timing, since processing follows stabilisation, rather than the modality chosen. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

Medication may help comorbid depression but does not treat the trauma or the dissociation, and deferring psychological work entirely leaves her without the skills she most needs. Stabilisation is psychological treatment, not a delay before it. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

Exposure is highly effective for single incident trauma in a person with intact regulation, but starting it during active dissociation and recent overdoses risks escalating self-harm and dropout. The issue is sequencing rather than whether exposure is ever appropriate for her. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

Australian guidelines recommend a phased approach for complex presentations with prolonged repeated trauma, significant dissociation and recent self-harm, because memory processing without regulation capacity can precipitate decompensation and increase risk. Stabilisation builds the affect tolerance and grounding skills that make later trauma processing survivable and effective. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

Prolonged admission for people with chronic self-harm and complex trauma is generally counterproductive, tending to reinforce crisis presentations and erode autonomy. Brief admission has a place for acute risk, but not as the setting for a course of trauma therapy. (Source: RANZCP: Personality Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Personality Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and substance use disorders co-occur far more often than chance, and the relationship runs in both directions: impulsivity and reward sensitivity raise the likelihood of early substance use, while untreated symptoms make sustained abstinence harder. The diagnostic challenge is distinguishing the disorder from the cognitive effects of chronic stimulant use, and the evidence that settles it here is a documented childhood diagnosis with symptoms persisting through a five month abstinent period. Australian guidance supports treating both conditions concurrently rather than sequentially, since withholding treatment until abstinence is achieved commonly means never treating at all. Where stimulant use is active, a non-stimulant avoids the prescriber contributing to the problem, and stimulants can be revisited with long-acting preparations and supervised dosing once use is stable.
key_points: Treat the neurodevelopmental disorder and the substance use disorder concurrently, not sequentially
Symptoms persisting during abstinence support a primary diagnosis rather than drug effect
Non-stimulants are preferred while stimulant use is active
Atomoxetine takes six to eight weeks for full effect, unlike the immediate effect of stimulants
Long-acting formulations with supervised dosing are the safer stimulant option later
explanation.pearls: Atomoxetine carries a specific warning for hepatotoxicity, so unexplained nausea with right upper quadrant pain, dark urine or jaundice during treatment requires immediate cessation and liver function testing rather than dose reduction.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Bupropion has modest evidence in adults with this condition and is sometimes used for concurrent nicotine dependence, but it is not a recommended first line agent. It also lowers the seizure threshold, which matters in someone using stimulants heavily. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Requiring prolonged abstinence before treating an untreated neurodevelopmental disorder is a common but counterproductive stance, since impulsivity and inattention themselves undermine the capacity to stop using. Effective treatment of the disorder supports rather than competes with substance use treatment. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: A long-acting preparation with supervised dosing is the reasonable stimulant option once substance use is stable or abstinent, and it may well become appropriate for him later. Starting it while he is using several times a week places the prescriber in the position of supplying a stimulant to someone actively using one. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: A non-stimulant with no misuse or diversion potential is preferred while stimulant use is active, and atomoxetine has the best evidence base among the non-stimulants for adults with this comorbidity. Its effect builds over weeks rather than within hours, which also removes the reinforcing immediate reward that complicates stimulant use. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: An immediate release stimulant during active methamphetamine use carries the highest risk of misuse and diversion of any option, and weekly dispensing does not remove that risk. Short-acting preparations are the least suitable stimulant formulation in this setting. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndrome of motor dysregulation that occurs across mood disorders, psychotic disorders and a wide range of medical and neurological conditions, and mood disorders are in fact its commonest psychiatric context. It is systematically underdiagnosed because its features are misread as severe depression, as negativism, or as a general medical deterioration, and the specific signs that distinguish it are motor rather than affective: waxy flexibility, catalepsy, gegenhalten, posturing, mutism, negativism, stereotypy, echolalia and echopraxia. The benzodiazepine challenge occupies an unusual position as both diagnostic test and treatment, with a substantial response confirming the syndrome and guiding ongoing dosing. The reason for urgency is malignant catatonia, in which fever, autonomic instability and rigidity supervene with a mortality that approaches that of untreated neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and which requires electroconvulsive therapy without delay.
key_points: Catatonia most commonly complicates mood disorders rather than schizophrenia
Waxy flexibility, gegenhalten, mutism, negativism and echolalia are the defining motor signs
The benzodiazepine challenge is simultaneously diagnostic and therapeutic
Antipsychotics may precipitate malignant catatonia and are withheld until it resolves
Electroconvulsive therapy is definitive when the challenge fails or malignant features appear
explanation.pearls: A raised creatine kinase in a catatonic patient signals sustained isometric muscle activity and impending rhabdomyolysis, so it warrants intravenous fluids and a shift towards electroconvulsive therapy rather than a further week of benzodiazepine titration.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Non-convulsive status is a genuine differential for an unresponsive patient and electroencephalography is worth obtaining, but waxy flexibility and gegenhalten are specific motor signs that point strongly to catatonia. The benzodiazepine challenge is faster and would improve both conditions if either were present. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Dopamine antagonists can precipitate malignant catatonia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome in a patient who is already catatonic, making this the most dangerous available choice. Antipsychotics are withheld until the catatonia has resolved. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Electroconvulsive therapy is the definitive treatment for catatonia and is indicated when the benzodiazepine trial fails or when malignant features are present, and it may still be needed here. Bypassing a trial that resolves most cases within hours and requires no anaesthetic is not the proportionate first step. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Nutrition and hydration do need urgent attention, but an antidepressant takes weeks and does not treat catatonia, leaving her immobile and at risk of venous thromboembolism, pressure injury and aspiration meanwhile. Supportive care is necessary but is not the treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Waxy flexibility, gegenhalten, mutism, immobility and echolalia constitute catatonia rather than psychomotor retardation, and a benzodiazepine challenge is both the diagnostic test and the start of treatment, with a marked response within 10 to 30 minutes in most cases. Recognising it matters because catatonia can progress to the malignant form with autonomic instability, rhabdomyolysis and death. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Delirium is an acute disturbance of attention and awareness that develops over hours to days, fluctuates across the day and is caused by an underlying medical condition, medication or substance. Dementia is the single strongest predisposing factor, which means the two coexist constantly, and delirium superimposed on dementia is both the commonest and the most frequently missed presentation because the baseline is already abnormal. Time course and attention separate them: dementia declines over months with preserved alertness, while delirium changes over days with impaired attention and a fluctuating conscious level. In a frail older person the precipitant is usually multiple and mundane, with urinary retention, constipation, infection, dehydration, pain and newly added medication accounting for most cases, and in Australia the Delirium Clinical Care Standard makes identifying and treating those causes the central obligation rather than managing the behaviour it produces.
key_points: Delirium is defined by acute onset, fluctuation, inattention and altered consciousness
Dementia is the strongest predisposing factor, so a changed baseline is the key history
Common precipitants are retention, constipation, infection, dehydration, pain and new drugs
Antipsychotics do not shorten delirium and are reserved for severe distress or danger
Benzodiazepines worsen delirium except in alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal
explanation.pearls: Hypoactive delirium is more common than the hyperactive form and carries a worse prognosis, yet it generates no staff request for review, which is why a brief attention test such as reciting the months of the year backwards should be applied to any older person whose alertness has changed rather than only to those who are agitated.

sources.label: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard

options.rationale: Benzodiazepines worsen and prolong delirium in older people other than in alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, and they increase falls in a man already trying to climb over bed rails. Delaying investigation overnight also delays treatment of the retention and constipation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Antipsychotics do not shorten delirium or improve outcomes and are reserved for severe distress or danger when non-pharmacological measures have failed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Charting a regular dose first treats the staff's request rather than the patient's illness. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard

options.rationale: Acute onset with fluctuating course, inattention and altered consciousness on a dementia background defines delirium, and three precipitants are already visible in urinary retention, constipation and newly started opioid. Treating the causes resolves the delirium, whereas sedating him leaves every cause untouched and adds to the confusion. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard

options.rationale: Dementia progresses over months and does not produce a two day change in attention and alertness, and this is the misattribution that makes delirium superimposed on dementia the most frequently missed presentation in aged care. Visual hallucinations that are new to a man with vascular dementia are a further pointer away from simple progression. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard

options.rationale: A fall four days ago in an older man does make subdural haemorrhage worth considering, and imaging should follow if he does not improve as the identified precipitants are corrected. Sending him to hospital for a scan before draining a palpable bladder addresses the least likely cause first. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard

explanation.summary: Tic disorders affect around 1 per cent of school-aged children and typically begin between 5 and 7 years, peak in severity around 10 to 12 years, and improve substantially through adolescence. The decision to treat rests on functional impairment rather than on tic frequency, since many children with visible tics need nothing more than education for the family and the school. Behavioural therapy is first line worldwide, and Australian practice follows that order, with medication added when therapy is unavailable or insufficient. Coexisting conditions drive much of the disability: attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and obsessive compulsive disorder are each present in a substantial minority and should be actively screened for. Where medication is needed, alpha-2 agonists such as clonidine and antipsychotics such as aripiprazole are the main options, chosen partly by which comorbidity is present.
key_points: Treat on functional impairment, not on tic count or visibility
Comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics is first line, using awareness training and a competing response
Screen for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and obsessive compulsive disorder, which drive much of the impairment
Clonidine and aripiprazole are the main pharmacological options when therapy is insufficient or unavailable
Tics usually peak around 10 to 12 years and improve substantially by late adolescence
explanation.pearls: The premonitory urge, an uncomfortable build-up relieved by performing the tic, is what separates tics from other movement disorders and is the specific target of the competing response in behavioural therapy.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for tic disorders

options.rationale: Clonidine is a reasonable pharmacological choice, particularly where attention deficit hyperactivity disorder coexists, but medication sits behind behavioural therapy in the treatment sequence for tics of this severity. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for tic disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for tic disorders

options.rationale: Aripiprazole has the best evidence among antipsychotics for tic reduction, but exposing a 9-year-old to metabolic and extrapyramidal risk before trying behavioural therapy inverts the recommended order. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for tic disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for tic disorders

options.rationale: Risperidone reduces tics but carries the highest prolactin elevation and weight gain burden of the commonly used agents in children, so it is a later choice rather than a first line one. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for tic disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for tic disorders

options.rationale: Watchful waiting is right for tics that cause no impairment, but he is being mimicked at school and is now avoiding it, which is functional impairment and an indication to treat. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for tic disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for tic disorders

options.rationale: Comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics combines awareness training, a competing response and functional strategies, and it has the strongest evidence base of any first line treatment with none of the pharmacological burden. The suppressibility and build-up of urge he describes are exactly the premonitory phenomena the therapy works on. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for tic disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for tic disorders

explanation.summary: Body dysmorphic disorder is a preoccupation with one or more perceived defects in appearance that are not observable or appear slight to others, accompanied by repetitive behaviours such as mirror checking, grooming, comparing or seeking reassurance. It sits in the obsessive compulsive and related disorders group rather than with the psychotic disorders, and around a third of patients hold their beliefs with delusional conviction without that changing the treatment. Prevalence is far higher in cosmetic surgery and dermatology clinics than in the general population, and outcomes after cosmetic procedures are poor. Suicidal ideation and attempts are common and should be asked about directly at every review. Treatment is cognitive behavioural therapy adapted for the disorder, with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor at higher than usual doses for more severe presentations.
key_points: Classified with obsessive compulsive and related disorders, not with psychotic illness, even when insight is absent
Cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention is first line treatment
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors need higher doses and a 12-week trial compared with depression
Cosmetic procedures rarely help and commonly shift the preoccupation elsewhere
Screen actively for suicidal ideation, which is frequent in this disorder
explanation.pearls: Muscle dysmorphia is the body dysmorphic disorder variant seen mostly in young men who believe they are insufficiently muscular, and it should prompt direct questioning about anabolic steroid use.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for body dysmorphic disorder

options.rationale: Cosmetic surgery in this setting usually leaves the preoccupation unchanged or transfers it to another body part, and dissatisfaction after operating is the rule rather than the exception. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for body dysmorphic disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for body dysmorphic disorder

options.rationale: Antipsychotic monotherapy is not effective for body dysmorphic disorder even when insight is poor, and the poor insight specifier does not convert the condition into a psychotic illness. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for body dysmorphic disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for body dysmorphic disorder

options.rationale: Benzodiazepines carry dependence risk in a young adult and treat only the surface distress, while allowing the avoidance and checking cycle that maintains the disorder to continue. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Cognitive behavioural therapy tailored to body dysmorphic disorder, targeting mirror checking, comparison and avoidance through exposure and response prevention, is first line treatment and works even where insight is poor. A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor is added where symptoms are severe or therapy alone is insufficient, typically at doses higher than those used for depression. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for body dysmorphic disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for body dysmorphic disorder

options.rationale: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors do help, but body dysmorphic disorder typically needs doses at the upper end of the range and a longer trial of 12 weeks, and medication alone is a weaker starting point than therapy. The distinguishing point from depression treatment is the dose and duration required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Hoarding disorder is a distinct diagnosis characterised by persistent difficulty discarding possessions because of a perceived need to save them, with accumulation that congests living areas and compromises their intended use. It must be separated from the accumulation seen in obsessive compulsive disorder, where saving is driven by contamination or harm obsessions, and from the neglect of squalor associated with frontal dementia, psychosis or severe depression, which is why cognitive screening and mental state examination matter at the outset. Insight is often poor and referral usually comes from a third party such as a family member, council or fire service rather than the person. Risk to the individual and to neighbours, from fire, falls and structural load, requires a coordinated response involving housing, council and fire services alongside clinical care. Forced clearance is the single most common and most counterproductive intervention, so a harm reduction approach with graded, negotiated clearance is preferred.
key_points: Hoarding disorder is a distinct diagnosis and is not simply a form of obsessive compulsive disorder
Exclude dementia, psychosis and severe depression with cognitive testing and mental state examination
Cognitive behavioural therapy with a home based sorting component is the treatment with the best evidence
Forced clearance causes distress, ruptures relationships and is followed by re-accumulation
Coordinate with council, housing and fire services for risk reduction while therapy proceeds
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically whether the stove, bath, bed and exits are usable; loss of function of these four is a better measure of severity and risk than any estimate of how much has been accumulated.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for hoarding disorder

options.rationale: She has intact cognition, manages her own affairs and has expressed no wish to move, so placement would be a disproportionate response that overrides her autonomy rather than treating a treatable disorder. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for hoarding disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for hoarding disorder

options.rationale: Hoarding disorder responds best to a cognitive behavioural approach that addresses beliefs about possessions, decision making and sorting skills, and that is delivered at least partly in the home where the behaviour occurs. Engagement is the central therapeutic task, and it is destroyed by imposed clearance, so building the working alliance first is what makes subsequent risk reduction possible. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for hoarding disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for hoarding disorder

options.rationale: Forced clearance produces severe distress, frequently ruptures family relationships and is followed by re-accumulation within months because the underlying beliefs and decision making difficulties are untouched. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for hoarding disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for hoarding disorder

options.rationale: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors have modest evidence in hoarding disorder and are used where depression or obsessive compulsive disorder coexists, neither of which is present here; medication alone is not the treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Guardianship requires impaired decision making capacity, and she demonstrates intact cognition and competent management of her affairs; disagreeing with her choices is not the legal test. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for hoarding disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for hoarding disorder

explanation.summary: Excoriation disorder and trichotillomania are the two body focused repetitive behaviours listed within the obsessive compulsive and related disorders, and both are commonly missed because patients present to dermatology rather than to mental health services. The behaviour is usually automatic and grooming-like, often occurring during sedentary activities, and it is distinguished from obsessive compulsive disorder by the absence of any preceding obsession, from body dysmorphic disorder by the absence of appearance preoccupation, and from deliberate self-harm by the absence of intent to injure. Habit reversal training, which pairs awareness training with a competing response, is the psychological treatment with the strongest support. N-acetylcysteine has replicated randomised evidence in trichotillomania and supportive evidence in excoriation disorder, and its favourable side effect profile makes it a reasonable adjunct. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are used where a mood or anxiety disorder coexists, with weaker direct evidence for the picking itself.
key_points: Automatic grooming-driven picking with no preceding obsession and no intent to injure defines excoriation disorder
Habit reversal training is the first line psychological treatment
N-acetylcysteine around 1200 to 2400 mg daily is the adjunct with the best randomised evidence
Distinguish it from obsessive compulsive disorder, body dysmorphic disorder and deliberate self-harm, which lead to different treatments
Repeated antibiotic courses for the lesions treat the consequence, not the behaviour
explanation.pearls: N-acetylcysteine typically needs 8 to 12 weeks before benefit appears, so patients stopping at 4 weeks because nothing has changed is the commonest reason an adequate trial is never completed.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for body focused repetitive behaviours

options.rationale: The lesions are self-induced, so dermatological treatment addresses the consequence rather than the behaviour and repeats the cycle that two antibiotic courses have already failed to break. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for body focused repetitive behaviours)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for body focused repetitive behaviours

options.rationale: Antipsychotics are not indicated for a body focused repetitive behaviour in the absence of psychosis or delusional infestation, and the metabolic burden is unjustified here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Excoriation disorder is not deliberate self-harm; she describes an automatic grooming behaviour with no intent to injure and no affect regulation function, which is the distinction that determines which therapy is offered. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for body focused repetitive behaviours)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for body focused repetitive behaviours

options.rationale: As-required benzodiazepines reinforce the urge-relief cycle, carry dependence risk and have no evidence base in body focused repetitive behaviours. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Habit reversal training is the psychological treatment of choice for excoriation disorder, and N-acetylcysteine at around 1200 to 2400 mg daily is the pharmacological adjunct with the best randomised evidence, thought to act through glutamate modulation in the corticostriatal circuits. The picking she describes is automatic and grooming-driven rather than obsessional, which is what places it in this group rather than with obsessive compulsive disorder. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for body focused repetitive behaviours)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for body focused repetitive behaviours

explanation.summary: Smoking rates among Australians with schizophrenia remain around two to three times the general population rate, and tobacco-related disease is a major contributor to the life expectancy gap in severe mental illness. Clinicians historically avoided varenicline in this group after post-marketing reports of neuropsychiatric events, but a large randomised trial comparing varenicline, bupropion, nicotine patch and placebo in cohorts with and without psychiatric disorders found no significant excess of neuropsychiatric adverse events, and regulatory boxed warnings were subsequently removed. Combination nicotine replacement, meaning a patch for background craving plus an oral form for breakthrough, is the alternative where varenicline is unsuitable. Behavioural support roughly doubles the effect of any pharmacotherapy and should always accompany it. One pharmacokinetic point is essential to remember: tobacco smoke induces cytochrome P450 1A2, so stopping smoking raises clozapine and olanzapine concentrations substantially and requires dose review and monitoring.
key_points: Varenicline is the most effective single agent and is not contraindicated in schizophrenia
Combination nicotine replacement, patch plus an oral form, outperforms patch alone
Behavioural support should accompany every pharmacological attempt
Withholding cessation therapy from people with severe mental illness widens the life expectancy gap
Smoking cessation raises clozapine and olanzapine levels through loss of cytochrome P450 1A2 induction
explanation.pearls: Clozapine plasma concentrations can rise by 50 to 100 per cent within 2 to 4 weeks of stopping smoking, so reduce the dose proactively and check a level when a clozapine-treated patient quits.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Supporting smoking cessation
RANZCP: Position statement on physical health of people with mental illness

options.rationale: Patch alone has already failed twice and does not address the intense morning cravings that defeated him; if nicotine replacement is used it should be combined patch plus an oral form for breakthrough craving. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Supporting smoking cessation)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Supporting smoking cessation

options.rationale: Bupropion is an effective option, but it is less effective than varenicline in head to head trials and lowers the seizure threshold, so it is generally the second choice when varenicline is available and tolerated. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Supporting smoking cessation)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Supporting smoking cessation

options.rationale: Varenicline is the most effective single agent for smoking cessation, and the large randomised safety trial in people with and without psychiatric illness found no excess of neuropsychiatric adverse events attributable to it, which removed the historical objection to its use in schizophrenia. Scheduled mental state review remains sensible practice in a person with a psychotic illness making a major behavioural change. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Supporting smoking cessation)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Supporting smoking cessation

options.rationale: Nortriptyline has modest evidence in smoking cessation but is unsubsidised for this purpose, has anticholinergic and cardiac effects, and sits well down the Australian treatment ladder. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Supporting smoking cessation)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Supporting smoking cessation

options.rationale: Withholding effective pharmacotherapy from people with severe mental illness is a recurring failure responsible for much of the roughly 15 to 20 year life expectancy gap in this population, and behavioural support alone has far lower quit rates. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on physical health of people with mental illness)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on physical health of people with mental illness

explanation.summary: Long term lithium therapy requires monitoring of renal function, thyroid function and calcium, and the calcium arm is the one most often forgotten. Lithium reduces the sensitivity of the calcium sensing receptor on parathyroid cells, so a higher serum calcium is needed before parathyroid hormone secretion is suppressed, producing a biochemical picture indistinguishable from primary hyperparathyroidism. The first interpretive step in any hypercalcaemia is the parathyroid hormone: if it is raised or inappropriately normal, the process is parathyroid-driven, whereas malignancy, myeloma, sarcoidosis and vitamin D excess all suppress it. Lithium-associated hyperparathyroidism differs from sporadic primary hyperparathyroidism in being more often multiglandular, which affects the surgical approach. Stopping lithium does not reliably reverse the abnormality once it is established, which is one reason the decision to change mood stabiliser is not automatic.
key_points: Check calcium alongside renal and thyroid function at least annually during lithium therapy
A raised or inappropriately normal parathyroid hormone with hypercalcaemia means a parathyroid-driven process
Malignancy, myeloma, sarcoidosis and vitamin D excess all suppress parathyroid hormone
Lithium raises the calcium set point of the calcium sensing receptor, mimicking primary hyperparathyroidism
Do not stop lithium reflexively; rebound mania and suicide risk must be weighed against mild hypercalcaemia
explanation.pearls: Lithium-associated hyperparathyroidism is frequently multiglandular rather than a single adenoma, so localisation imaging can be negative and the surgeon may need to explore all four glands.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.rationale: Abrupt lithium cessation carries a well described rebound risk of mania and of suicide, and the hypercalcaemia here is mild and asymptomatic apart from constipation, so the decision to change agents belongs to a planned discussion weighing endocrine against psychiatric risk. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.rationale: Acute hypercalcaemia treatment is reserved for levels above about 3.0 mmol/L or for symptomatic patients with confusion, vomiting or dehydration, and bisphosphonates do not address a parathyroid-driven process. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Myeloma causes hypercalcaemia by bone resorption independent of the parathyroid, so the parathyroid hormone would be suppressed rather than raised, and the serum electrophoresis is already clear. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Her level of 0.7 mmol/L is squarely therapeutic and she has none of the neurological features of toxicity; the abnormality is calcium metabolism, not lithium concentration. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Hypercalcaemia with a parathyroid hormone that is not suppressed is parathyroid-driven, and long term lithium causes exactly this picture by raising the calcium set point at which parathyroid hormone secretion is inhibited. Endocrine assessment decides between observation, parathyroid surgery and a change of mood stabiliser, which is a decision that should be made with the psychiatric risk of stopping lithium explicitly weighed. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

explanation.summary: Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant trinucleotide repeat disorder in which the psychiatric and cognitive features frequently precede the movement disorder by years and cause more day-to-day disability than the chorea itself. Irritability, apathy, depression and obsessionality are the commonest neuropsychiatric features, and apathy in particular is often mistaken by families for laziness or by clinicians for depression. Treatment of irritability begins with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, with an antipsychotic or valproate added or substituted when that fails, and the choice is influenced by whether chorea also needs suppression. Suicide risk is substantially elevated across the illness, peaking around the time of diagnosis and again when independence is lost, so it is asked about at every review. Care is multidisciplinary and includes genetic counselling for at-risk relatives, since predictive testing has implications for the whole family.
key_points: Psychiatric and cognitive symptoms often precede chorea and cause more functional impairment than the movements
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are first line for irritability and apathy, regardless of whether sadness is reported
Antipsychotics treat both irritability and chorea but add metabolic and extrapyramidal burden
Tetrabenazine treats chorea but depletes monoamines and is associated with depression and suicidality
Suicide risk is elevated throughout, peaking at diagnosis and at loss of independence
explanation.pearls: A CAG repeat length of 40 or more is fully penetrant, 36 to 39 is reduced penetrance and 27 to 35 is an intermediate allele that does not cause disease but can expand on paternal transmission.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for Huntington disease

options.rationale: As-required benzodiazepines add sedation and fall risk to a progressive neurodegenerative illness and provide no sustained benefit for a symptom that is present most of the day. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Valproate is used for irritability where mood instability is prominent or an antidepressant has failed, but it is not the first agent and adds sedation, weight gain and hepatic monitoring burden. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for Huntington disease)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for Huntington disease

options.rationale: An antipsychotic is the next step if a serotonergic agent fails, and it has the advantage of also suppressing chorea, but it carries metabolic and extrapyramidal burden and his movements are not yet disabling. The distinguishing consideration is whether chorea needs treating at the same time. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for Huntington disease)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for Huntington disease

options.rationale: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are first line for irritability and apathy in Huntington disease and are effective even when the patient does not describe sadness, since irritability in this illness is a frontostriatal symptom rather than a marker of depression. Starting here also avoids the metabolic and movement burden that an antipsychotic would add. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for Huntington disease)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for Huntington disease

options.rationale: Tetrabenazine is licensed for chorea, not for irritability, and it depletes presynaptic monoamines, which causes or worsens depression and carries a recognised association with suicidality in a population whose suicide rate is already several times that of the general population. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Narcolepsy typically begins in adolescence or early adult life and is frequently misattributed to depression, laziness or poor sleep habits, with reported diagnostic delays of many years. The cardinal symptom is excessive daytime sleepiness with naps that are short and refreshing, which distinguishes it from the unrefreshing sleepiness of sleep apnoea, depression and insufficient sleep. Cataplexy, a sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion, most often laughter, with consciousness fully preserved, is specific to narcolepsy type 1 and reflects loss of hypocretin-producing neurons in the hypothalamus. Sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations complete the classical tetrad but are neither sensitive nor specific on their own. Diagnosis requires overnight polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test, and treatment combines scheduled naps with wake-promoting agents and specific therapy for cataplexy.
key_points: Short refreshing naps distinguish narcolepsy from the unrefreshing sleepiness of apnoea or depression
Cataplexy is emotion-triggered loss of tone with preserved consciousness and is specific to narcolepsy type 1
Diagnosis requires polysomnography first, then a multiple sleep latency test the following day
Retained interest, enjoyment and reactivity argue against major depression as the explanation
Treatment combines scheduled naps, wake-promoting agents and specific anticataplectic therapy
explanation.pearls: Antidepressants suppress rapid eye movement sleep and can mask the sleep onset rapid eye movement periods that the multiple sleep latency test relies on, so they usually need to be withdrawn about 2 weeks before the study under sleep physician supervision.

options.rationale: She retains interest, enjoyment and reactivity with no guilt or hopelessness, so the diagnosis rather than the dose is the problem; increasing it prolongs a 12-month diagnostic delay. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy guidance)

Sleepiness with refreshing naps and episodes of laughter-triggered weakness with preserved awareness describes cataplexy, and the diagnosis of narcolepsy requires overnight polysomnography to exclude other causes of sleep disruption followed by a multiple sleep latency test the next day. That sequence must be performed in the correct order, since a daytime test alone cannot be interpreted without knowing the preceding night's sleep. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy guidance)

Venlafaxine does suppress cataplexy and is sometimes used for that purpose, but switching antidepressants without recognising the underlying disorder treats one symptom while leaving the sleepiness and the diagnosis unaddressed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Obstructive sleep apnoea produces unrefreshing sleep and morning headache rather than refreshing naps, and her body mass index of 23 and absence of snoring make it improbable; oximetry alone is also a poor test in adolescents. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy guidance)

She has no difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep and sleeps 9 hours a night, so insomnia therapy targets a problem she does not have. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy guidance)

explanation.summary: Acute behavioural disturbance is a medical emergency in which the risk of harm to the patient and to staff has to be balanced against the risks of sedation itself. Australian practice follows a graded approach: environmental and verbal de-escalation first, then oral medication if accepted, then parenteral sedation, with physical restraint used only for the minimum time needed to give medication safely. Droperidol became the preferred parenteral agent in Australia after trials showed it achieved sedation faster than midazolam with fewer airway interventions, and concerns about QT prolongation at the doses used in this setting were not borne out. Synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonists and other novel psychoactive substances are not detected on routine urine drug screens, produce far more severe agitation, tachycardia and hyperthermia than plant cannabis, and are recognised causes of seizures and acute kidney injury. After sedation, the priorities are continuous monitoring, a temperature check for hyperthermia, creatine kinase for rhabdomyolysis, and reassessment for an organic cause.
key_points: De-escalate and offer oral medication before parenteral sedation, and restrain only for the minimum time needed
Droperidol 10 mg intramuscularly is the Australian first line parenteral agent, with midazolam second line
Ketamine is a rescue agent after failure of two sedatives, not a first choice
Synthetic cannabinoids are not detected on routine urine drug screens and cause more severe toxicity than plant cannabis
After sedation check temperature, creatine kinase and glucose, and reassess for a medical cause of the disturbance
explanation.pearls: Hyperthermia above 38.5 °C in a stimulant or synthetic cannabinoid presentation demands active cooling and a creatine kinase level, because it is the single best predictor of rhabdomyolysis and death in this group.

sources.label: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments

options.rationale: Droperidol 10 mg intramuscularly is the first line parenteral sedative in Australian emergency practice for acute behavioural disturbance, supported by randomised trials showing faster and more reliable sedation than midazolam with less respiratory depression. Its recorded corrected QT interval of 420 ms is well within the range at which droperidol at this dose has been shown to be safe.
