(Source: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments

options.rationale: Midazolam sedates effectively but causes significantly more respiratory depression and airway intervention than droperidol at equivalent effect, which is why Australian protocols moved it to second line. It remains the agent of choice where an antipsychotic is contraindicated. (Source: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments

options.rationale: This combination is used in some international settings but is not the Australian first line, and haloperidol at this dose carries a higher burden of dystonia and akathisia than droperidol without better sedation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Intramuscular olanzapine is a reasonable option but is slower in onset than droperidol and must not be combined with parenteral benzodiazepines because of cardiorespiratory depression, which limits its usefulness when escalation may be needed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Ketamine is a rescue agent for sedation failure after two agents, and using it first exposes the patient to emergence phenomena, hypersalivation and a higher rate of intubation than necessary. (Source: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments

explanation.summary: Adults with severe intellectual disability who have little or no speech communicate physical distress through behaviour, and a new or escalating behaviour of concern should be treated as a symptom needing a differential diagnosis rather than as a reason to increase psychotropic medication. Diagnostic overshadowing, the attribution of new symptoms to the intellectual disability or to a known psychiatric diagnosis, is the central error to avoid. The physical causes worth systematically excluding are dental disease, constipation, gastro-oesophageal reflux, urinary retention or infection, otitis media, fracture, menstrual pain and medication adverse effects including akathisia. Helpful clues are the abruptness of onset, whether anything in the environment changed, whether the behaviour targets a particular body region, and whether sleep and appetite changed at the same time. Psychotropic reduction rather than escalation is the direction of travel in Australian policy, given the long history of overprescribing in this population.
key_points: New behaviour change in a minimally verbal adult is a symptom requiring a differential diagnosis, not an automatic dose increase
Diagnostic overshadowing is the error of attributing new symptoms to the disability or existing diagnosis
Exclude dental disease, constipation, reflux, urinary and ear infection, fracture and akathisia
Behaviour targeting one body site with unilateral tenderness points to localised pain
Australian policy direction is psychotropic reduction with positive behaviour support, not escalation
explanation.pearls: Akathisia from an existing antipsychotic can itself present as agitation and self-injury, so a dose increase can worsen the very behaviour it is meant to treat; ask staff specifically whether the person can now sit still for a meal or a television program.

sources.label: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability

options.rationale: Increasing an antipsychotic in response to behaviour change without first excluding a physical cause is diagnostic overshadowing, and it adds metabolic and extrapyramidal risk while leaving the source of pain untreated. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability

options.rationale: Depression can indeed present as behaviour change and sleep disturbance in intellectual disability, but it is a diagnosis reached after physical causes are excluded, and nothing here explains the strictly unilateral facial signs. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability

options.rationale: New self-injury directed repeatedly at one body site, with food refusal, night waking and unilateral tenderness on that side, points to localised pain, and dental disease is the commonest treatable cause in adults with severe intellectual disability who cannot report toothache. Examination under sedation is often the only way to obtain an adequate look and to treat in the same episode. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability

options.rationale: Constipation is a leading cause of behaviour change in this population and is always worth considering, but his bowel chart documents a soft formed stool daily and his abdomen is soft and non-tender, which makes it an unlikely explanation here. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability

options.rationale: Functional behaviour assessment is a core part of management for established behaviours of concern, but it starts from the premise that the behaviour is environmentally maintained, and here the history of abrupt onset with no environmental change and localised physical signs points elsewhere first. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability

explanation.summary: When a person with schizophrenia relapses, the reflex explanations are non-adherence and substance use, and these account for the majority of cases, which is why a long-acting injectable register and a urine drug screen are checked first. Once both are excluded and plasma levels confirm adequate exposure, the differential moves to psychosocial precipitants, and the best studied of these is the emotional climate of the household. Research on expressed emotion has consistently shown that high levels of criticism, hostility or emotional over-involvement in relatives predict relapse, and that structured family intervention reduces it. Effective programs run for at least 10 sessions over 6 months or more and combine psychoeducation, communication training and structured problem solving with the whole family rather than the patient alone. Family intervention is recommended in Australian and international guidelines yet remains substantially underdelivered, in part because services default to individual work.
key_points: Exclude non-adherence and substance use first, using the depot register, plasma levels and urine screening
High expressed emotion at home, meaning criticism, hostility or over-involvement, predicts relapse
Behavioural family intervention of at least 10 sessions roughly halves relapse rates
Clozapine is for treatment resistance after two adequate trials, not for relapse in a drug-responsive illness
A therapeutic plasma level with rapid remission argues against the dose being the problem
explanation.pearls: Family intervention needs a minimum of 10 sessions over 6 months to show relapse benefit; single-session psychoeducation for relatives improves knowledge but has not been shown to change relapse rates.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.rationale: A therapeutic plasma level with symptom resolution in 10 days without any dose change argues that the dose was not the limiting factor, and escalating it adds extrapyramidal and prolactin burden without addressing what preceded both relapses. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.rationale: Behavioural family intervention is the intervention with the strongest evidence for relapse reduction in schizophrenia, roughly halving relapse rates over the following 2 years when delivered over at least 10 sessions, and it is specifically indicated where criticism and over-involvement are prominent at home. With adherence confirmed by the depot register and plasma level and substance use excluded twice, the family environment is the modifiable factor that both relapses point to. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.rationale: Anticonvulsant augmentation has little evidence in schizophrenia without a mood component or aggression, and it adds hepatic, haematological and teratogenic monitoring burden for no expected relapse benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Clozapine is indicated after failure of two adequate antipsychotic trials, whereas his symptoms remitted on his current agent both times, so this is relapse in a responsive illness rather than treatment resistance. The distinguishing question is whether the drug failed to control symptoms or whether something outside the drug precipitated relapse. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.rationale: Individual supportive contact maintains engagement and is valuable, but it has not been shown to reduce relapse in the way structured family intervention has, and it leaves the household dynamic that preceded both relapses unaddressed. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

explanation.summary: New antisocial or criminal behaviour beginning in mid to later life with no prior history is a neuropsychiatric red flag, and behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia is the diagnosis most often missed in this presentation. Its core features are early behavioural disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, perseverative or ritualistic behaviour, hyperorality with a shift towards sweet foods, and executive dysfunction with relative preservation of memory and visuospatial function. That preservation is exactly why brief bedside screening tools perform poorly and why formal neuropsychological assessment is needed. Structural imaging typically shows frontal and anterior temporal atrophy, and functional imaging can help where structural imaging is equivocal. Recognition matters legally as well as clinically, because it bears on fitness to plead, on criminal responsibility and on decisions about guardianship and driving, and it redirects the family from blame towards support and planning.
key_points: New offending in mid to later life without prior history should prompt a neuropsychiatric assessment
Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia features disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy and a shift towards sweet foods
Memory and orientation are preserved early, so bedside screening scores are often near normal
Formal neuropsychological testing plus structural imaging is the appropriate workup
Diagnosis has direct forensic implications for fitness to plead and criminal responsibility
explanation.pearls: Offences in behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia are characteristically committed in the open with no attempt at concealment and no apparent concern about consequences, which is the behavioural signature that most reliably separates them from ordinary offending.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia
Dementia Australia: Frontotemporal dementia clinical information

options.rationale: Closing the assessment at this point misses a syndrome that is plainly emerging in the collateral history, and a fitness opinion given without completing the neuropsychiatric workup is not defensible. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia

options.rationale: Kleptomania requires a build-up of tension before the theft and pleasure or relief at the time, both of which she explicitly denies, and it usually begins in adolescence or early adult life rather than in the seventh decade with new behavioural change. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia

options.rationale: Apathy and social withdrawal in frontotemporal dementia are frequently misread as depression, but neither she nor her husband reports low mood, and the disinhibition, dietary change and loss of empathy do not fit a depressive episode. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia

options.rationale: New criminal behaviour committed openly without concealment, together with loss of empathy, dietary change towards sweet foods, and executive deficits on a preserved overall cognitive score, is the recognisable behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia picture, and neuropsychological testing with structural imaging is the appropriate workup. Bedside screening tools are insensitive to this syndrome because memory and orientation are preserved early, so a near-normal score cannot be used to exclude it. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia
Dementia Australia: Frontotemporal dementia clinical information

options.rationale: Psychological treatment for impulse control presumes intact capacity to learn and apply strategies, which is undermined by the executive impairment demonstrated here, and it would proceed without a diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia

explanation.summary: This scenario turns on keeping three legal frameworks separate: mental health legislation, which authorises treatment for mental illness; guardianship legislation, which governs consent to medical treatment for adults who cannot consent for themselves; and the common law emergency doctrine. A community treatment order or involuntary status under mental health legislation gives no authority to treat a physical illness, a point frequently misunderstood on medical and surgical wards. Capacity is decision specific and time specific, and it is assessed against the ability to understand the information, retain it, weigh it in the balance and communicate a choice, not against whether the clinician agrees with the outcome. In New South Wales the person responsible hierarchy allows a spouse, carer or relative to consent for major medical treatment, but that pathway closes when the patient objects, at which point the guardianship tribunal must decide. A psychotic illness does not by itself remove capacity, but it does so where the delusional content directly displaces the relevant reasoning, as it does here.
key_points: Mental health legislation authorises treatment for mental illness only, never for physical illness
Capacity is decision specific and rests on understanding, retaining, weighing and communicating
The person responsible can consent for major medical treatment, but not when the patient objects
An objecting patient without capacity requires an application to the guardianship tribunal
A psychiatric diagnosis never removes capacity by itself; the delusional content must displace the relevant reasoning
explanation.pearls: Terminology and thresholds differ by jurisdiction: New South Wales uses the person responsible under the Guardianship Act, Victoria uses a medical treatment decision maker under its own legislation, so state the state before naming the substitute decision maker.

sources.label: NSW Guardianship Act 1987 and NSW Health consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual
NSW Health: Consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual
RANZCP: Clinical practice resources on capacity and consent

options.rationale: Capacity is decision specific, so it must be assessed and documented for this operation rather than inferred from her psychiatric diagnosis or her treatment order. In New South Wales the person responsible may consent for someone who lacks capacity, but that authority falls away when the patient objects to the treatment, and consent must then be sought from the guardianship tribunal. (Source: NSW Guardianship Act 1987 and NSW Health consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual)
source_refs: NSW Guardianship Act 1987 and NSW Health consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual
RANZCP: Clinical practice resources on capacity and consent

options.rationale: Mental health legislation authorises treatment for mental illness only, and a community treatment order confers no authority over surgical or other physical health treatment. This is the most tempting wrong branch because the legal framework is already in place for a different purpose. (Source: NSW Health: Consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual)
source_refs: NSW Health: Consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual

options.rationale: The husband would ordinarily be the person responsible and could consent for someone lacking capacity, but the legislation expressly removes that authority once the patient objects to the treatment, which she has done clearly and repeatedly. (Source: NSW Guardianship Act 1987 and NSW Health consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual)
source_refs: NSW Guardianship Act 1987 and NSW Health consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual

options.rationale: Emergency provisions cover treatment needed urgently to save life or prevent serious damage when there is no time to obtain consent, and with a normal lactate, no fever and a 48-hour window there is time to follow the proper process. (Source: NSW Health: Consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual)
source_refs: NSW Health: Consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual

options.rationale: Accepting a refusal requires the person to be able to understand, retain, weigh and communicate the decision, and she cannot retain or weigh the central fact that she may die, because a delusional belief displaces it. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources on capacity and consent)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources on capacity and consent

explanation.summary: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder is distinguished from the far more common premenstrual syndrome by the severity of the mood component and the functional impairment it causes, and from an underlying mood disorder by the complete absence of symptoms in the follicular phase. Prospective daily charting over at least two cycles is required for diagnosis because retrospective recall consistently overattributes symptoms to the premenstrual window, and a substantial proportion of women referred with this presentation turn out to have premenstrual exacerbation of an underlying condition instead. The pathophysiology appears to involve differential central sensitivity to normal luteal progesterone metabolites rather than abnormal hormone levels, which is why measuring hormones is unhelpful. Serotonergic antidepressants work unusually quickly here, allowing luteal phase only dosing that halves drug exposure. Second-line options include continuous combined hormonal contraception, with ovarian suppression and, rarely, oophorectomy reserved for severe refractory disease.
key_points: Diagnosis requires prospective daily symptom charting across at least two cycles
Complete symptom resolution in the follicular phase separates this from an underlying mood disorder
Serotonergic agents are first-line and act within days, permitting luteal phase only dosing
Hormone measurement is unhelpful because levels are normal and sensitivity is the abnormality
Ovarian suppression is reserved for refractory disease because of hypo-oestrogenic bone loss
explanation.pearls: Luteal phase dosing typically starts around day 14 or at symptom onset and stops at the onset of menstruation, which distinguishes this from every other antidepressant indication where abrupt cessation risks discontinuation symptoms.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines

options.rationale: Tricyclics have not demonstrated the rapid luteal phase efficacy that serotonergic agents show and carry greater anticholinergic burden and overdose toxicity. A tricyclic would be a later-line consideration in treatment-resistant major depression rather than in this cyclical presentation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Two years of a prospectively charted symptom pattern confined to the luteal phase with complete follicular resolution establishes premenstrual dysphoric disorder, for which serotonergic agents are first-line. Response occurs within days rather than the weeks required in major depression, which is what makes intermittent luteal phase dosing effective and well tolerated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Antipsychotics have no established role in premenstrual dysphoric disorder and carry metabolic and movement disorder risks disproportionate to the indication. They would be appropriate as augmentation in psychotic or treatment-resistant mood disorder, which is not the picture here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Ovarian suppression is effective but induces a hypo-oestrogenic state with bone loss and is reserved for severe symptoms refractory to first and second-line therapy, usually with add-back oestrogen. It would be considered after serotonergic agents and hormonal contraception have failed. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)

Progestogen-only preparations do not reliably suppress ovulation at conventional doses and progestogens themselves can provoke the mood symptoms being treated. A combined preparation containing drospirenone taken continuously is the hormonal option with supporting evidence. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)

explanation.summary: Hair pulling disorder sits within the body-focused repetitive behaviours alongside skin picking, and it is classified near but separately from obsessive compulsive disorder because its treatment response differs markedly. The pulling is often automatic rather than deliberate, occurring during sedentary absorbed activities, and the absence of an obsessional belief driving it distinguishes it from a compulsion performed to neutralise an intrusive thought. Examination findings are characteristic: an irregular patch containing hairs of many different lengths, because regrowth is continually interrupted, with no scarring, scaling or inflammation. Onset typically occurs around puberty and the condition is substantially more common in females presenting to services. Habit reversal training is the treatment of choice, and asking about trichophagia is important because swallowing pulled hair can produce a gastric trichobezoar requiring surgical removal.
key_points: Tension before pulling and relief afterward, without an obsessional belief, characterises the disorder
Hairs of varying lengths in an irregular non-scarring patch distinguish it from alopecia areata
Habit reversal training is first-line; serotonergic antidepressants have largely negative trial data
Pulling is frequently automatic and occurs during sedentary absorbed activities
Screen for comorbid depression and anxiety, which commonly accompany the disorder
explanation.pearls: Ask directly whether she swallows the hair she pulls: trichophagia can form a gastric trichobezoar with a tail extending into the small bowel, which presents with obstruction and needs surgical removal.

sources.label: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.rationale: Serotonergic agents are effective in obsessive compulsive disorder but trials in hair pulling disorder have been largely negative, which is one reason the two conditions are now separated. An antidepressant would be indicated if a comorbid depressive or anxiety disorder were present alongside. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Topical steroid treats inflammatory alopecia such as alopecia areata, which produces smooth round patches without hairs of varying lengths. It would be correct if examination showed exclamation mark hairs and completely bare, non-irregular patches. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

Habit reversal training is the intervention with the strongest evidence in hair pulling disorder and works by building awareness of the behaviour and substituting a competing response at moments of urge. It is first-line ahead of medication because no drug has consistent trial support in this condition. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Antipsychotics are sometimes used as augmentation in refractory cases but carry metabolic and extrapyramidal risks unjustified as an initial approach in an adolescent. They would be considered only after behavioural therapy and other options had failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

The history of pulling with tension and relief and the finding of hairs at varying lengths without scarring make this a clinical diagnosis requiring no biopsy. Biopsy would be justified if there were scarring, scaling or diagnostic uncertainty about a primary dermatological cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Night terrors are disorders of arousal from slow wave sleep, which is concentrated in the first third of the night, and this timing is the most useful single feature separating them from nightmares. A child having a nightmare wakes in the second half of the night, can be consoled, and recalls the dream, whereas a child having a night terror appears awake but is not, cannot be consoled, and has no memory of it. Parents often find the amnesia hardest to believe and are reassured to learn that the child is not suffering in the way the screaming suggests. Precipitants are anything that increases slow wave sleep pressure or fragments sleep: insufficient sleep, irregular schedules, febrile illness, a full bladder and obstructive sleep apnoea. There is a strong familial tendency, and the great majority of children outgrow the episodes by adolescence without any specific treatment.
key_points: Slow wave sleep arousals occur in the first third of the night; nightmares occur in the later half
Unresponsiveness during the event and complete morning amnesia are characteristic
Sleep deprivation and irregular schedules are the commonest precipitants
Attempting to fully wake the child prolongs and worsens the episode
Screen for obstructive sleep apnoea, since sleep fragmentation triggers arousals
explanation.pearls: Scheduled awakening, gently rousing the child about 15 to 30 minutes before the usual event time for a couple of weeks, interrupts the slow wave cycle and is the behavioural option when events are frequent and predictable.

sources.label: Sleep Health Foundation: Parasomnias in children

options.rationale: Nocturnal frontal lobe seizures are the differential but they are brief, stereotyped, occur multiple times per night and often involve dystonic posturing, none of which is described. An electroencephalogram would be indicated for stereotyped clustered events, daytime seizures or abnormal neurological findings. (Source: RCH CPG: Sleep problems)

Benzodiazepines suppress slow wave sleep and are occasionally used for dangerous or very frequent parasomnias, but they are not appropriate for a self-limiting condition in a preschool child. Medication would be considered for episodes causing injury or persisting despite optimised sleep. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Attempting to rouse a child from a slow wave sleep arousal typically prolongs the episode and increases agitation, because he is not awake and cannot be consoled. Gentle guidance back to bed without full waking is the correct approach during an event. (Source: RCH CPG: Sleep problems)

Events arising 90 minutes after sleep onset with unresponsiveness, autonomic arousal and complete amnesia are night terrors from slow wave sleep, and insufficient sleep is the main precipitant given the recent later bedtime. Management is reassurance, restoring adequate sleep duration and making the environment safe, since the child may get out of bed during an event. (Source: RCH CPG: Sleep problems)

Night terrors are not caused by psychological trauma and the child is well, developing normally and has no daytime distress. Trauma assessment would be warranted if there were nightmares with recall, behavioural regression, or disclosure or suspicion of adverse experiences. (Source: RCH CPG: Sleep problems)

explanation.summary: Faecal soiling in a school-aged child who was previously continent is overflow incontinence from chronic constipation in the great majority of cases, and the history of infrequent enormous stools with daily leakage between them is close to diagnostic. The mechanism explains why punishment and reward systems fail: the rectum becomes chronically distended, stretch receptors adapt so the child stops sensing fullness, and softer stool tracks passively around the impacted mass without any voluntary control. Hiding soiled underwear reflects shame rather than defiance, and reframing this for the family is a therapeutic act in itself. Treatment has two distinct phases that must happen in order, disimpaction followed by maintenance, and the most common reason for failure is stopping maintenance laxatives too early, before the stretched rectum has regained normal tone and sensation. Red flags warranting further investigation include constipation from birth, delayed meconium, failure to thrive, an empty rectum, abnormal anal position or sacral and neurological signs.
key_points: Daily leakage with infrequent large stools indicates overflow incontinence, not voluntary soiling
Disimpaction must precede maintenance therapy and behavioural work
Rectal distension blunts sensation, so the child genuinely cannot feel the leakage
Maintenance laxatives continue for months after soiling resolves to allow rectal tone to recover
Red flags include constipation from birth, delayed meconium, failure to thrive and sacral or neurological signs
explanation.pearls: Warn families that soiling often worsens for the first few days of a macrogol disimpaction regimen as the retained mass mobilises, because parents who are not warned commonly stop the treatment at exactly that point.

sources.label: NICE: Constipation in children and young people

options.rationale: Behavioural work is a valuable adjunct but achieves little while a rectal faecal mass continues to cause involuntary leakage, and framing the problem behaviourally sustains the blame the child is already receiving. It becomes useful once disimpaction has occurred and toileting routines are being established. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

Faecal loading is already evident on palpation and radiography adds radiation without changing management or correlating reliably with symptoms. Imaging would be considered where examination is unreliable or an alternative diagnosis is suspected. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

These investigate Hirschsprung disease, which typically presents with delayed meconium passage in the newborn period and an empty rectum rather than with overflow soiling after years of normal continence. They would be indicated for constipation from birth with failure to thrive or an empty rectum on examination. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

A stimulant alone will not clear an established impaction and can cause severe cramping when driving peristalsis against a hard retained mass. Stimulants are used as adjuncts to osmotic laxatives when maintenance with macrogol alone proves insufficient. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

Daily leakage around a palpable faecal mass is overflow incontinence from chronic retention rather than voluntary soiling, and it cannot improve until the impaction is cleared. Maintenance laxative and scheduled post-meal toileting then continue for months, because relapse is common if treatment stops as soon as soiling resolves. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

explanation.summary: Akathisia and restless legs syndrome are confused constantly in psychiatric practice because both produce an urge to move in someone taking a dopamine antagonist, and getting the distinction right determines whether an effective antipsychotic is unnecessarily reduced. Restless legs syndrome follows a circadian pattern that worsens in the evening and at rest, is relieved by movement, and is focused on the legs, whereas akathisia is present throughout the day, is experienced as generalised mental restlessness as much as physical, and is not relieved by walking. Periodic limb movements during sleep accompany restless legs syndrome in the majority of cases and are a useful collateral clue from a bed partner. Iron deficiency is the most important reversible contributor, and the treatment threshold uses a ferritin considerably higher than that used for anaemia because brain iron status is the relevant variable. Dopamine antagonists can certainly unmask or worsen restless legs syndrome, so the two conditions can coexist with the same precipitant.
key_points: Circadian worsening at rest and in the evening with relief on movement indicates restless legs syndrome
Akathisia is continuous, generalised and subjectively mental as well as motor, and is not relieved by walking
Periodic limb movements reported by a bed partner support restless legs syndrome
Replace iron when ferritin is below 75 micrograms/L or transferrin saturation below 20 per cent
Dopamine agonists risk augmentation and are not first-line despite their efficacy
explanation.pearls: The ferritin threshold for treating restless legs syndrome is below 75 micrograms/L, far above the threshold used to diagnose iron deficiency anaemia, because central nervous system iron availability rather than red cell production is the target.

options.rationale: A circadian urge to move confined to rest and the evening, relieved by walking and associated with sleep kicking, is restless legs syndrome rather than akathisia, and low ferritin with reduced transferrin saturation identifies a reversible cause. Iron replacement is first-line when ferritin is below 75 micrograms/L, and correcting it frequently resolves symptoms without any change to antipsychotic therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Dose reduction is the correct response to akathisia, but akathisia produces continuous subjective inner restlessness with observable fidgeting that does not follow a circadian pattern or resolve with walking. Reducing the dose here risks psychotic relapse without addressing the actual cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Propranolol is a recognised treatment for akathisia but has no established role in restless legs syndrome. It would be appropriate if the patient described generalised inner restlessness present throughout the day with visible motor manifestations. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Anticholinergics treat drug-induced parkinsonism and acute dystonia, and examination shows no tremor, rigidity or bradykinesia to support either. Benzatropine is notably ineffective for akathisia as well, so it does not fit any of the plausible drug-induced alternatives here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Dopamine agonists are effective in restless legs syndrome but carry a substantial risk of augmentation with long-term use and would also antagonise the antipsychotic effect being relied on. They are reserved for persistent symptoms after iron has been replaced and non-dopaminergic options considered. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Drug-induced hyponatraemia in older adults is common, underdiagnosed and frequently attributed to the wrong agent because patients typically take several implicated drugs at once. The diagnostic framework is unchanged regardless of the culprit: confirm true hypo-osmolality, assess volume status clinically, and use paired serum and urine osmolality with urine sodium to separate the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis from hypovolaemia and from renal salt wasting. Thyroid and adrenal insufficiency must be excluded because both mimic it exactly. Attribution then rests on timing, and a documented normal sodium before the new drug is the single most valuable piece of evidence, which is why baseline electrolytes before starting an antidepressant in an older patient are worth the trouble. Serotonergic agents typically cause hyponatraemia within the first 2 to 4 weeks, and risk is substantially higher with advanced age, female sex, low body weight and concurrent diuretic use, all of which compound here.
key_points: Confirm hypo-osmolar hyponatraemia and assess volume status before attributing a cause
Urine osmolality above 100 mmol/kg with urine sodium above 30 mmol/L in a euvolaemic patient indicates inappropriate antidiuresis
Exclude hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency, which mimic the syndrome
Serotonergic antidepressants typically cause hyponatraemia within the first 2 to 4 weeks
Correct chronic hyponatraemia slowly; hypertonic saline is only for severe neurological symptoms
explanation.pearls: Check electrolytes at baseline and again about 2 weeks after starting a serotonergic antidepressant in anyone over 65, particularly if they also take a thiazide, because the fall is usually asymptomatic until sodium drops below about 125 mmol/L.

options.rationale: Thiazides are a classic cause of hyponatraemia and would be the answer if the timing fitted, but she has taken it for 6 years with a normal sodium 3 months ago. It would be the correct target if the antidepressant were long-established and the diuretic recently started. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Euvolaemic hypo-osmolar hyponatraemia with concentrated urine and urine sodium above 30 mmol/L is the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, and the temporal link to a drug started 4 weeks ago in a normonatraemic patient identifies the culprit. Serotonergic antidepressants characteristically cause this within the first few weeks, most commonly in older women, and stopping the drug with fluid restriction corrects it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptoms such as seizures, coma or marked confusion, and rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia risks osmotic demyelination. It would be indicated if she presented with a seizure or a depressed level of consciousness. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Isotonic saline treats hypovolaemic hyponatraemia but can worsen sodium in the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, because the salt is excreted while the water is retained. It would be correct if she were clinically volume deplete with a low urine sodium. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Tricyclics also cause the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis and add anticholinergic and cardiac conduction risks that are poorly tolerated in this age group. A switch would be considered later, to an agent such as mirtazapine or agomelatine, after the sodium has normalised. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Antipsychotic-associated corrected QT prolongation is a genuine but often mismanaged risk, and the practical decisions turn on two numbers: an absolute corrected QT interval above 500 ms, or an increase of more than 60 ms from baseline, both of which mark a materially elevated arrhythmia risk. This patient meets both. Before attributing the change to the drug, reversible contributors must be corrected, since hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia, bradycardia and hypothyroidism all prolong repolarisation and are far easier to fix than a psychotropic regimen. Antipsychotics differ substantially in this effect, with haloperidol, particularly intravenously, and ziprasidone among the higher risk agents, while aripiprazole, lurasidone and brexpiprazole have minimal effect. Because untreated psychosis carries its own substantial mortality, the answer is almost never to stop antipsychotic treatment altogether but to move to an agent with a better repolarisation profile and repeat the electrocardiogram once the new drug is at steady state.
key_points: A corrected QT interval above 500 ms or a rise of more than 60 ms from baseline requires action
Correct potassium, magnesium, calcium and thyroid abnormalities before attributing prolongation to a drug
Haloperidol and ziprasidone are higher risk; aripiprazole and lurasidone have minimal effect
Stopping all antipsychotic treatment is rarely correct given the mortality of untreated psychosis
Repeat the electrocardiogram once the replacement agent reaches steady state
explanation.pearls: Intravenous haloperidol prolongs the corrected QT interval considerably more than the oral route at equivalent doses, which is why continuous cardiac monitoring is advised whenever it is given intravenously for acute behavioural disturbance.

options.rationale: Although the effect is dose-related, continuing the same agent above a corrected QT interval of 500 ms leaves the patient exposed to arrhythmia for the sake of convenience. Dose reduction would be a reasonable response to a modest prolongation in the 460 to 500 ms range with close monitoring. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Ziprasidone produces greater corrected QT prolongation than most other antipsychotics, so substituting it exchanges one repolarisation risk for a similar or larger one. Ziprasidone and aripiprazole are both effective antipsychotics but sit at opposite ends of the repolarisation risk spectrum. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

A corrected QT interval above 500 ms carries a materially increased risk of torsades de pointes and requires the offending agent to be stopped rather than continued at a lower dose. Aripiprazole has among the least effect on cardiac repolarisation of the available antipsychotics, making it the rational replacement when antipsychotic cover must continue. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Citalopram is an antidepressant with its own dose-dependent corrected QT prolongation and would leave the psychotic symptoms untreated. An antidepressant might be added later for the affective component once an antipsychotic with a favourable cardiac profile is established. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Magnesium is the treatment for established torsades de pointes and for correcting hypomagnesaemia, and this patient's magnesium is already normal with no arrhythmia. It would be given immediately if he developed polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Delusional misidentification, in which a familiar person is believed to have been replaced by an identical impostor, is far more often a sign of organic brain disease than of a primary psychiatric disorder, particularly when it appears for the first time in later life. The task is to identify what underlies it, and the collateral history usually carries the diagnosis where the mental state examination alone cannot. Here the combination of fluctuating cognition, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, spontaneous parkinsonism and rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder gives the core clinical features of dementia with Lewy bodies. Recognising it has immediate and serious practical consequences because severe sensitivity to antipsychotics occurs in a substantial proportion of patients and can produce irreversible parkinsonism, sedation, autonomic instability and death. Cholinesterase inhibitors, by contrast, are often strikingly effective for the hallucinations and cognitive fluctuation, so the correct diagnosis changes treatment in the opposite direction to instinct.
key_points: New misidentification delusions in later life suggest organic disease rather than primary psychiatric illness
Fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and dream enactment define the core clinical picture
Dream enactment behaviour often precedes cognitive symptoms by years and predicts synucleinopathy
Severe antipsychotic sensitivity can cause irreversible deterioration and death
Cholinesterase inhibitors frequently improve hallucinations and cognitive fluctuation
explanation.pearls: If an antipsychotic is unavoidable in suspected Lewy body disease, quetiapine at the lowest possible dose is the conventional choice, and typical agents such as haloperidol are avoided entirely because of the risk of irreversible parkinsonism and death.

sources.label: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia

options.rationale: Delirium is a genuine contributor to the acute deterioration, but it does not explain 8 months of progressive parkinsonism, visual hallucinations and over a year of dream enactment reported by the family. A purely delirious picture would be correct if collateral history described normal baseline cognition and function. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia

options.rationale: Very late onset schizophrenia-like psychosis typically features persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations without parkinsonism, fluctuating attention or dream enactment. It would be the diagnosis if motor signs and cognitive fluctuation were absent and cognition were otherwise preserved. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia

options.rationale: Alzheimer disease presents with prominent early episodic memory loss and does not typically produce early parkinsonism, marked cognitive fluctuation or dream enactment behaviour. Both cause dementia with psychotic features, but visual hallucinations and parkinsonism arise early in synucleinopathy and late in Alzheimer disease. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia

options.rationale: Fluctuating cognition, well-formed visual hallucinations, spontaneous parkinsonism and a long history of dream enactment together identify dementia with Lewy bodies, of which delusional misidentification is a recognised feature. The dream enactment behaviour is particularly telling, since it frequently precedes cognitive symptoms by years and is strongly predictive of an underlying synucleinopathy. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia

options.rationale: Vascular cognitive impairment produces stepwise deterioration with focal neurological signs and imaging evidence of infarction or extensive white matter disease, and this scan shows atrophy only. It would be the diagnosis with a stepwise history and corresponding vascular lesions on imaging. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia

explanation.summary: Delusional infestation is the most common somatic delusional disorder and presents almost exclusively to dermatology and general practice rather than to mental health services, because the patient's explanatory model is dermatological. The defining feature is that the delusion is encapsulated: outside this single belief, thought form, mood, perception and social and occupational functioning are entirely intact, which is why involuntary treatment is rarely justified and why the person seems so credible. Secondary causes must be excluded first, including substance use, particularly stimulants, thyroid disease, B12 deficiency, diabetes, human immunodeficiency virus infection and dementia, since any of these can produce an identical picture with a different treatment. The specimen sign, in which the patient brings collected material as proof, is characteristic and should be examined seriously and microscopically rather than dismissed, because taking the complaint seriously is the foundation of any therapeutic relationship. Antipsychotics achieve substantial improvement in most patients, but only a minority of the therapeutic effort is pharmacological and the rest is engagement.
key_points: An encapsulated delusion with otherwise preserved functioning defines delusional disorder
Exclude stimulant use, thyroid disease, B12 deficiency, diabetes, human immunodeficiency virus infection and dementia
Examine patient-collected specimens microscopically rather than dismissing them
Direct confrontation of the belief ends the therapeutic relationship without changing it
Antipsychotics are effective, but acceptance depends on framing treatment around distress and skin healing
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about methamphetamine and prescribed stimulants before diagnosing primary delusional infestation, because stimulant-induced formication with secondary delusional elaboration resolves with abstinence and needs no long-term antipsychotic.

options.rationale: Direct contradiction of a fixed delusion does not alter the belief and typically leads the patient to seek another clinician, continuing the cycle of presentations and self-treatment. Explaining negative results works where the belief is an overvalued idea held with doubt rather than a fixed delusion. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Prescribing an antiparasitic reinforces the delusional belief and exposes her to further unnecessary treatment while the underlying disorder progresses. Permethrin would be correct for genuine scabies, which produces burrows and webspace involvement and typically affects household contacts. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

Involuntary assessment requires risk to the person or others that cannot be managed voluntarily, and she is functioning independently and engaging with services. It would become appropriate if self-treatment escalated to serious harm or if she refused all care while deteriorating markedly. (Source: RANZCP: Mental health legislation)

Serotonergic antidepressants have a role in body dysmorphic disorder and in obsessional preoccupations held with insight, but not in a fixed delusion of infestation. An antidepressant would be added if a comorbid depressive disorder emerged alongside antipsychotic treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

A single fixed delusion with preserved functioning in every other domain is delusional disorder of the somatic type, which responds to antipsychotic treatment but only if the patient accepts it. Treating the visible skin damage first and framing medication around distress and skin healing rather than around belief is what makes acceptance possible, since direct confrontation reliably ends the therapeutic relationship. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Corticosteroid-induced psychiatric disturbance is common, dose-related and frequently missed because the patient is on a medical ward being treated for something else. Risk rises substantially above prednisolone 40 mg daily, symptoms typically appear within the first week, and elevated mood, irritability and insomnia predominate on initiation, whereas depressive symptoms are more characteristic of prolonged therapy or withdrawal. The absence of any prior psychiatric history, of family history and of previous reaction to lower-dose courses does not exclude the diagnosis, since the reaction is dose-dependent rather than idiosyncratic. Management is a negotiation with the treating team, because the corticosteroid is often genuinely needed, and symptom control with an antipsychotic buys time while the dose is reduced. Documenting the reaction matters for the future, since recurrence on re-exposure at similar doses is likely and prophylaxis can be planned.
key_points: Risk rises markedly above prednisolone 40 mg daily, with onset usually in the first week
Mania and irritability predominate on initiation; depression is more typical of prolonged use or withdrawal
Reducing or withdrawing the corticosteroid is the primary treatment where the medical condition allows
Antipsychotics give symptom control during the taper; antidepressants can worsen the elevated phase
Sustained attention and orientation distinguish this from hyperactive delirium
explanation.pearls: Symptoms usually resolve within about 6 weeks of stopping the corticosteroid, so document the reaction clearly in the record, since re-exposure at a similar dose carries a high risk of recurrence and may warrant prophylactic cover.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines

options.rationale: Manic symptoms emerging within days of high dose corticosteroid in someone with no psychiatric history are a substance-induced mood disturbance, and the primary treatment is to reduce or withdraw the causative agent as the respiratory condition allows. An antipsychotic provides symptom control during the taper, since symptoms persist for days to weeks after the steroid is reduced and the behaviour carries real financial and interpersonal risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Committing to long-term mood stabilisation treats this as a primary bipolar disorder when the temporal relationship to a known precipitant has not yet been tested by withdrawing it. Lithium would be appropriate if manic episodes recurred independently of corticosteroid exposure. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines

options.rationale: Antidepressants can precipitate or worsen manic symptoms and have no role in an elevated mood state. They would be considered for the depressive phase that sometimes follows corticosteroid withdrawal, not for the manic phase. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Structural imaging is warranted for first-episode mania with focal neurological signs, atypical age of onset or altered consciousness, none of which is present alongside an obvious pharmacological precipitant. Deferring treatment also leaves the disinhibited spending and calling unaddressed. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines

options.rationale: Hyperactive delirium features impaired attention, disorientation and a fluctuating course, and this man is oriented with sustained attention and a sustained elevation of mood. Delirium management would be correct if attention were impaired and the picture waxed and waned across the day. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Aggression after traumatic brain injury is one of the strongest predictors of poor community reintegration and of carer breakdown, and it is usually the behaviour that determines whether someone can return home. Frontal injury impairs inhibition of responses to frustration, which is why outbursts are typically triggered, brief, followed by remorse, and clustered around specific care activities. Two steps precede any prescription: excluding treatable medical contributors such as pain, constipation, urinary retention, infection, sleep disruption and post-traumatic seizures, and implementing a structured behavioural plan, since environmental antecedents are modifiable and drugs cannot substitute for consistent handling. Where medication is needed, beta blockade is best supported, though often at doses higher than those used in cardiology and requiring several weeks for full effect. The overarching principle is to avoid agents that dull arousal, because rehabilitation gains depend on the patient being alert enough to participate.
key_points: Exclude pain, constipation, retention, infection, sleep disruption and seizures before prescribing
Implement a structured behavioural plan first, since triggers are identifiable and modifiable
Beta blockade has the strongest evidence for aggression after traumatic brain injury
Antipsychotics may impair motor and cognitive recovery and are reserved for psychotic drivers
Benzodiazepines risk paradoxical disinhibition and impair new learning
explanation.pearls: Propranolol for post-injury aggression often requires doses well above cardiac dosing and takes several weeks to show full benefit, so review pulse and blood pressure at each increment rather than abandoning it as ineffective at low dose.

sources.label: RANZCP: Neuropsychiatry of acquired brain injury
BMJ Best Practice: Traumatic brain injury

options.rationale: Antipsychotics are widely used but animal and clinical data suggest dopamine blockade may impair motor and cognitive recovery after brain injury, and sedation compromises rehabilitation participation. Risperidone would be reserved for aggression driven by psychotic symptoms, which are absent here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Beta blockade has the strongest evidence base of any drug class for aggression following traumatic brain injury, and it is added here because a properly implemented behavioural plan has given only partial benefit. It is preferred over sedating alternatives because it does not impair the arousal and attention on which ongoing rehabilitation depends. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Benzodiazepines can cause paradoxical disinhibition in frontal lobe injury and impair the memory consolidation needed for new learning in rehabilitation. They have a role in brief acute sedation for immediate safety, not in ongoing management of recurrent outbursts. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Anticonvulsant mood stabilisers are sometimes used for post-injury agitation but the supporting evidence is weaker than for beta blockade, and the electroencephalogram shows no epileptiform activity to justify it on seizure grounds. Valproate would be more attractive if post-traumatic seizures coexisted. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Serotonergic antidepressants help where irritability arises from post-injury depression or emotional lability, and he is euthymic between episodes with no depressive symptoms. Sertraline would be appropriate if a depressive disorder were driving the irritability. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor encephalitis characteristically begins with a viral-like prodrome and then produces psychiatric symptoms that are indistinguishable from a primary psychotic illness for days to weeks, which is why many patients are admitted to mental health units before the diagnosis is made. The features that should redirect thinking are neurological and autonomic rather than psychiatric: new seizures, orofacial dyskinesia, catatonia, autonomic instability and a decreased level of consciousness, particularly in a young woman with no psychiatric history. Standard investigations are frequently unremarkable, since computed tomography is typically normal, magnetic resonance imaging is normal in around half of cases, and inflammatory markers may be only mildly raised, so a normal first-line workup does not exclude it. Cerebrospinal fluid antibody testing is essential because serum testing alone has lower sensitivity and can be falsely negative. Treatment with corticosteroids, immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, plus removal of any associated teratoma, produces good recovery in the majority, and delay in immunotherapy is the strongest modifiable predictor of a poor outcome.
key_points: A viral prodrome followed by subacute psychosis, seizures, dyskinesia and catatonia is the characteristic sequence
Computed tomography is normal and magnetic resonance imaging is normal in roughly half of cases
Cerebrospinal fluid antibody testing is required, since serum testing alone misses cases
Ovarian teratoma is present in a substantial minority of affected young women and must be sought
Time to immunotherapy is the strongest modifiable determinant of outcome
explanation.pearls: Orofacial dyskinesia persisting while the patient is otherwise still is the single most discriminating bedside sign, because it does not occur in primary psychotic illness in an antipsychotic-naive patient.

options.rationale: An electroencephalogram is a reasonable adjunct and may show the extreme delta brush pattern, but it will not establish the cause and antiseizure treatment alone leaves the underlying process untreated. It would be the priority if the question were whether ongoing non-convulsive status was present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome requires exposure to a dopamine antagonist, and she has taken no antipsychotic medication, nor does she have the lead-pipe rigidity and marked hyperthermia typical of it. Creatine kinase would be central if she had received antipsychotics and developed rigidity with high fever. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Subacute psychosis with a viral prodrome, new seizures, orofacial dyskinesia, catatonia and autonomic instability in a young woman is the recognised presentation of anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor encephalitis, and cerebrospinal fluid antibody testing is the definitive investigation. Cerebrospinal fluid testing is specifically required because serum testing alone misses a meaningful proportion of cases. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Tumour screening is an essential part of management once the diagnosis is established, since an ovarian teratoma is found in a substantial minority of affected young women, but it follows rather than precedes antibody confirmation. It becomes the next step once cerebrospinal fluid antibodies return positive. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Wilson disease can present with psychiatric symptoms and movement abnormalities in this age group but evolves over months to years with hepatic involvement and Kayser-Fleischer rings, not over 3 weeks with seizures and fever. It would be worth testing in a subacute psychiatric presentation with tremor, dysarthria and deranged liver function. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Hoarding disorder was separated from obsessive compulsive disorder in DSM-5 because its phenomenology, course and treatment response differ. The defining features are persistent difficulty discarding possessions regardless of their value, distress associated with discarding, and consequent accumulation that congests living areas, with excessive acquisition present in most cases and specified when it occurs. The differential includes obsessive compulsive disorder where hoarding is driven by contamination or harm obsessions, a depressive episode with amotivation, psychosis with delusional beliefs about the objects, autism spectrum collecting, and frontotemporal dementia when onset is late and accompanied by other behavioural change. Insight is specified as good, poor or absent, and poor insight is common and does not exclude the diagnosis. Response to treatment is slower and less complete than in obsessive compulsive disorder, and the safety issues of fire risk, falls, vermin and structural load often need parallel attention from fire services and council.
key_points: Hoarding disorder requires difficulty discarding plus distress plus congestion of living areas
The absence of obsessions and rituals distinguishes it from obsessive compulsive disorder
Adapted cognitive behavioural therapy is first line; serotonergic medication has weaker evidence
Forced clearance without participation causes distress and rapid reaccumulation
New onset hoarding in later life warrants consideration of frontotemporal dementia
explanation.pearls: Animal hoarding is a distinct and more severe presentation, almost always accompanied by absent insight and squalor, and it carries much higher recidivism after intervention than object hoarding, so it warrants involvement of animal welfare services from the outset.

sources.label: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.rationale: Serotonin reuptake inhibitors at high dose are first line for obsessive compulsive disorder, where they act on the obsessions that drive the compulsions, and the evidence for them in hoarding disorder as a standalone condition is much weaker. Medication is added when a comorbid depressive or obsessive compulsive disorder is present or when therapy alone has not worked. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.rationale: Forced clearance without the person's participation reliably produces acute distress and rapid reaccumulation, because it removes the objects without changing the beliefs and decision-making difficulties that generated them. Enforced clearance is reserved for genuine public health or fire risk and is done alongside therapy, not instead of it. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.rationale: An antipsychotic would be considered if the beliefs about the possessions were held with delusional intensity, for instance that the objects were sentient or had special powers. She retains insight that the accumulation is a problem, which places this outside the psychotic spectrum. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.rationale: Difficulty discarding possessions with distress on parting from them and excessive acquisition, in the absence of obsessions and compulsive rituals, is hoarding disorder, and the treatment with the best evidence is a specifically adapted cognitive behavioural therapy. It targets the decision-making and categorisation difficulties, the beliefs about the objects, and the acquisition behaviour, typically with in-home sorting practice alongside clinic sessions. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.rationale: Cognitive assessment matters when hoarding emerges for the first time in later life with other features of frontal or degenerative disease, and a Montreal Cognitive Assessment of 28 out of 30 argues against that. Deferring treatment for testing that is unlikely to change management wastes the therapeutic window. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

explanation.summary: Narcolepsy type 1 results from loss of hypothalamic orexin producing neurons, probably through an autoimmune mechanism in genetically susceptible people, and it is defined by excessive daytime sleepiness plus cataplexy or a low cerebrospinal fluid orexin concentration. The classic tetrad of sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis and hypnagogic or hypnopompic hallucinations represents intrusion of rapid eye movement sleep phenomena into wakefulness, although fewer than a third of patients have all four. Cataplexy is the one feature that is close to pathognomonic and is distinguished from syncope and seizure by the emotional trigger, the preserved consciousness and the rapid complete recovery. Naps that are short and refreshing help separate it from the unrefreshing sleepiness of depression, sleep apnoea and insufficient sleep. Treatment combines scheduled naps and sleep hygiene with modafinil or another wake promoting agent for sleepiness, and venlafaxine or sodium oxybate for cataplexy, alongside mandatory discussion of driving and notification requirements.
key_points: Cataplexy is brief bilateral weakness triggered by emotion with consciousness fully preserved
Short refreshing naps separate narcolepsy from depressive and apnoeic hypersomnia
Diagnosis needs overnight polysomnography then a multiple sleep latency test
Diagnostic criteria are mean sleep latency of 8 minutes or less with two or more sleep onset rapid eye movement periods
Do not start a stimulant before the sleep studies, as it invalidates the result
explanation.pearls: Untreated narcolepsy with cataplexy makes a person unfit to drive in Australia; a conditional licence can be granted once treatment has produced satisfactory control, documented by a sleep physician, and the patient carries a legal obligation to notify the driver licensing authority.

options.rationale: The hypersomnia of a depressive episode is unrefreshing, is accompanied by low mood, anhedonia and diurnal variation, and does not produce brief episodes of muscle weakness triggered by emotion. A Patient Health Questionnaire 9 score of 3 with a bright reactive mood makes depression an implausible explanation. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

Treating first and investigating later removes the ability to interpret the sleep studies, because stimulants alter sleep latency and suppress rapid eye movement sleep. Formal diagnosis is also required in Australia for subsidised access and for the driving and occupational advice that follows. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

Brief bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by laughter with preserved consciousness is cataplexy, and combined with daytime sleepiness, sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations this is narcolepsy type 1. Diagnosis requires overnight polysomnography to exclude another cause of disrupted sleep followed immediately by a multiple sleep latency test, which shows a mean sleep latency of 8 minutes or less with two or more sleep onset rapid eye movement periods. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

Insufficient sleep syndrome is the commonest cause of sleepiness in this age group and responds to extending sleep opportunity, but her diary already shows nine hours of consolidated sleep. Sleep hygiene advice is a useful adjunct in narcolepsy alongside scheduled naps, not a substitute for diagnosis. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

Obstructive sleep apnoea produces unrefreshing sleep with snoring and witnessed apnoeas, typically in an older or higher weight patient, and naps are not restorative. A body mass index of 22 kg/m2 with refreshing short naps and cataplexy points elsewhere. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

explanation.summary: Body dysmorphic disorder is a preoccupation with one or more perceived defects in physical appearance that are not observable or appear slight to others, accompanied by repetitive behaviours such as mirror checking, grooming, skin picking, reassurance seeking or comparing. It is under-recognised because sufferers present to dermatologists and cosmetic surgeons rather than to mental health services, and insight is frequently poor, with a substantial minority holding their beliefs with delusional conviction. Suicidality is high, exceeding that seen in obsessive compulsive disorder and major depression, so risk is assessed at every review. Treatment combines a specifically adapted cognitive behavioural therapy with a serotonin reuptake inhibitor, and the doses required are consistently higher and the time to response longer than in depression, which is why premature dose-limited trials are the commonest reason for apparent treatment resistance. Cosmetic intervention rarely satisfies the concern and often shifts it to another body area.
key_points: The perceived defect is absent or slight to an observer, while the distress and time cost are large
Serotonergic doses must reach the upper end of the range, as in obsessive compulsive disorder
An adequate trial is 12 weeks at the maximum tolerated dose before declaring failure
Suicide risk is higher than in obsessive compulsive disorder or major depression
Cosmetic procedures usually leave the preoccupation unchanged or displaced elsewhere
explanation.pearls: Muscle dysmorphia, the belief that the body is insufficiently muscular, is a specifier of body dysmorphic disorder that occurs almost entirely in men and carries a high rate of anabolic androgenic steroid use, so ask directly about supplement and injectable use.

sources.label: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders
BMJ Best Practice: Body dysmorphic disorder

options.rationale: Cosmetic procedures in body dysmorphic disorder leave the preoccupation unchanged or worse in the great majority of cases, and his own experience after rhinoplasty demonstrates exactly that. Surgery would be appropriate only if there were an objective deformity, and his nose has a normal contour. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.rationale: An antipsychotic is used as augmentation when beliefs are held with delusional conviction and a properly dosed serotonergic trial has failed, not as a substitute for optimising that trial. His insight is poor rather than absent, which does not by itself change first-line treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Body dysmorphic disorder characteristically requires serotonergic doses at the upper end of the range, comparable to those used in obsessive compulsive disorder, and 50 mg of sertraline is a starting dose rather than an adequate trial. An adequate trial is defined as 12 weeks at the maximum tolerated dose, so treatment failure cannot be declared until the dose has been pushed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Clomipramine is the one tricyclic with evidence in this disorder because of its potent serotonin reuptake inhibition, and other tricyclics have none. Switching agents before optimising the current one also loses whatever partial response has accrued. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Generic supportive counselling has no evidence in body dysmorphic disorder, which responds to a specifically structured cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention and perceptual retraining. Withdrawing medication at the same time removes the one active treatment he is receiving. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

explanation.summary: Gambling disorder is classified among the substance related and addictive disorders because it shares the reward pathway, tolerance and withdrawal-like features of substance dependence, and in Australia electronic gaming machines account for the majority of harm. It is almost never the presenting complaint, surfacing instead through insomnia, anxiety, depression, relationship breakdown or financial crisis, so asking about gambling directly is what makes the diagnosis. The diagnostic features to elicit are preoccupation, escalating stakes to achieve the same excitement, repeated failed attempts to cut down, chasing losses, lying to conceal involvement, and jeopardising relationships or employment. Suicide risk is substantially elevated and rises sharply at moments of financial disclosure or crisis, so it is asked about at every contact. First-line treatment is cognitive behavioural therapy targeting erroneous cognitions about randomness, combined with financial counselling and practical restriction of access to funds, with pharmacotherapy reserved for non-response.
key_points: Gambling presents through insomnia, mood, relationship or financial problems rather than directly
Ask about preoccupation, escalation, chasing losses, concealment and failed attempts to stop
Cognitive behavioural therapy plus financial counselling is first line
Free state-based Gambling Help services provide both components
Suicide risk is elevated and peaks around financial disclosure and crisis
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about dopamine agonists in any patient with new onset gambling: pramipexole and ropinirole prescribed for Parkinson disease or restless legs cause impulse control disorders in up to 17 per cent of users, and the behaviour resolves when the drug is withdrawn.

options.rationale: Opioid antagonists have modest evidence in gambling disorder and are considered when structured psychological therapy has failed or when there is a strong family history of alcohol use disorder. Starting a drug before any psychological or financial intervention inverts the treatment hierarchy. (Source: RANZCP: Gambling disorder)

Cognitive behavioural therapy addressing the erroneous beliefs about randomness and near misses, combined with financial counselling to restructure access to money, is first line and is available free through Gambling Help services in every Australian state. Addressing the debt is part of treatment rather than separate from it, because unmanaged financial pressure is itself a driver of chasing behaviour and of suicide risk. (Source: RANZCP: Gambling disorder)

Antidepressants treat a comorbid depressive disorder but do not reduce gambling behaviour in their own right, and his low mood is described as entirely reactive to the financial situation. Treating the mood alone would leave the behaviour and the debt untouched. (Source: RANZCP: Gambling disorder)

Self-exclusion is a useful adjunct that reduces access to particular venues, but it is readily circumvented, does not cover online platforms, and does nothing about the cognitions that sustain the behaviour. It belongs within a treatment plan rather than as the whole of it. (Source: RANZCP: Gambling disorder)

Residential withdrawal exists to manage the physiological withdrawal syndromes of alcohol, opioids and benzodiazepines, and gambling has no such syndrome requiring medical supervision. He drinks two standard drinks weekly and uses no other substances. (Source: RANZCP: Gambling disorder)

explanation.summary: Selective mutism is classified as an anxiety disorder and is defined by consistent failure to speak in specific social situations where speaking is expected, despite speaking normally in others, for at least one month beyond the first month of school. It is commonly misread as shyness, wilful refusal, a language disorder or autism, and the delay to referral averages several years, which matters because outcomes are better with earlier intervention. The diagnostic work is largely exclusionary: confirm normal hearing, confirm fluent age-appropriate speech in at least one setting, and confirm that social reciprocity is intact outside the feared situations. Comorbid social anxiety disorder is present in the majority, and a smaller group has a coexisting speech or language difficulty that warrants its own assessment. Treatment is behavioural, using stimulus fading, shaping and graded exposure delivered collaboratively across home, clinic and classroom, with a serotonin reuptake inhibitor reserved for severe or treatment resistant cases.
