key_points: Speech is fluent in at least one setting, which distinguishes this from a language disorder
Duration must exceed one month beyond the first month of schooling
Preserved eye contact, shared enjoyment and imaginative play argue against autism spectrum disorder
Behavioural therapy with school involvement is first line; medication is second line
Most children have comorbid social anxiety disorder, which is treated at the same time
explanation.pearls: Pressing a mute child to speak, or rewarding a single word in front of the class, reliably worsens the avoidance; the effective technique is stimulus fading, in which a new person is gradually introduced into a setting where the child is already speaking comfortably.

sources.label: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

options.rationale: Hearing assessment is essential in any child with reduced speech output and has already been done with a normal result at school entry. Repeating it delays treatment and cannot explain speech that is fluent at home and absent at school. (Source: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

options.rationale: A serotonin reuptake inhibitor is added when a structured behavioural program has been properly delivered and has not produced progress, or when the impairment is severe and entrenched. Medication as the opening move skips the intervention with the strongest evidence in this age group. (Source: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

options.rationale: Reduced speech at school would raise this question, but she maintains eye contact, shows spontaneous sharing, plays imaginatively and sustains reciprocal friendships, all of which argue against a pervasive social communication difficulty. The selectivity of the mutism by setting is itself the discriminating feature. (Source: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

options.rationale: Consistent failure to speak in specific social situations despite speaking fluently elsewhere, persisting beyond a month of school and interfering with education, is selective mutism, an anxiety disorder rather than a language or oppositional problem. Behavioural treatment using stimulus fading and graded exposure delivered jointly by clinician, family and school is first line, and early intervention prevents the pattern becoming entrenched. (Source: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

options.rationale: A brief settling-in period of up to a month after starting school is expected and does not warrant diagnosis, which is why the criteria require a duration beyond one month. Fourteen months of complete mutism is well past that point, and delay is associated with poorer outcomes. (Source: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD requires several symptoms to have been present before the age of 12, impairment in two or more settings, and symptoms not better explained by another disorder, and the childhood onset criterion is the one that substance use most often obscures. Collateral evidence from school reports, parents or a long-term partner is therefore central to the assessment rather than optional. Substance use disorders are two to three times more common in adults with ADHD than in the general population, and the relationship runs both ways, with untreated ADHD predicting earlier onset and poorer treatment retention. The Australian guideline recommends treating both conditions concurrently rather than sequentially, favouring non-stimulants or long-acting stimulant formulations where diversion or misuse is a concern. Stimulant prescribing for adults in Australia additionally requires a state or territory authority and is generally initiated by a psychiatrist, and driving and occupational implications are discussed at initiation.
key_points: Childhood onset before age 12 must be established, ideally with contemporaneous collateral evidence
Treat ADHD and substance use disorder concurrently; abstinence is not a precondition
Non-stimulants and long-acting stimulants are preferred where misuse or diversion is a concern
Immediate release stimulants carry the highest diversion potential
Adult stimulant prescribing in Australia requires a state authority and usually psychiatrist initiation
explanation.pearls: Atomoxetine takes 4 to 6 weeks to reach full effect, unlike stimulants which work within hours, so patients must be warned in advance or they will discontinue it in the second week believing it has failed.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Australian guidance is explicit that ADHD treatment should not be withheld while a substance use disorder is addressed, because untreated ADHD worsens substance use outcomes, and the two are treated concurrently. A non-stimulant such as atomoxetine has no misuse or diversion liability and is preferred while methamphetamine use is active, with a long-acting stimulant considered once use is stable. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Immediate release stimulants have the highest misuse and diversion potential of the available options and share a pharmacological class with the drug he is already using. If a stimulant is used at all in this setting it is a long-acting preparation, and only once the substance use is stable. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Requiring abstinence before treatment is an outdated position that the Australian guideline specifically rejects, since untreated ADHD is itself a driver of continued substance use and of attrition from drug and alcohol services. Abstinence is a goal of the concurrent treatment, not a precondition for it. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Deferring the diagnosis would be defensible if the only evidence of inattention came from the period of substance use, since stimulant use can mimic the symptom profile. Contemporaneous school reports documenting symptoms from Year 2 establish onset well before age 12 and before any drug exposure. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Antipsychotics have a role in methamphetamine induced psychosis and in acute behavioural disturbance, and he has never had psychotic symptoms. They do not treat inattention and carry metabolic and extrapyramidal burden without benefit here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Electroconvulsive therapy is the most effective acute treatment for severe depression with psychotic features, with remission rates well above those of antidepressant pharmacotherapy, and relapse after a successful acute course is high enough that maintenance treatment is offered to patients with a recurrent pattern. Consent is specific to the procedure, must be informed and voluntary, and is reconfirmed before each treatment rather than obtained once for an open-ended course. Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific, and is assessed against whether the person can understand and retain the relevant information, weigh it in arriving at a decision, and communicate that decision. Where capacity is absent, each Australian state and territory has its own statutory pathway, typically involving a mental health tribunal or guardianship body rather than family consent, and these differ enough that local legislation must be checked. The documented cognitive effect is anterograde and retrograde amnesia around the treatment period, which improves over weeks to months and is reduced by right unilateral ultrabrief pulse electrode placement.
key_points: Capacity is decision-specific: understanding, retaining, weighing and communicating
A relative cannot consent for, or veto treatment for, a capacitous adult
Consent for electroconvulsive therapy is reconfirmed before each treatment in a course
Maintenance treatment substantially reduces relapse after a successful acute course
Where capacity is absent, a statutory tribunal pathway applies, and it varies between states
explanation.pearls: Right unilateral ultrabrief pulse placement produces markedly less retrograde amnesia than bitemporal placement but needs stimulation at around six times seizure threshold to match its efficacy, which is why an inadequately dosed unilateral course is a common reason for apparent non-response.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Depression in adults

options.rationale: A relative has no legal authority to veto treatment for an adult with decision-making capacity, and deferring on that basis would expose her to relapse of an illness that has previously involved food and fluid refusal. Family concerns are addressed by discussion with her consent, not by suspending her treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive therapy)

Substitute decision making processes are engaged only when a person lacks capacity for the decision in question. Invoking a tribunal for a woman who demonstrably retains capacity removes her rights rather than protecting them. (Source: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive therapy)

Antidepressant monotherapy has already failed to prevent four episodes, and relapse rates after a successful acute course are substantially higher without maintenance electroconvulsive therapy in this group. Stopping would also be a unilateral decision against the expressed wish of a capacitous patient. (Source: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive therapy)

Consent signed by another person is valid only where that person holds a formal substitute decision making role and the patient lacks capacity. Obtaining a relative's signature for a capacitous adult is legally ineffective and would invalidate the consent. (Source: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive therapy)

She retains, understands, weighs and communicates the relevant information, which satisfies the test for decision-making capacity, and consent for electroconvulsive therapy in Australia rests with the patient whenever capacity is present. The right response to the son's concern is to offer, with her permission, a discussion of the actual evidence on cognitive effects, while documenting the capacity assessment and re-confirming consent before each treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive therapy)

explanation.summary: Australian guidelines place trauma-focused psychological therapies, principally trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing, ahead of pharmacotherapy for post-traumatic stress disorder on the strength of their effect sizes. Medication is offered when psychological therapy is unavailable, declined or insufficient, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are the usual first choice. Trauma processing requires a baseline of safety and stability, meaning the person is not living under continuing threat, has somewhere to live, and is not in uncontrolled substance withdrawal; where those conditions are absent, practical and stabilisation work comes first. For people from refugee backgrounds the assessment must also consider the effects of the settlement process itself, including visa insecurity, family separation and the loss of occupational identity, all of which can maintain symptoms independently of the original trauma. Engaging a professional interpreter, rather than a family member, is a requirement of safe and effective care and is arranged as a matter of course rather than on request.
key_points: Trauma-focused psychological therapy is first line and outperforms medication
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are second line; supportive counselling is not recommended
Trauma processing requires baseline safety and stability in housing, threat and substance use
Never use a family member as interpreter, particularly in trauma work
Settlement stressors such as visa insecurity and family separation maintain symptoms independently
explanation.pearls: Prazosin, titrated from 1 mg at night, has the best evidence of any drug specifically for trauma related nightmares, and the dose-limiting problem is first dose postural hypotension rather than any central effect.

sources.label: Foundation House: Working with interpreters in mental health

options.rationale: Dose escalation is reasonable when psychological therapy is unavailable or declined, and medication is a second-line option in post-traumatic stress disorder rather than the treatment with the best effect size. Escalating without offering the more effective intervention accepts a partial response unnecessarily. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

Using a family member as interpreter is not acceptable practice in any clinical setting and is particularly damaging in trauma work, where the patient will censor disclosure to protect the relative and the relative may be re-traumatised or may filter the content. Professional interpreters are engaged even when the family offers to help. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

Antipsychotic augmentation has limited evidence in post-traumatic stress disorder and carries metabolic and sedative burden, so it sits well down the list of options. Prazosin has better evidence specifically for nightmares if a pharmacological adjunct is needed after trauma-focused therapy has been offered. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

Non-directive supportive counselling performs no better than waiting list in post-traumatic stress disorder and is specifically not recommended as a substitute for trauma-focused therapy. Delivering it in a language she cannot follow compounds the problem. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

Trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing are the first-line treatments with the largest effect sizes, and she has the stability in housing, immigration status and substance use that makes trauma processing appropriate now. A professional interpreter, ideally the same one across sessions and briefed about the content, is essential so that she can disclose freely and the therapy retains its fidelity. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonists are sprayed onto plant material and sold as herbal smoking blends, and their toxicity differs sharply from that of cannabis because they are full rather than partial agonists at the cannabinoid receptor and carry no cannabidiol to moderate the effect. The clinical picture includes severe agitation, psychosis, vomiting, seizures, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, and occasionally acute kidney injury or myocardial ischaemia, which are essentially unseen with cannabis itself. Routine urine immunoassays target delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol metabolites and do not cross-react with these compounds, so a negative cannabis screen is expected and must not be used to exclude the exposure. The chemical structures are altered continually to stay ahead of scheduling, which means potency and effect vary unpredictably between batches sold under the same brand name. Management is supportive, centred on titrated benzodiazepine sedation, active cooling, fluids, and monitoring for rhabdomyolysis and renal impairment.
key_points: Synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonists are full agonists and far more potent than cannabis
Routine urine immunoassay does not detect them, so a negative screen is uninformative
Seizures, hyperthermia and severe agitation distinguish them from cannabis intoxication
Titrated benzodiazepine sedation is the first-line treatment, not an antipsychotic
Monitor for rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury after significant agitation or hyperthermia
explanation.pearls: Check a creatine kinase and renal function in anyone sedated after synthetic cannabinoid toxicity: acute kidney injury has been reported in clusters with these products even without prolonged struggling or marked hyperthermia.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Synthetic cannabinoid toxicity

options.rationale: Butyrophenones lower the seizure threshold, impair thermoregulation and prolong the corrected QT interval, all of which are active hazards in a patient who has already seized and is hyperthermic. Antipsychotics are second line in stimulant-type toxicity and only after adequate benzodiazepine loading. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Opioid toxicity presents with pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression and reduced conscious state, which is the opposite of this hyperadrenergic picture with 6 mm pupils and tachypnoea. Naloxone would achieve nothing and would precipitate withdrawal if opioids were also on board. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Charcoal has no role after an inhaled exposure, since the drug has bypassed the gut entirely, and administering it to an agitated patient risks aspiration. Decontamination is relevant to recent large oral ingestions with a protected airway. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonists are full agonists at the cannabinoid receptor, far more potent than delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, and are not detected by the routine immunoassay, which is why a negative screen in a classic presentation does not exclude them. Treatment is supportive with titrated benzodiazepine sedation, which simultaneously controls agitation, raises the seizure threshold, reduces the adrenergic drive and lowers heat generation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Olanzapine is a reasonable adjunct once benzodiazepines have been loaded and agitation persists, and it is not the first agent when seizures and hyperthermia are present. Its anticholinergic burden also impairs sweating in a patient who is already at 38.4 degrees. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia is the commonest cause of dementia with onset before 60 years and is defined by progressive change in personality and social conduct rather than by amnesia. The diagnostic criteria require three of six features: behavioural disinhibition, apathy or inertia, loss of sympathy or empathy, perseverative or compulsive behaviour, hyperorality or dietary change, and a dysexecutive neuropsychological profile with relative sparing of memory and visuospatial function. That sparing is precisely why bedside screening tools perform poorly, since instruments weighted towards memory and orientation can return a near normal score in a person whose social functioning has collapsed, and the commonest misdiagnoses are depression, bipolar disorder and a primary personality disorder. New onset criminal behaviour in middle age, particularly theft, trespass and sexually inappropriate conduct, is a recognised presentation and carries obvious medicolegal implications for culpability and for driving. Around 40 per cent of cases have a family history and a significant proportion carry mutations in the C9orf72, MAPT or GRN genes, so genetic counselling is part of specialist assessment.
key_points: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia presents with conduct change, not memory loss
Diagnosis needs three of six features including disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy and hyperorality
A near normal Montreal Cognitive Assessment does not exclude it, as memory is spared early
New onset criminal behaviour in middle age is a recognised presentation
A family history is present in around 40 per cent, so genetic counselling forms part of assessment
explanation.pearls: Cholinesterase inhibitors are not indicated in frontotemporal dementia and can worsen disinhibition and agitation, which is the opposite of their effect in Alzheimer disease, so an empirical trial while awaiting the specialist opinion is actively unhelpful.

options.rationale: Progressive disinhibition, loss of empathy, apathy, compulsive repetitive behaviour and hyperorality with carbohydrate craving are the core diagnostic features of behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia, and the imaging corroborates them. Memory is characteristically preserved early, so a near normal cognitive screen argues for the diagnosis rather than against it, and specialist assessment is needed for neuropsychology, genetic counselling and medicolegal input into the charges. (Source: Dementia Australia: Frontotemporal dementia)

Kleptomania requires rising tension before the theft and relief or gratification afterwards, with the person recognising the act as wrong, and it typically begins in adolescence or early adulthood. He shows puzzlement rather than tension or remorse, and the onset in middle age alongside other behavioural change points to an acquired cause. (Source: Dementia Australia: Frontotemporal dementia)

Opioid antagonists are used for impulse control disorders such as gambling and are not a treatment for behaviour arising from frontal degeneration. Treating the symptom pharmacologically without establishing the cause would also leave the driving, financial and medicolegal consequences unaddressed. (Source: Dementia Australia: Frontotemporal dementia)

Apathy in frontotemporal dementia is frequently misread as depression, and this is the commonest initial misdiagnosis, but he reports no low mood, no sleep disturbance and no anhedonia, and apathy without subjective sadness is the distinguishing pattern. Serotonergic agents can help the compulsive and disinhibited behaviours later but do not substitute for making the diagnosis. (Source: Dementia Australia: Frontotemporal dementia)

Feigning would be a consideration if the presentation had begun after the charges and served an obvious external incentive, whereas his wife dates the change to two years before any legal involvement. Structural imaging showing focal atrophy also provides objective corroboration that exaggeration cannot produce. (Source: Dementia Australia: Frontotemporal dementia)

explanation.summary: Trichotillomania sits within the obsessive compulsive and related disorders but differs from obsessive compulsive disorder in both phenomenology and treatment response. Pulling is preceded by mounting tension or an urge and followed by relief or gratification, and it occurs in both a focused mode, where the person is aware and often distressed, and an automatic mode during sedentary activities such as reading, studying or screen time. There are no obsessions, and the absence of appearance related preoccupation distinguishes it from body dysmorphic disorder, in which hair removal is driven by a belief that the hair itself is defective. The dermatological differential matters because irregular patches with hairs of varying length and normal underlying skin point to pulling, whereas smooth patches with exclamation mark hairs suggest alopecia areata and scaling with broken hairs suggests tinea capitis. Habit reversal training, usually delivered within a broader behavioural package, is first line, and unlike obsessive compulsive disorder the condition responds poorly to serotonin reuptake inhibitors, with N-acetylcysteine having modest supporting evidence as an adjunct.
key_points: Premonitory tension with relief after pulling is the defining phenomenology
Automatic pulling during sedentary activity requires awareness training to address
Serotonin reuptake inhibitors work in obsessive compulsive disorder but not in trichotillomania
Irregular patches with varying hair lengths and normal skin distinguish it dermatologically
Habit reversal training within a behavioural package is first line treatment
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about trichophagia, because swallowing pulled hair can form a trichobezoar that extends into the small bowel as Rapunzel syndrome and presents with obstruction, and it requires surgical rather than psychiatric management.

sources.label: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.rationale: Antipsychotics have some evidence as augmentation in refractory cases but carry metabolic burden that is hard to justify as an initial step in a young woman. They sit well behind behavioural therapy in the treatment sequence. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Trichotillomania is a chronic condition with a waxing and waning course that rarely remits without treatment, and this advice offers a fragment of a therapeutic technique without the structure that makes it work. It also risks her hearing her distress as trivial. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.rationale: Hair pulling with premonitory tension and subsequent relief, without obsessions or appearance related beliefs, is trichotillomania, for which habit reversal training within a behavioural package has the strongest evidence and outperforms any medication. Awareness training addresses the automatic pulling that occurs during sedentary activities. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.rationale: Serotonin reuptake inhibitors are effective in obsessive compulsive disorder but trials in trichotillomania have been largely negative, which is one of the clearest pharmacological differences between these related conditions. They remain useful for a comorbid depressive or anxiety disorder. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.rationale: The clinical picture of irregular alopecia with hairs of differing lengths and intact skin is characteristic of pulling, whereas alopecia areata gives smooth round patches with exclamation mark hairs and tinea capitis gives scaling with broken hairs. Biopsy and topical steroid treat neither the behaviour nor its cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Caffeine is the most widely used psychoactive substance in Australia and is a recognised cause of a discrete anxiety syndrome, with intakes above roughly 400 mg per day in adults commonly producing restlessness, tremor, palpitations, gastrointestinal upset and insomnia. Energy drinks and pre-workout supplements make the exposure easy to miss, because a single can may contain 80 to 160 mg and pre-workout powders frequently contain 200 mg or more per serve alongside other stimulants, so a young person can consume well over a gram daily without thinking of themselves as a heavy coffee drinker. The temporal relationship between escalating intake and symptom onset, the absence of pervasive worry or situational avoidance, and the presence of tremor and insomnia should all direct the assessment towards intake before a primary anxiety disorder is diagnosed. Reduction should be gradual because abrupt cessation produces headache, fatigue, irritability and poor concentration that typically last two to nine days and frequently cause people to resume. Thyrotoxicosis, phaeochromocytoma, arrhythmia and stimulant use are the other differentials to consider, and a normal thyroid function test with a normal electrocardiogram addresses the most common of these.
key_points: Intakes above roughly 400 mg of caffeine daily commonly produce an anxiety syndrome
Energy drinks and pre-workout powders conceal very large doses from the patient
Absent pervasive worry and situational avoidance argues against a primary anxiety disorder
Taper rather than stop abruptly to avoid withdrawal headache and relapse
Exclude thyrotoxicosis and arrhythmia with thyroid function and an electrocardiogram
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about pre-workout supplements and energy drinks by name rather than asking how much coffee someone drinks, because a single pre-workout serve can exceed 200 mg of caffeine and patients almost never count it as caffeine intake.

options.rationale: Serotonergic therapy is first line for a primary anxiety disorder, but he lacks the pervasive worry, avoidance or unexpected attacks outside the stimulant context that would define one. Treating before removing the pharmacological driver means an antidepressant is credited with a response that dietary change would have produced. (Source: RANZCP: Anxiety disorders)

Benzodiazepines have a narrow role in short term crisis management and carry dependence risk in a young man with an ongoing stimulant exposure. Sedating the effects of a stimulant he continues to consume treats neither the symptom nor its cause. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Cognitive behavioural therapy is effective for panic disorder, and interoceptive exposure deliberately provokes the bodily sensations that are feared. Delivering it while a pharmacological agent is generating those same sensations undermines the therapy and the formulation. (Source: RANZCP: Anxiety disorders)

Cardiac investigation is warranted for palpitations with syncope, exertional onset, structural signs or an abnormal resting electrocardiogram, and none of these are present. Repeated negative testing tends to entrench health anxiety rather than resolve it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

His daily intake from energy drinks, pre-workout powder and coffee sits far above the threshold at which caffeine reliably produces anxiety, tremor, palpitations and insomnia, and the symptoms began as the intake rose. Reducing gradually rather than abruptly avoids the withdrawal headache and fatigue that otherwise drive relapse. (Source: RANZCP: Anxiety disorders)

explanation.summary: The menopause transition carries a well documented increase in the risk of depressive symptoms and of first onset major depression, mediated by fluctuating oestradiol, vasomotor symptom burden, sleep fragmentation and concurrent life stressors. The clinical task is to separate a major depressive episode, which requires antidepressant or psychological treatment in its own right, from subthreshold depressive symptoms driven principally by vasomotor sleep disruption, which respond to treating the flushes. Menopausal hormone therapy improves mood in perimenopausal women with vasomotor symptoms, an effect that is not reliably reproduced in women who are well past the final menstrual period, so the timing of the window matters. In a woman over 45 with characteristic symptoms the diagnosis is clinical and hormone measurement adds nothing, since levels fluctuate markedly from week to week. Transdermal oestradiol is preferred over oral where thrombotic risk is a consideration, and any woman with a uterus requires a progestogen, with micronised progesterone favoured for its breast and metabolic profile.
key_points: Distinguish major depression from subthreshold symptoms driven by vasomotor sleep loss
Hormone therapy improves mood in the perimenopausal window but not reliably later
The diagnosis is clinical over age 45; hormone levels fluctuate too widely to be useful
Transdermal oestradiol avoids the first pass thrombotic risk of oral therapy
A progestogen is required for any woman with an intact uterus
explanation.pearls: Vasomotor symptoms in the menopause transition are now also treatable with non-hormonal neurokinin 3 receptor antagonists such as fezolinetant, which act on the hypothalamic thermoregulatory pathway and offer an option for women with a hormone sensitive cancer history.

options.rationale: Hormone levels fluctuate widely during the perimenopause and a single measurement cannot confirm or exclude the transition in a woman over 45, in whom the diagnosis is clinical. Waiting on the result delays treatment without adding information. (Source: Australian Menopause Society)

Depressive symptoms arising for the first time during the perimenopause alongside prominent vasomotor symptoms and sleep disruption improve with hormone therapy, which treats the flushes driving the sleep loss and has independent antidepressant effects in this window. She has no contraindication, and the transdermal route avoids the additional venous thromboembolism risk of oral oestrogen. (Source: Australian Menopause Society)

An antidepressant is the right choice for a major depressive episode, particularly with a previous history, and some agents also reduce flushes. Here the mood symptoms are subthreshold and clearly secondary to vasomotor sleep disruption, so treating the flushes addresses the cause rather than the consequence. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders)

A contraceptive pill is a reasonable choice for a perimenopausal woman who also needs contraception and has no cardiovascular contraindication, but it delivers supraphysiological ethinylestradiol. Where symptom control is the sole aim, oestradiol based therapy is preferred. (Source: Australian Menopause Society)

Cognitive behavioural therapy helps with the distress and sleep disruption of the menopause transition and is a useful adjunct. It cannot abolish fifteen hot flushes a day, which is the mechanism keeping her awake. (Source: Australian Menopause Society)

explanation.summary: People experiencing homelessness have rates of psychotic and mood disorders many times those of the general population, together with very high rates of substance use, traumatic brain injury and untreated physical illness, and they die decades earlier than the housed population. Clinic based models fail this group systematically, because attendance depends on the cognitive organisation, stable contact details and transport that the illness and the circumstances remove. Assertive community treatment and street outreach models deliver care in the person's own environment, maintain contact through repeated low demand engagement, and integrate housing, income support and physical health care with psychiatric treatment. Housing First approaches provide permanent accommodation without requiring treatment adherence or abstinence as a precondition, and have better housing retention than staircase models that make housing conditional. Legal coercion through community treatment orders may have a place once the statutory criteria are met, but it is not a substitute for a service model capable of reaching the person.
key_points: Repeated non-attendance usually reflects a service model mismatch, not refusal of care
Assertive outreach reduces admissions and improves continuity in this population
Housing and clinical treatment run in parallel rather than in sequence
Untreated physical illness contributes substantially to the mortality gap
A community treatment order requires both statutory criteria and a means of delivery
explanation.pearls: Leg ulceration, foot problems and untreated dental disease are among the commonest reasons people sleeping rough will accept a first clinical contact, so offering wound care is often a more effective route into psychiatric engagement than offering psychiatric care directly.

sources.label: RANZCP: Service delivery for people with severe mental illness
Australian Institute of Health and Welfare: Homelessness and mental health

options.rationale: Discharging for non-attendance penalises the symptom, since disorganisation and persecutory beliefs are precisely what prevent attendance. This approach is associated with escalating emergency use and premature death in this population. (Source: RANZCP: Service delivery for people with severe mental illness)
source_refs: RANZCP: Service delivery for people with severe mental illness

options.rationale: Housing is central and should not wait, but sequencing treatment behind it recreates the treatment first model in reverse and leaves psychosis untreated meanwhile. Contemporary practice delivers housing and clinical care in parallel rather than making one a precondition of the other. (Source: Australian Institute of Health and Welfare: Homelessness and mental health)
source_refs: Australian Institute of Health and Welfare: Homelessness and mental health

options.rationale: Waiting for the next crisis is a reactive plan that has already failed four times this year and depends on him meeting involuntary criteria on the day. Admission without a community structure to receive him simply restarts the cycle. (Source: RANZCP: Service delivery for people with severe mental illness)
source_refs: RANZCP: Service delivery for people with severe mental illness

options.rationale: Repeated non-attendance at a fixed clinic in a man who engages readily on the street is a mismatch between the service model and the patient, and assertive outreach with in-reach to where he actually is has the strongest evidence for reducing admissions in this group. Integrating housing and wound care matters because untreated physical illness and homelessness drive the relapses. (Source: RANZCP: Service delivery for people with severe mental illness)
source_refs: RANZCP: Service delivery for people with severe mental illness

options.rationale: A community treatment order requires the statutory criteria to be met and a practical means of delivering the treatment, and he was judged not detainable at his last presentation. An order without an outreach team to enact it produces a legal document that nobody can implement. (Source: RANZCP: Service delivery for people with severe mental illness)

explanation.summary: Suicide rates in rural and remote Australia exceed those in major cities, with the gap driven substantially by access to firearms, occupational and financial stress, alcohol use and distance from services. Risk assessment rests on clinical formulation rather than on scale scores, which have repeatedly been shown to lack the predictive accuracy needed for individual disposition decisions, and an explicit statement of intent with a formed plan and immediate access to lethal means is among the strongest available indicators of imminent danger. Means restriction is the single intervention with the best evidence for reducing suicide deaths, and in a firearm owner it means arranging removal of weapons through police or a nominated person immediately, independent of the treatment setting. Where a patient refuses voluntary care at this level of risk, involuntary assessment provisions exist in every jurisdiction and should be used, with retrieval organised in parallel rather than sequentially. Rural clinicians should use telehealth psychiatry to support decision making and to plan aftercare, but it does not provide the containment that a high risk disposition requires.
key_points: Formed plan, stated intent and immediate lethal means access indicate imminent danger
Structured risk scales must not determine disposition; formulation does
Means restriction has the strongest evidence of any single suicide prevention intervention
Family supervision does not substitute for statutory containment at high risk
Use telehealth in parallel with, not instead of, arranging transfer
explanation.pearls: Firearm access should be asked about directly in every rural suicide risk assessment and acted on the same day, because the case fatality of a firearm suicide attempt approaches 90 per cent compared with a few per cent for intentional overdose, leaving almost no opportunity for rescue.

sources.label: Australian Institute of Health and Welfare: Suicide and self-harm monitoring

options.rationale: A formed plan with stated intent to act tonight and immediate access to a highly lethal means, in a patient refusing any voluntary plan, meets the threshold for involuntary assessment and transfer in every Australian jurisdiction. Means restriction through police firearm removal is the intervention with the largest single effect on outcome and must happen regardless of where he is treated. (Source: RANZCP: Suicide prevention)

Telehealth review is a valuable rural resource and should be used in parallel, but it cannot provide containment for a man who has said he will act tonight and whose relative has said she cannot prevent him leaving. Family supervision is not a substitute for statutory containment at this level of risk. (Source: RANZCP: Suicide prevention)

Structured scales have poor predictive accuracy at the individual level and are not endorsed as the basis for disposition decisions, which rest on clinical formulation. Using a score to override an explicit stated intent inverts the evidence. (Source: RANZCP: Suicide prevention)

Antidepressants take weeks to act and do nothing for tonight, and a safety plan requires a patient willing to engage with it, which he has explicitly refused. A next day appointment offers no protection across the interval of greatest danger. (Source: RANZCP: Suicide prevention)

Local admission with continuous observation may be a necessary interim step while retrieval is arranged, but routine sedation of a calm, cooperative and sober patient is not justified and intermittent fifteen minute checks are inadequate at this risk level. The legal framework and means restriction still have to be addressed first. (Source: RANZCP: Suicide prevention)

explanation.summary: Before labelling a depression treatment resistant, three things must be verified: that the diagnosis is correct, that the trials were adequate in dose and duration, and that adherence was real. Obstructive sleep apnoea is among the most commonly missed medical mimics, because its daytime consequences of fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, low motivation and reduced libido overlap almost entirely with a depressive syndrome, while the features that separate them are the absence of sadness, guilt, anhedonia and hopelessness alongside prominent unrefreshing sleep and somnolence. Supporting features include obesity, a neck circumference above about 43 cm in men, witnessed apnoeas, morning headache, nocturia and hypertension that is difficult to control. Treatment with continuous positive airway pressure improves mood scores substantially in this group and antidepressants do not. Fitness to drive is a separate and immediate obligation, since untreated moderate to severe sleep apnoea with excessive daytime sleepiness disqualifies a commercial driver under the Australian standards until treated and demonstrably controlled.
key_points: Verify diagnosis, trial adequacy and adherence before declaring treatment resistance
Somnolence and unrefreshing sleep without guilt or anhedonia suggest a medical mimic
Obesity, large neck, witnessed apnoeas and resistant hypertension support the diagnosis
Sedating and weight promoting agents worsen the underlying airway obstruction
Commercial driving must cease until the condition is treated and control demonstrated
explanation.pearls: Untreated moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnoea with excessive daytime sleepiness makes a commercial vehicle driver unfit under the Austroads standard, and the treating doctor must advise the patient to stop driving and document that advice, with reporting to the licensing authority if the advice is disregarded.

options.rationale: Mirtazapine improves sleep continuity in depression but causes appetite stimulation and weight gain, which directly worsen obstructive sleep apnoea. Sedating an untreated airway obstruction is counterproductive. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Antipsychotic augmentation is an evidence-based step in genuine treatment resistant depression, but it is being applied here to a syndrome that is not primarily depressive. Adding a drug that causes sedation and weight gain would worsen both the somnolence and the underlying airway problem. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders)

Obesity, a large neck, witnessed apnoeas, unrefreshing sleep, resistant hypertension and somnolence without core depressive cognitions point to obstructive sleep apnoea masquerading as treatment resistance, which no antidepressant will fix. Driving advice is a legal as well as clinical obligation in a commercial driver who has fallen asleep at the wheel. (Source: Austroads: Assessing fitness to drive)

Electroconvulsive therapy is highly effective for severe or refractory depression, particularly with psychotic or melancholic features, and none of those are present. Applying it to undiagnosed sleep apnoea exposes him to anaesthesia in an untreated difficult airway. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders)

A wakefulness promoting agent masks the symptom that is the diagnostic clue while leaving nocturnal hypoxaemia and its cardiovascular consequences untreated. It also gives false reassurance about driving safety. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
